9098902b3156.title: When to use this skill
9098902b3156.content: When a content change is being reviewed and the reviewer (or the author) needs to see the rendered result before merging. The staging deployment puts the feature branch’s rendered site at: . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<branch-slug>/ . A preview is the general publication step with a different root. The push itself is render-kg-to-cdn with branches/<branch-slug>/ as the publication root URL and the gh-pages Tool as the target — the same step a release takes with the site root. What this skill owns is everything around that call: the slug, the banner and staging.json, the render log, the PR comment, and taking the preview down. Which site — the repository the change lives in . <owner>/<repo> above is the repository that holds the change, not the repository of the index the agent happens to be working in. Read that repository’s index.config.json first: . | the change lives in | its preview is at | published by | . | a repository with its own site (its index.config.json has a site entry) | https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<slug>/, and the root from its default branch | that repository: stage-local.ts --repo . from its checkout when it declares site.agentRun (below), else its own staging.yml | . | a layer an index mounts and publishes as part of its own site (no site of its own) | branches/<slug>/ on the index’s site | a staging re-pin: a pull request on the index that points the mount at the branch’s commit, recorded with bun run cat mount:remote --staging (basis staging, no consent needed) | . A repository with a site of its own is previewed there, even when an index also mounts it. The index’s site shows it as one layer among its layers, which is the wrong page for that repository’s reviewers. If the repository’s own build cannot run yet (its publisher refuses for a missing cache or an undeclared input), say what is missing and ask. Never fall back to the index’s site in silence.

17d5d9964b19.title: How it works
17d5d9964b19.content: 1. Feature branch → staging deployment . When an agent pushes to a feature branch with an open pull request, drafts included, feature-staging.yml automatically: . | Builds the docs site (Jekyll + TypeDoc + BPMN diagrams) | Writes the build’s facts — commit SHA, timestamp, branch, PR, issue, build log — once, to staging.json at the preview root | Injects a constant staging banner at the top of every HTML page, which reads those facts in the browser | Comments on the PR that the preview is staged and queued, with the earliest push time and when it should be live | Waits for the rate-limit window (§8), then deploys to gh-pages/branches/<branch-slug>/ only the files that differ from the live site (staging-share.ts apply). The preview’s staging-sw.js serves the rest from the live site in the browser and puts the banner back on its pages; the live site’s root 404.html (staging-share.ts write-404, written by docs-site.yml) installs that worker for a deep link opened before it exists. A page is shared only when it matches the live one once the per-preview edits are set aside (banner, SEO strip, fa-staging and fa-search-index, TypeDoc’s title suffix); anything else keeps the preview’s own copy. The footer build stamp is filled in the browser on every build, the live site’s from build.json, so an unchanged page is byte-identical across deploys | Rewrites the same comment: pushed at a time, live by about five minutes later | . 2. The staging banner . Every staged page carries a muted-sage banner: . 🔀 FEATURE BRANCH — claude/update-schedule · commit a1b2c3d · built 2026-09-18T00:30:00Z · PR #42 · issue #215 · compare with main ↗ · build log . Its colour, #4F6F52, measures 5.63:1 against its white text, above the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold. Check any replacement the same way; the pale decorator sages (#9CAF88, #87A96B) land near 2.5:1. The facts are fetched, not baked — and that is a storage decision . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-banner.ts injects a fragment that is byte-identical on every page and across every rebuild, and the browser derives its preview root from location.pathname, fetches staging.json and fills the banner in. A per-build value in the fragment makes every page unique on every build, so each re-push adds the whole site to gh-pages as new objects. Three rules: . | Nothing per-build may go back into the fragment. staging-banner-constant.test.ts runs two builds with different facts and compares the emitted bytes, so any leak fails regardless of how it is spelled. Add the fact to staging.json instead. | A failed fetch must still say PREVIEW. The static markup carries “FEATURE BRANCH” before any fetch happens, and the fetch only ever ADDS detail. “Could not determine” is never rendered as “this is the real site” — the same third-state rule the rest of the repository runs on, and here the failure mode is a reviewer approving the wrong artefact. | Every value from the JSON goes in as textContent, never as markup. Git ref names may contain <, > and " — they are not in git’s forbidden set, which stops at space, ~, ^, :, ?, *, [, \ and the control characters. staging-banner.e2e.ts pins this with a branch name carrying an onerror payload. | . Pages still differ between previews, because Jekyll’s relative_url prepends the baseurl to ~235 hrefs per page and the fa-translation-index island publishes site.baseurl to JavaScript. Both are coupled to the language switcher. 3. Commit SHA stamping — and the four fields staging must NOT write . Both builds write docs/_data/build.yml, and they do not write the same fields. The difference is deliberate: it is the second half of the deduplication above. |   | docs-site.yml (main) | feature-staging.yml (a preview) | . | sha, short_sha, built_at, run_url | written | DELIBERATELY ABSENT | . | branch, staging, staging_slug, pr_number, search_index | — | written | . Why staging omits them. site-chrome/_includes/footer_custom.html renders short_sha, built_at and run_url into the footer of every page, so writing them per build changes every page on every deploy. The client fills those three in from the same staging.json the banner already fetches — one request, two consumers — and a failed fetch leaves Jekyll’s | default: 'dev' in place rather than blanking the footer, which is the same third state §”The facts are fetched, not baked” requires of the banner. On main there is one copy and nothing to deduplicate, so the include’s own reason stands: “a stale browser cache and a deploy that has not run look identical.” . Adding a per-build field back to the staging stamp will not fail a test. staging-banner-constant.test.ts compares the banner fragment, which is genuinely constant; the footer is not in it, because it lives in a Jekyll include rather than in the workflow’s injection step. Check the deploy commits on gh-pages, not the code, to confirm pages do not differ across rebuilds. A Jekyll layout can read site.data.build.sha to display the deployed version — on main. Under a preview, read it from staging.json. 4. Before/after comparison . The reviewer opens both URLs side by side: . | Surface | URL | What it shows | . | Main (current) | <pages-url>/ | The published state on main | . | Staging (proposed) | <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | The feature branch’s changes | . The commit SHA on each page confirms exactly what is being compared. 5. Cleanup . When the PR is merged or closed, the cleanup job in feature-staging.yml removes branches/<slug>/ from gh-pages so stale previews don’t accumulate. The full retention rules — merged vs closed-unmerged, the label, the dispatch — are in staging-review §”Staging retention”. 6. The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off . Previews are capped by size, at 3 GB in total, and the oldest are rotated off. The cap is by size rather than count because one preview can run to hundreds of megabytes. Per-PR cleanup bounds nothing in total, every preview is a full copy of the site, and a gh-pages branch past GitHub’s 10 GB Pages limit freezes the live site. So every stage run, inside its push loop, runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-rotate.ts: it stamps the preview it is staging (branches/<slug>/.staged-at), keeps that one plus the most recently updated others while the total fits MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES (3 GB, 3 x 1024^3 bytes, defined there and nowhere else), and removes the rest, oldest first — each with a removed render-log entry, its record retired into branches/_retired/, and a line (slug, age, size) in the commit message and job log. _retired/ and non-preview entries are never touched. Two things to know when editing it: . | The push loop re-reads gh-pages on every attempt; it does not rebase. The commit carries removals decided against one read of the branch, and a replayed removal is a stale one — it could delete a preview another run has just refreshed. Same shape as publish-gh-pages.sh. | A rotated-off preview is regenerated by the next push to its PR branch. It can reach an OPEN PR’s preview; the cost is a 404 until the author pushes, not lost work. Detail and the reviewer’s remedy: staging-review §”The cap”. | . 7. The cone — a preview rebuilds only what a changed file can reach . A preview rebuilds only the dependency cone of the changed files, at FILE level, with each derived directory’s generator declared as writer. The rule is general across rendered kinds. A rendered directory is in the cone when a changed file is . | under its own path (its pages, or its source data), or | in the import closure of a writer it declares, or under a writer directory (a path ending in /: what a generator reads, such as its templates, rather than imports), or | in a directory it is derivedFrom, transitively (check:derived-from --downstream <instance/id> prints that half on its own). | . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-cone.ts computes it; compose-docs.ts carriedInstances applies it to the composed layers. Three rules: . | Any doubt carries. No file list, a writer that does not exist, or an import that does not resolve carries the directory, with the reason in the build log. A preview missing the pages under review misleads a reviewer, while an oversized one only costs bytes. | A computed import() is bounded, not ignored. It can load only a module, so it carries on a changed module file and never on a page. The two such sites a generator reaches today (harness-config.ts’s contributes loader and block-module.ts’s block loader) have DECLARED targets and are walked exactly; DECLARED_COMPUTED_IMPORTS lists them. | The instance-prefix match is a floor. The cone can only add to it. Narrowing below it is a separate decision, made once the cone has been measured in previews. | . A skill-only change carries no IG; a change to gen-ig-pages.ts or to the DAK layer’s themes/chrome.json carries all three. staging-cone.test.ts holds these cases as tests. Built sites follow the same rule. An IG’s own Jekyll site and its AST site are BUILT in the preview from an upstream repository pinned in the layer’s own files, not composed from the checkout. stage-ig-sites.ts and stage-ast-sites.ts take --changed-files and stage only the layers siteInCone reaches. Its reasons, in order: no file list; a change to the build environment (SITE_ENVIRONMENT: the docs Gemfile and this workflow); a change under the layer; the cone reaching any of the layer’s directories (a theme change arrives this way); or a change in the stager’s closure. Each decision is printed with its reason. When you add a generated directory, declare its writer and derivedFrom. Without them the cone cannot reach it through code or data, and the prefix floor is all it gets. 8. The rate limit — a preview never cancels the main site’s Pages build . Staging previews are pushed to gh-pages at a limited rate. GitHub’s pages build and deployment keeps only the NEWEST run, so every push cancels the build in flight, the main site’s included; a build takes about three minutes. So before each push attempt the stage job re-reads gh-pages and runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-push-gate.ts gate, which holds the push until the branch tip is old enough: . | tip of gh-pages | wait until it is | . | a staging commit (staging(...)) | STAGING_WINDOW_MS — 5 min | . | anything else: the main-site publish, publish.yml, any other publisher | MAIN_WINDOW_MS — 10 min | . The numbers live once, in that script. Exit 75 means it slept until the window should open (plus up to a minute of jitter) and the loop must re-read and ask again; exit 1 means the job has waited MAX_WAIT_MS (two hours) and fails rather than pushing; exit 2 is an unreadable tip, never read as open. Three things to know when editing it: . | git’s fast-forward rule is the lock. Two jobs that both find the window open both build on the same tip; one push is rejected, re-reads, finds a tip younger than the window, and waits. So at most one staging push lands per window with no shared state. A rejection whose tip MOVED is therefore a lost race, sent back to the gate without spending one of the three attempts; only a rejection with the tip unmoved counts as a failure. | No concurrency group, and none should be added. Every waiting preview would pend in one group and each arrival would cancel the last. The per-branch group at the workflow level stays: a newer push to the same PR cancels a preview still waiting at the gate, so a superseded preview is never pushed at all. | A staging push BEFORE a main-site push is harmless; only one AFTER it cancels the build that matters. The main push then cancels the staging build, and the build that runs carries both. That is why the gate looks at the tip, and why it does not wait for docs-site runs that have not pushed yet. | . A rate limit is used rather than a batching flush job because the gate is one script and one loop whose correctness rests on git, while a flush job needs a second workflow, an artifact round trip per preview, a record of what is deployed, a best-effort schedule and a write token over content built from a pull request. The cost is latency under load: with K previews waiting, the last one pushes about 5 × K minutes later, and the PR comment gives its own estimate. The cleanup and cleanup-dispatch jobs do NOT pass through the gate. They push once per closed PR rather than once per push. 9. Build types — preview and full . There are two build types. A public comment (PC) build is a full build, and so is a release. | build type | used for | builds | . | preview | every pull request’s branches/<slug>/ preview | only what the change can reach (the cone, §7); every whole-corpus index is main’s copy, put back rather than rebuilt | . | full | the main site deploy, a public comment release, a release | everything; every index rebuilt from the tree being published | . An index is computed over the whole corpus: the search index, the LSI viewer, the SQLite slices, the handler index, the glossary pages, the translation status pages and the node-kind pages. A builtAtPublish entry says so with index: true; a writer is borrowed only when every entry it writes says so. Rebuilding an index in a preview shows the reviewer almost nothing and costs minutes, so in a preview derive:publish puts back main’s copy from main’s writer-cone recording and logs borrowed <writer>; the search index is served from main the same way (§”Serve the published search index” in the preview workflow). So a preview of a glossary, translation or node-kind change shows main’s copy of those pages: review such a change on a full build (dispatch with build_type: full) or in its source. The switch is CAT_BUILD_TYPE (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/build-type.ts). Any doubt builds full: unset means full, and a value that is neither word is refused. A preview whose main recording holds no copy of an index builds it. A public comment release must be frozen from a full build. A frozen release is cited by page and line for the whole comment period, so its search and slices must describe the draft, not main. Dispatch the preview workflow for the branch with build_type: full, then run pc:release freeze. Freeze refuses a copy whose staging.json says buildType: "preview", and records the build type in release.json. 10. Agent-built previews — deferred on the critical path, verified by a full CI rebuild . When an agent builds and pushes a preview with stage-local.ts, it writes branches/<slug>/_build-record.json (scripts/preview-record.ts) recording builder: "agent", the git tree hash tree of the source tree it built (HEAD^{tree} or the merge tree with origin/main), the head and base commit SHAs, and the SHA-256 of every deployed file outside the per-build metadata (staging.json, _build-record.json, .staged-at, build.yml). When feature-staging.yml runs on the pull request: . | Defer on the critical path. conflict-gate checks branches/<slug>/_build-record.json on gh-pages. When builder is "agent" and record.tree equals MERGE_SHA^{tree} (refs/pull/<n>/merge), the preview is already live for that exact merge tree: the workflow sets the preview/agent-build commit status on the PR head to pending, posts a <!-- preview-build-verify --> notice on the PR, and skips the critical-path stage build so the runner is free. Any missing record, CI-built record, or tree mismatch (including when main moved under the branch) builds on the critical path as usual. | Verify off the critical path. preview-verify-sweep.yml (triggered when feature-staging.yml completes and on a 15-minute schedule) checks that no Feature Staging run is queued or in progress, finds the oldest open PR whose head commit has preview/agent-build in state pending, and dispatches feature-staging.yml with verify_pr=<number>. | Compare or replace. The verify run rebuilds refs/pull/<n>/merge in full and runs preview-record.ts compare against the agent’s _build-record.json on gh-pages: . | Files match (same=true): nothing is redeployed; preview/agent-build is set to success (or failure if a built-site check failed) and the PR comment records the verified tree. | Files differ (same=false) or the base moved (same=stale): CI’s build is deployed to branches/<slug>/ (guarded so a newer preview tree is never overwritten) with a rendered log entry, and when the agent’s build differed, preview/agent-build is set to failure with the differing file paths listed in the PR comment. | Merge guard: merge-guard check 5 (src/coordinator/merge-guard.ts) reads preview/agent-build alongside check runs; pending holds the PR as not ready, and failure refuses the merge. | . | .

46c0d711e3ea.title: Agent workflow
46c0d711e3ea.content: When an author requests a content change: . | Detect scope — use content-graph and integration-watcher to identify affected blocks and downstream implications | Create feature branch — branch from main, open PR immediately | Make changes — edit content blocks, deterministic logic, translations | Push — on a folio whose staging.yml runs on push, the staging deployment happens automatically. On an agent-run repository, run stage-local.ts (below). | Report staging URL — tell the author the preview is at <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | Iterate — each push updates the staging deployment with a new SHA | . The BPMN for this workflow is the content core’s processes/content/content-change-review.bpmn. Publishing without a runner — stage-local.ts, one command . When the Actions queue is backed up, the agent can build and publish itself: it already has the checkout, the platform and bun. On an agent-run repository (below) this is not a shortcut. It is the only publish path. It is one command for a preview and for the main site, for a folio and for a FHIR IG: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --plan # what it would do; nothing built bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --dry-run # build, compose the commit, push nothing bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> # build and push bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --artifact <dir> . It prints its plan first, every time: which workflow it mirrors, where the output lands, what it replaces and what it keeps, the commit message, and what it does not run. The size review. Owner, 2026-11-10: “add size review as part of authoring process”. Every build, preview or main, prints a size report before its push (site-size.ts, bun run cat site:size). The report gives the total against the published root, the top directories, the size by extension, the biggest files, byte-identical duplicates, source maps, the directories named after another layer of index.lock.json, and the directories the shared-assets host could serve. It writes site-size.json beside the build, never into the site. The review is advisory: growth over 10% or 10 MB is a warning, and nothing is refused. Read the report before you hand over the preview. The usual culprits each have one fix: . | another layer’s pages copied in: link that layer’s own site; | the same bytes under several names: publish one index, and serve each file once; | vendored libraries: serve them from the shared-assets host; | .map files: do not publish them. | . When the growth holds and none of these fixes applies, raise a decision card with the owner, with the comparison line and the top contributing directories on it. Which publisher is read from the repository’s own workflow files, from the reusable workflow each one calls: . | a caller of folio-staging.yml is a folio. The build inputs (build_command, site_dir, publish_branch, …) are read from that caller. | a caller of a reusable workflow that a mounted layer declares as a site publisher is that publisher’s kind. The IG layer declares one: a caller of its fhirbuild.yml or ghbuild.yml is an IG, published by that layer’s own code, which stage-local.ts reaches through the layer’s declared site-publisher-ig pipeline slot and never by path. The reusable workflow is fetched at the ref the caller names, and its build job is run step by step as written: run: blocks with the environment a runner gives them, docker:// steps in their image. Steps that read a secret, push to the source branch, or need an Actions runtime are skipped, and the plan names each one with its reason. fhirbuild.yml itself only triggers build.fhir.org’s auto-build, so the Pages build is the ghbuild.yml beside it, and the plan says so. | a repository that calls both (smart-ra carries an IG under input/) gets the folio, unless --publisher ig is given. The folio owns the publish root. An IG’s root deploy is a clean one, and it is refused on a publish branch that holds a folio’s branches/, _render-log/ or _main-site.json. | . Main site or preview follows the branch, as the workflows do. The default branch publishes the main site; any other branch publishes a preview. --main says the same explicitly, and it is refused off the default branch. The main site is published only from a HEAD that is the pushed tip of the default branch. |   | folio | IG | . | preview | branches/<slug>/, replaced wholesale; held by the rate-limit gate (§8); commit staging(<slug>): from <sha>; render log staging-preview | branches/<last path component>/, nothing deleted; commit Deploy candidate branch | . | main site | the root, through publish-main-site.ts: only the files the last publish’s _main-site.json lists are replaced, and branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are kept; commit main-site: from <sha>; render log main-site for / | the root, cleaned except for the deploy step’s clean-exclude (branches, sitepreview) and the action’s own exclusions; commit Deploy main branch | . Every path refuses an empty build before it deletes anything. | Pushing removes the first wait and not the second. Pages deploys on a runner, so say the page is live once that deploy has run, never sooner. | --artifact <dir>: no GitHub at all. It writes the same build as a bundle for a claude.ai Artifact: index.html plus the files listed in <dir>/artifact.json. Publish that, and it is live in about a minute, private until shared. | An Artifact holds at most 254 files plus the page per publish. Whole top-level directories are left out to fit, the ones with the most files first. artifact.json names each one, and links into a left-out directory 404. | Before publishing a folio whose content belongs to a real organisation (a WHO draft, say), ask the author: an Artifact is a new place that content appears. | . | What it does not do, and says in its plan: . | the folio preview’s QA sweep, screenshots, review-comment ingestion and PR comment (the banner says the preview was built locally); | the IG workflow’s PR comments, its branch-history page and README write-back (each reads a token, or writes the source branch); | the IG deploy action’s single-commit, which force-pushes one orphan commit and erases the publish branch’s history. This path commits on top and never force-pushes. | . | An IG build needs what its workflow needs. The workflow runs IG Publisher in a Docker image, so a machine with no Docker daemon gets the plan from --dry-run, and a real run stops naming the missing prerequisite. | An IG repository’s own site is built from its AST, not from the Publisher’s HTML. The repository declares site.build in its index.config.json entry (inline — never a <instance>.config.json), and that recipe’s first step restores the AST from its cache branch and refuses one that is not valid for the commit. The cache is refreshed by a Publisher run on a runner, through the IG layer’s reusable refresh workflow. It is the one workflow an agent-run IG repository dispatches, and only a person, or an agent the owner names for that run, dispatches it. The layer that owns IG builds owns the rule and the workflow; this skill names no IG step. | . Agent-run repositories — the GitHub Actions path is documented, not run . A repository is agent-run when it says so in its own index.config.json: "site": { "agentRun": true }. An agent builds and publishes its site, and its publish workflow keeps only workflow_dispatch. This skill keeps no list of them: the declaration is the list, and stage-local.ts says in every plan whether the repository declares it. For these repositories the GitHub Actions path is documentation. It says what the workflow does, so that the agent path can match it. It is not a fallback for an agent to take. | what | agent path | GitHub Actions path (documented, not run) | . | a folio preview at branches/<slug>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | folio-staging.yml job stage | . | a folio’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | folio-staging.yml job publish-main | . | an IG preview at branches/<branch>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy candidate” | . | an IG’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy main” | . | QA sweep, screenshots, review comments, PR comments | not run (the plan says so) | jobs in the workflows above | . Never dispatch the workflow, to cover a gap or for any other reason: a dispatched run contradicts the repository’s agent-run setting. When the agent path cannot do a step, say which step it is and ask. Skills that drive GitHub Actions are not to be implemented. Document what the workflows do, here and in the workflow files, so that an agent-run step can be checked against them — stage-local.ts reads the workflow files rather than restating them, so a change to a workflow’s build or layout is a change to the agent path too.

4a2f655c1fba.title: Staleness detection
4a2f655c1fba.content: The SHA stamp means staleness is always detectable: . | Staging matches PR head → the staging preview is current | Staging SHA ≠ PR head → the staging preview is stale (push again) | Main site SHA = merge commit → the publication is current | Main site SHA ≠ latest main → docs-site.yml needs to run | .

7230337e0683.title: Example — a change that spans several blocks
7230337e0683.content: An author needs to change the immunization schedule: . | Agent detects the change affects: . | Narrative content in the immunization chapter | Decision logic (CQL) for scheduling the next visit | Indicators that count doses administered | Referral logic for follow-up visits | . | Agent creates feature/update-immunization-schedule | Agent edits all affected blocks, assesses downstream impact | Push → staging deployment → author reviews | Author submits to the guidance review committee | Committee compares main vs branches/feature-update-immunization-schedule/ | Committee approves → merge → staging cleaned up → main site updated | .

6ae95b0e3dcf.title: Before you hand a staging URL to a person
6ae95b0e3dcf.content: Check the ref, then say how long and come back. A preview push is not a served page, and the bot’s “Staging preview” comment reports at most the first, not the second — and while it says queued, not even that. List branches/<slug>/ on refs/heads/gh-pages before relaying the URL; quote the comment’s own push and live-by times (the rate limit in §8 can hold a push for several windows), or say the stage job takes about 22 minutes plus the wait and Pages adds 3 to 4 on top; schedule the re-check rather than promising it. The three states, and why the third is not yours to assert, are in staging-review §”Before you hand a staging URL to a person (STRICT)”. It is the same rule and it is written once, there.

6f612da814aa.title: Before you report a staging URL as broken
6f612da814aa.content: Look at the publish ref, not the site. A staging URL is LOOKED UP in gh-pages under branches/<branch-slug>/, never composed from the source path — cat-harness/docs/guides/x.md publishes to /docs/cat-harness/guides/x.html, and composing it from the source path yields a 404 for a page that is there. From an agent container a curl against a Pages URL fails on the proxy regardless, so a failed fetch is not evidence either way. Full rule: github-state-inspection (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

0c86ba7e39d3.title: Staging links
0c86ba7e39d3.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

06d3d7b576a8.title: feature-staging (skill)
06d3d7b576a8.content: The skill feature-staging as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/feature-staging.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

8a6e1837f6fa.title: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe
8a6e1837f6fa.content: Named by: Questionnaire wireframe review, SMART Guideline end to end, L2 DAK to L3 FHIR IG . Skill id: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Process: questionnaire-wireframe-review.bpmn (Process_QuestionnaireWireframeReview). Show a built FHIR Questionnaire the way a person will meet it — a mid-fidelity wireframe at web and mobile width, and a live form — have it reviewed as a design, check that it says what the wireframe it was derived from says, and take change requests on either side back through authoring. Sourcing. What a Questionnaire means is defined by the FHIR specification and the Structured Data Capture IG; what the live form supports is defined by NLM’s LHC-Forms. This skill states how the two are wired in this harness.

d63d9193ce35.title: Rules
d63d9193ce35.content: . | The renderer is NLM LHC-Forms, vendored into the site: never a CDN at runtime. Its BSD-style notice travels with the vendored files. | The field ↔ item check is scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts (Tool check-wireframe-questionnaire). It knows nothing about any one IG; a layer above uses it by name. | Either side may be edited. A change request says whether the Questionnaire or the wireframe was changed, and the agent brings the other back in line. Neither is regenerated from the other. | .

5ff6afe21395.title: Inputs and outputs
5ff6afe21395.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-questionnaire-wireframe/: . | in — questionnaire (required: one built JSON path; several are several runs), mode, wireframe, renderer, assetDir, suggest, issueForm, channels, branch | out — the output shape of wireframe-design-review (use, topic, assetDir, candidates[] each with its source HTML, web and mobile screenshots and their staging links, chosen, changedAssets, stagingLinks), plus renderer, fidelity[] (the checker’s findings per layout), sdcChecks[] (step 4b) and changeRequests[] (issue URL, which side was edited, status). | . stagingLinks is an inline copy of cat-harness schemas/staging-comparison.schema.json, as every contract carrying it keeps one; changedAssets is the staging preview graph’s changed-assets record, with three kinds of its own: questionnaire-wireframe, questionnaire-rendering, questionnaire-screenshot.

779248749cde.title: Roles
779248749cde.content: | role | does | . | fhir-modeller | authors: renders, runs the checks, applies change requests | . | business-analyst | reviews the form against the workflow it serves | . | clinical-sme | reviews what the form asks and in what order | . | build-pipeline | the mechanical steps: rendering, screenshots, the fidelity check | .

96fc3adddde7.title: Steps
96fc3adddde7.content: . | Read the built Questionnaire JSON, never FSH: fsh-generated/resources/Questionnaire-<id>.json, or the IG’s published Questionnaire-<id>.json. FSH is what the author wrote; the JSON is what every renderer and reader receives, so it is what is judged. | Render. | A mid-fidelity wireframe: one field per answerable item, in item order, each carrying data-element="<id>" (the item’s definition, or its code) and sitting in a data-layout="web" or data-layout="mobile" subtree. Monochrome, the item’s own text, no placeholder text — the rules of wireframe-design-review step 2. | A form view: the same JSON in <lhc-forms>, from the vendored LHC-Forms build, on the IG site’s Questionnaire form page (build-ig-site). | . | Screenshots at web and mobile width with the cat-harness Tool wireframe-check (1280×800 and 390×844; renders, no-overflow, no-placeholder). A candidate missing either viewport does not enter review. | Fidelity, when an L2 wireframe exists — the form was designed first and the Questionnaire derived from it: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts <wireframe.html> <Questionnaire.json> . Each layout is judged on its own: a field with no item, an item with no field, an item naming no data element, a data element twice, the first place the order differs. Exit 0 faithful, 1 a finding, 2 cannot tell — and 2 is never a pass. The findings go in fidelity[], per layout. This is fidelity, not design: a faithful form can still be a poor one. 4b. SDC build checks, with CSIRO’s libraries (Apache-2.0; used for checks, not UI), Tool sdc-checks: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/sdc-checks.ts --ast output-ast --fixtures input/tests/questionnaires [--out <dir>] . | check | library | passes when | . | assemble | @aehrc/sdc-assemble 2.0.3 | an assemble-root’s sub-forms all resolve in this IG; --out writes the assembled Questionnaire, so assembly is a build step too | . | template-extract | @aehrc/sdc-template-extract 1.0.16 | extraction from the fixture’s response.json yields every resource in extract-expected.json | . | populate | @aehrc/sdc-populate 4.7.2 | FHIRPath pre-population from populate-context.json gives the answers in populate-expected.json | . | behaviour | @aehrc/questionnaire-test-toolkit 0.1.0 | the IG’s behaviour.test.tsx passes. Warn-only: the toolkit is early, and needs its React and Smart Forms peers installed with the IG’s tests | . The fixtures are the IG’s, one directory per Questionnaire id. Nothing is fetched from a server. not-applicable, no-fixture and could-not-determine are said, and never read as a pass. The results go in sdcChecks[], one entry per Questionnaire. | Review by wireframe-design-review, as-is use for a form that exists, design use for one being designed: blind, per criterion, at both viewports, adjudicated where reviewers disagree. That skill is the method; this one does not restate it. | Stage by feature-staging, and ask for review with staging-review: one deep link per rendered Questionnaire and wireframe, before and after. Where the request goes — the conversation, an issue, the pull request — is a judgement, and more than one may be right: staging-review’s deep-link rule, point 5. | Change requests come in in one of two ways, and both end as an issue: . | ✍ suggest, in its Questionnaire mode, on the form page: the reviewer edits the Questionnaire or the wireframe and the editor opens an issue; | the questionnaire-change issue form, filled by hand. | . Each goes to content-feedback for triage (to public-comment when a review round is open), then to l3-fhir-authoring, which edits the side the request did not touch so the two agree again, then back to step 1. changeRequests[] records each issue, which side was edited, and where it stands. | .

fccafa20ea1a.title: The change-request payload
fccafa20ea1a.content: What the ✍ editor writes into the issue’s body, and what the issue form asks for, by these field ids, when it is filled by hand: . | field id | holds | . | questionnaire | the Questionnaire’s canonical URL or Questionnaire/<id> | . | edited | questionnaire or wireframe: the side the reviewer changed | . | patch | an RFC 6902 JSON Patch over the built Questionnaire, its paths annotated with the item’s linkId | . | items | a readable before/after table of the items that changed | . | source | the FSH file and line the item comes from, when known | . | rationale | why | . The issue form is templates/ig-repo-site/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/questionnaire-change.yml, which an IG repository copies to .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/, as it copies the workflows beside it. It is for people filing by hand: the ✍ editor does not open it, because GitHub ignores a prefilled body when template= names an issue form, and the patch would be lost. The editor opens a plain issue whose body carries everything. A pre-filled link longer than about 7000 characters is too long for GitHub; the body then goes to the clipboard and a stub issue opens, as the ✍ runtime does.

df47c26559d2.title: The form view and the ✍ Questionnaire mode
df47c26559d2.content: build-ig-site writes one page per Questionnaire in the IG’s AST, Questionnaire-<id>-form.html, through scripts/questionnaire-form.ts: . | the form, drawn by the vendored LHC-Forms build (scripts/assets/vendor/lhc-forms/<version>/, its NLM LICENSE.md beside it, vendored.json recording the npm tarball and a SHA-256 per file) from a rendered copy of the built JSON, questionnaires/Questionnaire-<id>.json. The source Questionnaire is never changed. eb259545c34d.title: The suggest checker
eb259545c34d.content: checkSuggestion(before, after, { wireframe }) in check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts is the checker a suggest editor runs on the reviewer’s edit, in the editor-checker shape { errors, warnings }: . | errors are syntax only — not JSON, not a Questionnaire; | warnings never block, and only what the edit introduces is reported, computed against the editor’s own round-trip of the original: a duplicate linkId, an enableWhen naming no item, and the fidelity findings of step 4 when a wireframe is given. | . It is not declared as an editor-checker profile (contentType: questionnaire; a folio-editor-checker/v1 node naming open, check and issue with extensions: [".json"]): the editor-checkers typology is declared by folio-assistant-sci, which this layer does not need. The page config names the profile directly (QUESTIONNAIRE_PROFILE in questionnaire-form.ts).

bb2dc5bd8cd5.title: What this skill does not do
bb2dc5bd8cd5.content: . | It does not build the IG: l3-fhir-authoring and ig-publication do. | It does not regenerate one side from the other on its own. Which side is the source of a change is the change request’s to say. | A clean fidelity check is not a design review, and a clean design review is not conformance: fhir-validation still decides that. | .

b7d28e6e1e92.title: fhir-validation
b7d28e6e1e92.content: Named by: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes . Skill id: fhir-validation · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Named by l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Validate against profiles, Build pipeline — SUSHI · validator · IG Publisher lane) and ig-incremental-build.bpmn (Validate the cone (fhir_validate), Publisher + validator services (JVM) lane). Validate an IG’s FHIR artefacts against the profiles and packages they claim to conform to. Sourcing. Conformance is defined by the FHIR specification and by the packages an IG depends on; the validator is HL7’s. This skill states how it is invoked in this harness and what each outcome is allowed to mean.

23ecd2941835.title: Inputs and outputs
23ecd2941835.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-validation/: . | in — igRoot (required), validationLevel, targetProfiles | out — overallStatus (required), sushiResult, publisherResult, conformanceResults | . SUSHI compiling is not conformance. FSH can compile to JSON that the validator then rejects, so a green sushiResult with an unrun publisherResult is not a pass.

49595dd60326.title: The binaries
49595dd60326.content: The package declares these capabilities (providesCapabilities in package-manifest.json); each is defined, with its detection command, in scenarios/capabilities/: . sushi --version # sushi-compiler (requires node-runtime) java -jar "${FHIR_VALIDATOR_JAR}" -version # fhir-validator (requires java-runtime) java -jar "${IG_PUBLISHER_JAR}" --version # ig-publisher (requires java-runtime) . fhir-validator is the standalone validator, distinct from ig-publisher, which builds a whole IG. An authoring loop runs the validator on single resources between builds; a release is cut from the publisher.

3f7859f4a153.title: When a package host refuses you
3f7859f4a153.content: SUSHI and the Publisher resolve the IG’s dependencies: from packages.fhir.org. Where that host is refused, the failure looks like a broken IG and is not one. Ask for the remedy: . bun run cat tools:remedy packages.fhir.org # → fhir-cache-seed-npm, with its command . Every network-dependent Tool declares remedies per host it reaches (check:tools enforces it), and fhir-harness/scripts/ig-cache.sh doctor prints the same answer for each host it finds unreachable. For packages.fhir.org it is fhir-cache-seed-npm --sushi-config sushi-config.yaml, and for versions npm does not carry, --mirror from a repository that fhir-package-mirror filled on a machine that reaches the host. Pin that repository with --mirror-commit <full 40-character SHA>: git cannot fetch an abbreviated SHA from a remote, and the seeder refuses one. A cloud session can fill the mirror without a person’s device, through a GitHub Actions runner: push a claude/mirror-* branch that edits packages.txt in the mirror repository, wait for its mirror.yml run, merge, re-seed. SUSHI also adds packages that sushi-config.yaml does not list, such as hl7.fhir.uv.tools.r4#latest. A #latest needs the registry to name a version, so offline it fails with errors that look like the IG’s own (for example logical-target … does not exist), even with the package in the cache. Serve the mirror as a registry on localhost, answering GET /<name> with dist-tags.latest and GET /<name>/<version> with the tarball, and run FPL_REGISTRY=http://127.0.0.1:<port> sushi build .. Check which version latest resolves to: it is the mirror’s highest, which is only right when the mirror holds the current release. Do not report “SUSHI cannot run here” before running tools:remedy. A refusal that tools:remedy answers with none is “could not determine” in the sense of the next section: say so, with the reason it gave.

ba427a0542a5.title: A capability that is absent did not pass
ba427a0542a5.content: If a probe fails, overallStatus is not a pass with an empty findings list. It is “could not determine”, and it is reported as such: a clean run over a validator that never started looks exactly like a clean IG.

d2ef99b653aa.title: Validating a cone
d2ef99b653aa.content: ig-incremental-build.bpmn validates a restricted cone — the artefacts a change touches — rather than the whole IG, and reports the cone it chose. That is a latency optimisation for the authoring loop. It does not gate a release: the full publisher build in l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn does. Do not let a green cone stand in for a green IG: a profile the change did not touch can still be broken by it.

759ef291dfb2.title: After validation
759ef291dfb2.content: Quality gates on the aggregate are quality-control; publishing is ig-publication. A validator’s verdict is an input to the QC reviewer’s decision, not the decision.

2bc39410ea3b.title: Figure rebuild: a figure is data, not a picture
2bc39410ea3b.content: Skill figure-rebuild: Turn a figure into a computable diagram: every figure of a source publication when a folio is built from its L1 entry, and any hand-drawn figure in a folio, an IG or a demonstrator that is redrawn from a source. Every declared figure gets a block, and each one is rebuilt in the form its type calls for: an ArchiMate view, BPMN, DMN, a FHIR logical model, or an SVG generated from data, always from one schema-backed source. The PDF crop stays beside the rebuild as the cited source, and the rebuild keeps the original’s layout. The figure-coverage check counts what is missing and what is still only a picture. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . A folio built from an L1 entry must carry every figure its source declares, and carry it as data rather than as a picture. Two things go wrong otherwise: . | Figures go missing silently. A vector arm that matches only Fig. and Figure misses a handbook that writes Fig 1., and nothing compares the publication’s declared figures with the folio’s blocks unless figure:coverage does. | Figures arrive as pictures. A figure block whose file is vfig-pNNN.png has a caption, a page and glossary links in the KG. Its boxes, arrows and labels are pixels: no query can reach them. | . The rebuild form is picked by figure type (step 2).

23be13551846.title: Not only L1 folios
23be13551846.content: The routes and rules here apply to any figure that is redrawn from a computable source, not only the figures of an L1 publication: a hand-drawn PNG on an IG’s home page, a demonstrator’s overview, a handbook figure in a DAK. The coverage steps (1 and 6) are the L1 part; everything else binds wherever a picture becomes data. Failure this prevents (smart-ips-pilgrimage, 2026-11-07): the IG’s hand-drawn overview of actors, systems and numbered flows was redrawn in PlantUML. Two rules below were missed because this skill read as L1-only: the figure draws actors and systems, so its route is an ArchiMate view (and declaring that view turns on the ArchiMate subgraph); and PlantUML lays the boxes out itself, so the redraw no longer looked like the original. The commit said it “draws the same figure” with no picture to show it.

d1a9fd9f6649.title: The redraw keeps the original’s layout
d1a9fd9f6649.content: A rebuild is a transcription of the drawing, and where a box sits is part of the drawing: readers know the figure by its shape. So, for every route: . | Take the coordinates from the original. Each box goes where the original draws it, scaled to the original’s canvas: bpmndi bounds for BPMN, Archi <bounds> for an ArchiMate view, the data file’s positions for a generated SVG. Groups and regions the original draws (a country, a lane, a phase) keep their place too. | Never hand the layout to an auto-layout tool. PlantUML, Graphviz and Mermaid place boxes themselves and cannot hold a position, so they are a rendering, never the source of a redrawn figure (§”Mermaid and PlantUML are renderings, never a source”). | Show a side-by-side before asking for review. Render the rebuild and put it next to the original in the PR or review row. “Draws the same figure” is a claim a reviewer checks by looking, so give them the picture. | Say what differs. ArchiMate notation draws typed boxes, not the original’s icons; list such differences in the PR rather than hiding them. | . A pictured figure keeps its pictures: a styled view from the same model . When the original draws people and systems as pictures (avatars, devices, logos) rather than boxes, readers expect to see those pictures. Keep the computable view and add a styled one; never trade one for the other. | Two views, one source. The ArchiMate (or BPMN) view stays the source of record. A script reads the built model and draws an “as drawn” SVG from it: the same element positions, a pictogram per role, the same flows. Offer both on the page with a toggle. The script has a --check mode, like every generated file. | Pictograms come from the original, traced, not redrawn. Crop each pictogram from the original image, upscale it, smooth it (a Gaussian blur), sharpen it (threshold again), then trace the outline to an SVG path (potrace). Keep the paths in a data file next to the model (for example archimate/icons.json) with a note on where each came from. A hand-drawn stand-in looks wrong next to the original and invites “use the original”. | Logos come from the owner’s own logo file. Ask for it and trace it, or embed it. Never redraw a logo or emblem freehand. When the original combines a logo with an illustration (an IPS logo over a health-exchange diagram), trace the illustration too and keep the two together. | Everything is a link. Each pictogram links to its role or actor page. Each step marker links to its journey moment. Each narrative links to its transaction (or its moment). Codes such as transaction ids go into the link and its tooltip, not into the printed text. | What a flow carries is drawn with its narrative. A QR code, a key or a document sits before the narrative, as one block, at the height of the text. It must not float on its own beside the arrow. | Respect the original’s geometry. Anchor a figure to the dividers the original draws (for example a person’s head on the central dashed line). Draw nearly level arrows level. Keep text at a readable size, with a line height that does not crowd. | Review by looking. Share the generated SVG (not a PNG) and a side-by-side with the original, and iterate on the owner’s notes. | .

2b8191f65305.title: The steps, after the folio is seeded
2b8191f65305.content: . | Every declared figure has a block. Run bun run cat figure:coverage --entry <library>/<doc-id> --folio folio/<doc>. A missing figure is a bug in extraction or seeding. Fix that (re-run the vector arms, inspect, place the block) rather than excluding it. The one legitimate block exclusion is content the folio may not copy, such as a third-party figure used by permission. It is signed off by a person (scope: "block"), and the folio says in prose what the figure was. | Classify each figure by what it draws, by looking at the render, never by its labels alone (see l1-document-ingestion, “the text layer is not the figure”): . | The figure draws | Rebuild as | Where it lives | . | actors, systems, components, layers of an architecture | an ArchiMate view | the reference architecture the folio mounts (e.g. smart-ra tools/archimate-dth/), linked from the block’s meta.figureViews | . | a workflow with tasks, gateways, lanes | BPMN 2.0 | the folio’s processes/, or the DAK it is adapted from | . | a decision or a transition rule | DMN 1.3 | processes/decisions/ | . | classes, attributes, cardinalities | FHIR logical models (FSH), drawn as a UML class diagram generated from them | the upstream IG (e.g. smart-pcmt), else a litlfred FSH repo | . | a graph of named boxes and arrows | find what the boxes ARE (processes, actors, systems) and model it as ArchiMate elements and relationships | the reference architecture, or for an IG or demonstrator its own archimate/ model (declared with graph typology archimate, so the archimate-pages visualiser draws it) | . | phases, layers, nested shapes, a tree, a staircase | an SVG generated from data: a data file plus a generator Tool. The DIIG phases chart is the worked example: diig-phases-figure/v1 data on the L1 library entry of each publication that prints it, drawn by Tool diig-phases-svg | the data on the source’s L1 library entry; the folio commits the SVG, and adds only its own tiles in a diig-phases-adaptation/v1 file | . | a table of values drawn as a picture | a table block | the block | . | any of the above, kept looking as printed: the as-drawn companion of a model view, or a drawing no model route fits (an illustration, a diagram of pictograms, a country example the folio may copy) | an as-drawn SVG: as-drawn-figure/v1 data transcribed from the PDF by scripts/pdf-as-drawn.py, drawn by Tool as-drawn-svg (§”A drawing kept as printed becomes as-drawn data”) | the folio’s figure-data/as-drawn/; the folio commits the SVG | . | a country example, a photograph, a screenshot, a third-party figure | keep the cited picture (scope: "rebuild" exclusion, signed off) | unchanged | . One source, never a copy. Every rebuilt figure is generated from, or links to, ONE schema-backed source: an ArchiMate model, a BPMN or DMN file, a FHIR logical model, or a data file whose labels are glossary IRIs. A figure that appears in several publications (the DIIG phases chart, the SMART Guidelines layers, the ANC workflow) has one source in the layer they all mount, and each folio points at it. Content that already lives upstream (smart-pcmt’s FHIR models for dth-pc) is linked, never re-typed. | Start from the drawing’s own structure. pdf-vector-figures.py already records, per render, the labelled boxes (assembly.boxes) and which open strokes join two of them. That is a draft node and edge list. Check it against the render: the assembly does not know arrow direction or meaning, and a label in white space belongs to no box. | Keep the picture as evidence. The rebuilt block cites the PDF page and keeps meta.source.file pointing at the crop, so a reviewer can compare. Record how it was made in meta.source.method: archimate-view, bpmn, dmn, fhir-logical-model, generated or redrawn, plus generator when a script draws it and the source’s path or IRI. | Assert nothing the figure does not draw. A rebuild is a transcription of the drawing. A relation the figure does not draw is not added, and counts, dates and country facts stay cited source content, never model facts (the L2 DTH workplan rule: no empirical claims in formal content). smart-ra’s dth_sc.py states the same rule in its view documentation. | Re-run the check. --require-computable fails while any figure is still a picture or only linked, so a folio can adopt it as a gate once the rebuilds are done. | .

53050e875c30.title: Routes by figure type, in detail
53050e875c30.content: A workflow picture becomes BPMN XML . A figure drawn in BPMN notation (lanes, events, gateways, tasks, groups, subprocesses), such as the ANC workflow in dth-pc Fig. 6 and dth-sc Fig. 7, is transcribed into a .bpmn file. | Look for the source’s own BPMN first. If the publication it is adapted from (a DAK, a DTH, an IG) publishes the process as .bpmn, mount or cite that file; never redraw it. Otherwise transcribe it: WHO smart-anc, for example, publishes no .bpmn for its ANC workflow. | Transcribe exactly what is drawn. Keep the source’s activity numbers and names as task ids and names (10.5 Nutrition supplementation), the lanes, the gateway labels on their flows, a group as bpmn:group, and a subprocess as bpmn:subProcess. Include bpmndi coordinates taken from the render, so the diagram looks like the source. | What the figure emphasises becomes data, not colour. The purple outline on “connections to the supply chain” becomes a marker on those tasks, an extension element or a documented category, so a query can find them. | Shared processes live once, in the layer the folios mount (dth-sc for the supply chain handbooks), and each folio’s figure block points at that file. | Validate with the cat-harness bpmn-authoring checks, then render the SVG with the same tool the folio uses for its own processes. | . A data model becomes FHIR logical models, rendered as UML . A class diagram with attributes and cardinalities (dth-pc Fig. 9: Generic Product, Trade Item, Regulated Trade Item) is a data model. | Find the newer computable source first. dth-pc’s data model is carried forward in smart-pcmt: Product and ProductAuthorization logical models. Link to those, cite the handbook figure as the original, and list the differences rather than hiding them. Read WHO and smart-* repositories; never change them. | Only where no source exists, transcribe it as FSH Logical: models in a litlfred repository. sushi must run without errors before the commit. | Draw the figure as a UML class diagram generated from the StructureDefinitions, never from the picture. Show each entity as an IG-style structure tree, using the FHIR layer’s logical-model-schemas and ig-ast-render. | In mapping tables, every FHIR path links to the spec page for its version (https://hl7.org/fhir/R5/<resource>-definitions.html#<Resource.path>), and every entity links to its logical model or profile. State the FHIR version when the source and the mapping differ (smart-pcmt is 4.0.1; dth-pc maps to R5, where InventoryItem first exists). | . A layered or phased chart becomes an SVG generated from data . Charts such as the SMART Guidelines L1–L5 layers, the DIIG phases, nested strategies or a cost tree are not graphs. Write their content as a data file: layers, boxes, their text, and which feeds which. Then generate the SVG with a Tool. The DIIG phases chart is the worked example; the data lives in the L1 library: . | Each published version is transcribed once, as diig-phases-figure/v1 data on that publication’s L1 library entry, under figure-data/. DIIG Fig. 1.1.1 lives on 9789240010567-eng, and the product catalogue handbook’s Fig. 4 lives on 9789240116191-eng. | A folio that adds its own tiles (dth-hrh) writes only those tiles in a diig-phases-adaptation/v1 file that adapts the published version. | Tool diig-phases-svg (bun run figure:diig-phases) draws either one. The folio commits the SVG and records the data file in meta.source.generated. | The SMART Guidelines approach chart (L1–L5 layers and their country adaptations) follows the same pattern: smart-guidelines-approach-figure/v1 data (the product catalogue handbook’s Fig. 5 is on 9789240116191-eng), drawn by Tool smart-approach-svg (bun run figure:smart-approach). | A source’s own wording stays as printed, typos included (“prioritise outcomes”); a correction is a review comment, not an edit to the data. | Labels are SVG <text>, never pixels, so they can be searched, translated and read aloud. | A label that names a glossary concept (L1 Narrative, Digital adaptation kit, Localisation) links to the SKOS term, an <a href> around the text. | . A drawing kept as printed becomes as-drawn data . When the reader should see the figure as printed (every figure needs that companion beside a model view, and some figures have no model route), do not redraw it by hand. Transcribe it: . | python3 -I folio-assistant-core/scripts/pdf-as-drawn.py --entry <L1 entry> --pdf <its PDF> --out figure-data/as-drawn --glossary <file>=<IRI base>... writes one as-drawn-figure/v1 file per L1 render. It holds every path, clip, text run and image inside the render’s region, in paint order, at the printed coordinates, colours, line widths, dashes, font sizes and weights. Nothing is placed by hand, so the layout is the original’s by construction. The caption line is left out, because the block prints it. | bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/as-drawn-svg.ts figure-data/as-drawn --out-dir folio/<doc>/media draws as-drawn-fig-<N>.svg, and --check holds the SVGs to the data. Labels are SVG <text> held to their printed width. A label that equals a glossary prefLabel or altLabel links to the term, and nothing else is linked. | The block records meta.source.method: "generated" with the data, the tools and the PDF crop as evidence. For a figure that is also a model view, keep the view’s render as well, and name the as-drawn SVG in the ArchiMate config’s figures[].asDrawn. | Review by looking: render each SVG next to the L1 PNG. The extractor handles compound paths, clips, form XObjects, CMYK (as poppler converts it), rotated text and invisible text. It leaves out soft-masked paint (drop shadows) and counts it in omitted. Say so in the PR. | Skip, with --skip-page, a figure that already has a generated SVG, and third-party content the folio may not copy. That one gets a signed-off scope: "block" exclusion. | . Mermaid and PlantUML are renderings, never a source . Mermaid is a drawing language, not a schema. Nothing downstream consumes it: no KG import, no validator, and the document site does not render it. Its node names are local strings with no IRI, so they cannot link to a glossary term, an ArchiMate element or a FHIR model. A hand-written .mmd is therefore a second copy of content, which the one-source rule forbids. PlantUML is the same: its boxes are local strings, and its auto-layout cannot keep a redrawn figure’s layout. Mermaid or PlantUML may appear only as a view GENERATED from a schema-backed source, when it lays out better than the native renderer, and then the generated text and SVG are build output, not authored files. Drop the flattened figure text from the prose . Page-level seeding puts a figure’s text layer into the prose block of its page (“Fig. 1: Product master data Product identifier, Name, …”). That text is neither prose nor a figure. Once the figure has a block, remove its text from the prose, from the caption line to the end of the figure’s labels. The labels live in vector-labels.json and, after a rebuild, in the computable source. The l1-coverage check is unaffected, because figure labels are not normative sentences. Link table cells . Tables seeded from a publication hold names that the folio already defines. Link them: . | a chapter or section name links to its section anchor in the folio; | an organisation or role (Ministry of Health, National Regulatory Authority, Central Medical Stores, Data officer) links to its glossary term, and through that to the ArchiMate actor or role the term maps to; | a cross-reference to a figure or table (“Fig. 9”) links to the block. | . Match names only on an exact glossary label or altLabel. A cell with no match stays plain text and is listed for review. A guessed link is worse than none. Example data becomes FHIR example instances . A figure or table that shows example records, such as products, packs or identifiers with quantities, is instance data and not a drawing. Examples are dth-pc Fig. 11 (packaging variations) and the NPC01101001 table. Write the records once as FSH Instance:s of the upstream logical model (InstanceOf: Product, Usage: #example) beside that model. The figure or table is then generated from the compiled instances. For dth-pc these instances are in litlfred/smart-pcmt. The instances carry only what the source prints: . | A value the model requires but the source omits gets data-absent-reason#unknown, never a plausible guess. | Numbers that do not add up in the source are transcribed as printed, and the mismatch is listed in the PR. | A column with no clean element is left out and listed, not forced. | . A repeated activity header comes from the step records . A bar that repeats over each activity, such as INPUTS / STEPS / RESOURCES / OUTPUTS in dth-pc, is a view of that activity’s step-table record. Generate it from the record. Each input and output links the BPMN data object it names, and nothing is typed into the bar.

21c3d4af18a5.title: Reviewing the classification
21c3d4af18a5.content: An agent proposes, and a person decides. Review happens either in the folio’s Contributor Log sheet or in a GitHub issue, and the result always lands in the folio’s figures.json by a PR. | Propose. An agent looks at each figure’s render and vector-layer structure. It proposes a route from the table in step 2 and an upstream source to reuse, if one exists, and gives its evidence. | Review in the sheet. Write one row per figure, or per batch, to the Contributor Log’s Agent tab, one row per change set. The script copies the rows across, so the sheet needs no new columns: . | Title: Fig N: route | Selected Sections: the section that holds the figure | Feedback: Decision needed: <question>, followed by lettered options with the recommendation marked | Agentic status: Needs human | . An Editor accepts the recommendation by setting Ready for agent to Yes, or types another letter. The steps are in review-sheet-script, “A question to people goes in the sheet”. | Or review in an issue. One issue per figure, labelled figure-route, holding the same question. The row’s Issue column and feedback-issue.ts keep a sheet row and its issue linked, so either one can start the review and the decision closes both. | Record. Accepted routes are written to figures.json in a PR, with who approved each one. figure-coverage then holds the folio to them. | .

769688f42ca1.title: Reading the report
769688f42ca1.content: | State | Meaning | . | missing | declared by the publication, no block in the folio | . | excluded | no block, by a signed-off scope: "block" exclusion | . | picture | only crop or image blocks | . | linked | a picture whose block links a model view; the view may not draw the whole figure | . | computable | a diagram or table block, or a figure block with a rebuild method | . | cited | kept as a picture on purpose, by a signed-off scope: "rebuild" exclusion | . As in l1-coverage, an agent may propose an exclusion, but only a person signs one off. Declared figures are read with cat-harness-tools declaredFigureCaptions, the same reading check:l1-complete uses, so the two checks agree on what the publication declares.

959ed64c5b1f.title: When to use folio-init
959ed64c5b1f.content: Reach for folio-init when triage in getting-started or repo-conversion has settled that a new folio structure should be created: . | new-repo — a brand-new repository is being stood up to author a paper, document or DAK folio. | add-folio — an existing repository wants a new folio added alongside its existing directories (overlay), without overwriting its tracked files. | . Do not run folio-init when: . | The repository already has a <name>.json declaration and only needs a lower harness layer brought in at a pinned SHA — that is materialise, served by remote-mount (bun run cat mount:remote). | The user is converting existing prose in place (convert in repo-conversion.bpmn) — that uses ingestion, not a blank scaffold. | . Because folio-init runs before the target repository has a content type, the Tool is registered among the generic harness tools rather than inside a content-type adapter.

be7b3f276931.title: Write capability requirement and read-only degradation
be7b3f276931.content: folio-init is a writing verb: it creates directories, writes manifests and agent stubs, and (when the repository has an origin) creates the cat/<instance>/beans, cat/<instance>/todos and cat/<instance>/fsh-guts state branches it declares. Before invoking folio-init to write, check that at least one write capability is present (scenarios/capabilities/): . | git-push — local filesystem write plus git remote push capability for the target repository and its state branches. | github-api — GitHub API token (gh / REST / GraphQL) able to create or populate the target repository and refs. | github-connector — MCP GitHub connector able to push the scaffolded files into the target repository. | . When no write capability is available (a read-only container or an unauthenticated session), folio-init degrades cleanly via --dry-run (dry_run: true on the MCP tool): it computes and returns the complete Markdown report of every directory, manifest, builder shim and config file it would write, without touching the filesystem or git refs. Never attempt a partial write when write capability is absent, and never report a failed capability probe as a completed scaffold.

a0f065e1a82c.title: What folio-init writes
a0f065e1a82c.content: Given title and one or more authors (plus optional content_type, slug, dir, link, assistant_path, force, dry_run), folio-init lays down: . | The folio directories and initial manifests — folio/ (or content/), uploads/, library/, the root <slug>.json layer declaration and <slug>.config.json, and the root index.config.json that instantiates it (index-config). | The builder shim (content/schema/builders) — block manifests in the folio import ../schema/builders rather than importing the platform path directly. Writing the path to the harness once in the shim means re-linking a folio (submodule ↔ sibling ↔ remote mount) is a two-file edit rather than a sweep across every block manifest. | The link back to the platform (--link) — links the harness via sibling (--assistant-path ../folio-assistant) or submodule, and writes .mcp.json and the .claude/ session-start hook (bun run cat state:mount) pointing at that link. | The agent instructions — AGENTS.md and the one-line CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md stubs pointing to it. | The state branches — declares beans, todos and fsh-guts on cat/<slug>/<id> and creates each missing one, seeded empty with the standard layout, once main is on the remote. Each state graph in the result carries created (created, exists, denied, refused). Where it could not create one (no origin, an empty remote, or a token that cannot push), the note names bun run cat state:seed --init, and the first bun run cat state:mount creates it. That command then mounts a working store on the first session start (directory-conventions §”Where a NEW layer’s state lives”). | .

9bc13c5126ff.title: What to check afterwards
9bc13c5126ff.content: . | bun run cat state:seed --init --dry-run — every declared state branch is on the remote (nothing left to create). | bun run cat check:declaration-resolution — every directory and asset the new <slug>.json declares resolves on disk. | bun run cat index:render:check — the generated AGENTS.md matches the new index.config.json and layer declaration. | bun run cat state:status — the beans and todos stores are mounted and writable. | .
