b27c1b3fec1d.title: ig-publisher-fork
b27c1b3fec1d.content: Skill ig-publisher-fork: Requirements for an agent working a local experimental fork of the IG Publisher — which repositories, what the AST must carry, what must not change, and the acceptance criteria. Read before forking, and before reporting a fork’s work complete. Named by: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch . Skill id: ig-publisher-fork · Package: fhir-ig-base · Layer: fhir-harness . The brief for an agent taking a local, experimental fork of the FHIR IG Publisher, so that an AST can be emitted and cached.

68c35fd61407.title: Which repositories, and why only one
68c35fd61407.content: | repository | holds | needed for | . | HL7/fhir-ig-publisher | orchestration, the loaded resources, DependencyAnalyser, CqlSubSystem, the metadata exports | the dump, the toolchain record, the logic-layer dependency edges | . | hapifhir/org.hl7.fhir.core | the renderer, the validator, dependency loading | page-fragment provenance only | . The logic-layer edges are a publisher-side gap, not a core one: . | DependencyAnalyser is in the publisher (org.hl7.fhir.publisher.core/.../igtools/publisher/). Its analysePD and analyseAD are empty stubs, and Library and Measure are not dispatched. That is the whole criterion-2 gap. | CqlSubSystem already attaches CQL depends-on to each Library (AdjunctFileLoader), so Library→Library edges exist in memory; nothing exports them. | . Only page-fragment provenance needs core. Read upstream before re-quoting either claim.

5b3a91a26e56.title: The shape taken: a library ON TOP, not a fork IN it
5b3a91a26e56.content: Do not change existing Publisher code unless there is no other way: remarshal, reuse, subclass. The work is ast-export/, a separate Maven project on branch claude/ast-export of litlfred/fhir-ig-publisher. It depends on the released org.hl7.fhir.publisher.core from Maven Central, is not a module of the root pom, and changes no Publisher file. | AstPublisher extends Publisher and overrides nothing. It reads getFileList() after execute(). | AstFieldsAccess is a read-only view of package-private PublisherFields, declared in the Publisher’s package inside the library. A rename upstream fails to compile rather than failing at run time. | Upstream’s DependencyAnalyser is reused unchanged; LogicEdges sits beside it. | . That makes “behind a flag, default byte-identical” true by construction for the Publisher itself: a stock build never loads the library. What still needs measuring is that AstExportCli’s own build writes the same output/ as a stock one.

d6ad75714f4f.title: The tools an agent runs
d6ad75714f4f.content: In the fork, under ast-export/: . | tool | what | network | . | scripts/run-real-igs.sh [work] [--byte-identical] | W1/W2 on the WHO SMART Trust IG and the WHO SMART Immunizations IG, W2 per resource type | packages.fhir.org, tx.fhir.org | . | scripts/w7-round.sh <work> | one incremental round on a one-CQL-file change | same | . | AstExportCli, AstPlanCli, IncrementalBuildCli | export, plan a delta, rebuild the cone | export and rebuild: yes; plan: no | . Here, ig-ast-delta lists, checks, diffs and renders what those produce. The one CI path is .github/workflows/ig-ast-refresh.yml: it runs AstExportCli on a runner, at the pinned commit, to refresh an IG’s AST cache, calling the same exporter and ig-cache.sh. ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle” owns it. Any other CI calls these same scripts.

2fc8510fb9b8.title: Without packages.fhir.org: seeding the cache from trusted sources
2fc8510fb9b8.content: Some environments reach GitHub and registry.npmjs.org but not packages.fhir.org. The seeder fills the FHIR package cache from sources that are each a trust anchor: named by the owner, or the package’s own publisher. Nothing else is consulted. There are two copies: ast-export/scripts/seed-fhir-cache-from-npm.py in the fork, which ig-ast-refresh.yml runs, and scripts/fhir-cache-seed-npm.ts here, which the Tool fhir-cache-seed-npm invokes. | source | trust | what it holds | . | npm, account grahamegrieve | owner: trusted. Grahame Grieve founded HL7 FHIR | mostly the latest version of each HL7 package; core packages under @hl7/ | . | a publisher’s own published-site repository on GitHub | the publisher’s own published site | every released version that publisher hosts there | . | a template’s own repo at HEAD | FHIR/ig-registry/templates.json names it; owner: fhir.base.template is trusted | templates, #current included | . | --mirror | whoever ran mirror-fhir-packages.sh (Tool fhir-package-mirror) | what the others lack | . Rules: . | Exact versions only. A pin is never satisfied by another version; there is no “approximate” build with substituted versions. The one exception is the Publisher’s own rule: a patch wildcard (1.1.x) resolves to the highest 1.1.N a source lists, and the resolution is recorded. | Verified. npm tarballs against npm’s sha512. Every other source must carry a package/package.json naming exactly the requested package and version. npm’s 0.0.1-security malicious-package placeholder is refused. | Nothing computed once and kept. Load from the repositories every run; do not compute once and assume it fixed. The template registry, the IHE folder listing and any mirror clone are fetched fresh every run into a scratch directory deleted at exit. There is no table of package locations that could go stale behind the registry. | Provenance in ast-export-npm-provenance.json: the source, URL or commit, and hash of every package. | . Where it stands, measured over the WHO SMART Trust and Immunizations IGs: 20 packages install, including both templates. Missing are the pinned HL7 versions (IPS, terminology, extensions, CQL, CRMI, SDC, IPA), fhir.cqf.common and us.nlm.vsac. To close the gap: . | Run the seeder with --missing-out missing.txt. | Run mirror-fhir-packages.sh <repo> missing.txt on a machine that reaches packages.fhir.org. | Run the seeder again with --mirror <repo>. | . What the declared dependencies miss. Seeding from sushi-config.yaml alone leaves the build short (Publisher 3.0.0 / core 7.0.1): . | The template. It is named in ig.ini, not in sushi-config.yaml, so pass it to the seeder as a positional name#version. | A template seeded from its repo keeps the repo’s layout. The template’s own files go at the top of the cache entry, and only package.json goes under package/. The Publisher reads a cached template with NpmPackage.fromFolder, which files a top-level file under package/$root and unpacks it into template/. A file under package/ lands in template/package/, and the build fails with template/config.json not found. | Packages the Publisher loads by itself: . | hl7.fhir.pubpack at CommonPackages.VER_PUBPACK; | hl7.fhir.xver-extensions at CommonPackages.VER_XVER; | hl7.fhir.uv.tools.r<N> at Publisher.TOOLING_IG_CURRENT_RELEASE, for the IG’s FHIR release; | the latest milestone of hl7.terminology.r<N> and hl7.fhir.uv.extensions.r<N>, when the IG does not declare them. Read the versions from the release you build against. Never copy them from here, because they move with each release. | . | “Latest” offline is not exact. When it cannot reach the registry, getLatestVersion falls back to the highest version in the local cache. That silently breaks the exact-versions rule. Mirror the version the registry lists today, and record which version it was. | . An offline validator crash that is not ours. In core 7.0.1, InstanceValidator.checkTypeValue fetches the approved additional resources from fhir.github.io. When that fetch fails it dereferences a null set, so the build fails with an NPE on additionalResourceNames. Only an environment that cannot reach fhir.github.io meets it. It is upstream’s bug (org.hl7.fhir.core), and it is not patched here, because the library does not change Publisher code. Build with a terminology server. A -tx n/a build, which is run-real-igs.sh --no-tx, is only for finding faults before the real run. Its numbers are never recorded as measurements. A template the registry does not list is named by the caller with --template-repo <name>=<owner/repo>, on the command line, never stored. Publishers’ site repositories. The fork’s seeder keeps one fixed table mapping a package-name prefix to the publisher’s own GitHub repo. It can drift, which is tolerated only because every package fetched through it must name itself exactly in its own package.json, so a stale entry fails as “missing”, never as a wrong package. The copy here holds no such table: the caller maps each prefix with --site-repo <prefix>=<owner/repo>[@branch], none by default, because which publishers exist is not something fhir-harness may know. An IG’s package lock. An IG that pins its FHIR packages commits a fhir-packages.lock.json at its root, in the format of this layer’s scripts/sushi/fhir-packages.lock.json: {"packages": [{"name", "version", "tarball", "integrity"}]}, where tarball is an exact https URL (a commit-pinned one for a package a site repository publishes) and integrity is sha512-<base64> or sha256-<base64>; a hex sha256 may be given instead or as well, and every hash given must match. --lock <file> installs each pinned package from its URL only, refuses one whose bytes or package.json do not match, and does not follow its dependencies, so the lock lists the IG’s packages in full. ig-ast-refresh.yml (input package-lock, default fhir-packages.lock.json) and ig-ast-build.sh (--package-lock) run it before SUSHI and the Publisher, so neither fetches a package the lock pins. A package’s URL is named in the lock, never derived from its name.

fea8ec05bf22.title: The measurement that justifies the work
fea8ec05bf22.content: Using the Publisher’s current metadata exports as an AST proxy across two real IGs: . | export | the WHO SMART Trust IG | the WHO SMART Immunizations IG | . | valueset-ref-list.json ValueSet→CodeSystem edges | 17 over 14 | 431 over 252 | . | codesystem-ref-list.json uses populated | 0 of 15 | 0 of 14 | . | usage-stats.json extension→path | 6 | 35 (+5 profiles) | . Two findings: . | uses is declared and never populated — in both IGs. | Nothing exports Library / PlanDefinition / Measure dependencies — 458 artefacts, 61 % of the WHO SMART Immunizations IG, the decision-logic core, with zero edges. | . Re-derive both before quoting them. If a later Publisher release closes either, the fork’s scope shrinks accordingly.

70c0e1a78bdc.title: Acceptance criteria
70c0e1a78bdc.content: The AST must carry: . | one structured record per resource, keyed by canonical URL and version — an id alone collides across versions | dependency edges among Library, PlanDefinition and Measure — the gap above. Built as LogicEdges; not yet measured on the WHO SMART Immunizations IG. Measured as: every logic resource has at least one logic-to-logic edge in either direction. In graph terms, no vertex is isolated. Outgoing edges alone cannot be the test, because a finite acyclic dependency graph always has a sink: a library that others depend on and that depends on no logic itself. run-real-igs.sh prints both counts. | uses actually populated, or an explicit statement that it cannot be — a declared-and-empty field is worse than an absent one, because a consumer cannot tell “no dependencies” from “not computed” | page-fragment provenance — which source produced which output fragment, so a rendered page can be traced without re-running | the resolved dependency closure with pinned versions | terminology expansion provenance — which server, which version, and whether expansion actually happened; a build against a dead tx must be distinguishable from an IG with thin ValueSets | a toolchain object — publisher version, core version, SUSHI version. publisher.jar is re-downloaded from the latest release on every WHO build, so without this an AST cannot say what produced it | . And the fork itself must satisfy: . | emitted behind a flag, with default behaviour byte-identical when the flag is absent | upstreamable shape — a flag and an additional writer, not a rewrite; a fork that cannot be offered back has no exit | no change to validation or rendering semantics. If a fork build’s qa.json differs from an upstream build’s on the same input, that is a defect in the fork, and it is the first thing to check | .

dffbafd72a75.title: What the agent must not do
dffbafd72a75.content: . | Do not treat the AST as an authority. It is a cache: its indices, dependency edges and versions are unverified until a full run. Anything written to consume it says so — see ig-publisher-reduction §P3. | Do not vendor either repository into this one. The fork lives at its own remote; exactly one repository runs a thing. | Do not add WHO, DAK or SMART concepts to the fork. The AST is a property of a FHIR IG. A DAK-shaped field in it makes the fork unofferable upstream and breaks the layering fhir-harness exists to keep. | Do not fix uses by inferring it. If the information is not there, report that it is not there. An inferred edge in a dependency graph is indistinguishable from a real one downstream, and every ordering metric computed from it becomes unfalsifiable. | .

af12d4133325.title: Reporting
af12d4133325.content: A fork round reports: which repositories at which commits, which criteria are met, which are not, and what was measured rather than what was implemented. A criterion is met when an AST from a real IG is shown to carry the thing. The WHO SMART Immunizations IG is the right subject: it carries the 61 % gap.

892d9cc8f16d.doc: An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes
892d9cc8f16d.title: An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes
892d9cc8f16d.content: Process_IgRelease · advisory · 5 step(s) . How an IG repository’s release is cut, and how a missed one is caught up (skill ig-binary-artefacts §”Releasing”). (Owner, 2026-11-10: “need to add this to process (and how to catchup if not tagged) of build”.) . THE RULE. A release is a governance decision. The owner tags the IG’s CURRENT version from sushi-config.yaml, v<version>, on the default branch. The tag starts the IG’s ig-release.yml caller, which builds the tag in full and makes a GitHub DRAFT release carrying package.tgz (and its R4/R4B variants), ast-data.zip and SHA256SUMS. The owner publishes the draft. An agent never chooses a version, never pushes a tag and never publishes a release. THE CATCH-UP. Every AST refresh of the default branch runs ig-release.ts check (advisory, never failing the run): an untagged current version is reported with the commit that set it, for the owner to tag; a tag with no release is reported with the by-hand run of the release workflow; a draft is reported as waiting for the owner. The site is not the release: it is published from the AST cache (ig-ast-cache.bpmn) and carries none of these files. i i i i i

5830eefe4e8b.title: ig-render-jekyll
5830eefe4e8b.content: Skill ig-render-jekyll: Rendering a FHIR IG’s content through the just-the-docs pipeline instead of mounting the IG Publisher’s finished HTML — the JSON-only representation contract, navigation derived from sushi-config.yaml, and the LHS rail. Read before adding a representation, a menu entry, or a page kind. Named by: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs . Skill id: ig-render-jekyll · Package: fhir-ig-base · Layer: fhir-harness . Render an IG’s pages as folio pages — markdown with front matter, through Jekyll and just-the-docs — from the Publisher’s structured output, never its finished HTML. Publisher HTML has no front matter, so the navbar, language bar, QA badges and translation surface cannot reach it; a folio page gets them all. Whether an IG repository gets this rendering is asked when it is adopted (default yes); see ig-build-pipeline §”Who starts a build”.

9ec459ffad11.title: The three contracts
9ec459ffad11.content: 1. JSON only . The Publisher emits JSON, XML and Turtle; only JSON is taken, wrapped in JSON-LD / JSON Schema. RDF, where needed, is projected from the JSON-LD. A representation that arrives and is not taken is recorded as a refusal. Not linked either. The site does not link a resource’s .xml or .ttl copy: JSON-LD nodes carry only JSON encodings, and the site.data artefact variables only url.json. The refusal record still counts what each IG published in those forms. 2. Navigation is derived, never authored . sushi-config.yaml already carries both maps the site needs: . | pages: — an ordered map of source file to title. That is the page order. | menu: — the grouping, including nested subsections. | . Derive the navigation from them. Do not hand-author a nav file or write entries back into sushi-config.yaml. When the config names a page that does not exist, that is a finding, not a reason to create a placeholder. 3. LHS rail, and the theme is captured rather than replaced . Navigation goes in the left-hand rail, not the FHIR IG’s top bar. The rest of the IG theme — CSS, typography, resource-page furniture — is captured into the theme layer rather than discarded. Nav position is a layout setting; nav contents are derived per build.

aea40929bee7.title: What the render reads in the IG repository
aea40929bee7.content: Only what the repository declares. Every reader on this path (build-ig-site, ig-site-data, ingest-ig-menu, ig-repo-site) goes through scripts/ig-read-scope.ts, which honours contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json; anything outside it is not rendered. A repository with no section is read whole, with a warning. See ig-build-pipeline §”What this layer reads”.

46cefe087295.title: Where the variables come from
46cefe087295.content: artifactVariables (build-ig-site.ts) writes the per-artefact Liquid variables from the artefact index to _data/, read by the same Jekyll run: site.data.fhir.artifacts.<ResourceType>__<id> with url (canonical, page, json), text, link.html and elements.<key>, plus artifact_categories, artifacts_listed and artifact_lists. An element key the index does not hold is reported as not sourced, never written empty. The families and keys follow WHO’s generate_smart_liquid.py, a build script outside this layer, without its smart__ prefix: that prefix is WHO’s, and this layer does not know about WHO.

717e6cd4eedb.title: What parity means, and what it does not
717e6cd4eedb.content: Parity is a checklist of asset types and page kinds. A page kind the Publisher emits no data for cannot be rendered.

d3a3ff90262f.title: Thin pages, the default (--full-pages to opt out)
d3a3ff90262f.content: Every IG page is a thin HTML shell that loads its content from the JSON-LD graph, unless a build passes --full-pages. The shell is cat-harness-tools’ thinPageHtml. Artefact pages (gen-ig-pages.ts) . | Page address: artifact/<Type>-<id>.html, self-canonical. | The asset is a JSON-LD node, artifact/<Type>-<id>.jsonld, with no .json twin (every reader fetches the .jsonld), written by ig-artifact-jsonld.ts from the index (kind ig-artifact-jsonld; QA ig-artifact-jsonld.ts check over the built site). It uses the FHIR RDF class, dcterms, schema.org and PROV, and mints nothing. The page names the node as alternate. Its encodings list the reduced <Type>-<id>.json at the site root first (local), then the full copy in the AST cache by raw URL (mirror), then the IG’s published file (upstream); artifact/index.jsonld names each root file on its entry (schema:contentUrl; fhir-harness#359). | One shared renderer. assets/ig-artifact.js fetches the node, then the resource’s full copy (the mirror, else the local one), draws the description, facts, identity table and elements, concepts or includes, and hands the narrative and JSON to ast-resource.js. The page carries only its title, key and a <noscript> link to the node and resource. | The rail is linked: folio-navbar: linked, and the rail pass (rail-standalone-pages.ts) links its style and scripts rather than inlining them. | The tab views are thin pages too, written beside the page wherever the site serves the artefact’s JSON: a compiled copy (--compiled-data) or, failing that, the Publisher’s own <Type>-<id>.json carried as data (--publisher-data <dir>, from the docs root). An IG repository’s site (ig-site:compose) passes only --compiled-data .: the AST’s copy, served once at the root as <Type>-<id>.json. Each view keeps the Publisher’s file name: . | -definitions: the snapshot’s element table, differential marked; | -mappings: each mapping declaration with the elements mapped to it; | the JSON view (.profile.json for a StructureDefinition, else .json), drawn by ast-resource.js; | -examples, for every StructureDefinition: the instances claiming it in meta.profile, or a note that there are none. | . Each uses the same shell (thinArtifactView) and renderer; the artefact’s page links them in a tab bar, and the narrative’s links to them are relinked. The change history, testing, XML and Turtle views are neither rendered nor published. The IG API view pages stay full pages. | Nothing under comparison-v*/ is published. ig-site:publisher-pages serves the AST’s data and reads no Publisher output. | In an IG site the docs root is the site root, so --compiled-data . points each resource at ../<Type>-<id>.json from artifact/. No ast-data/ mirror is published. | . The artefact list and the table of contents (build-ig-site.ts) . | One index node, artifact/index.jsonld (family folio-ig-artifact-index-jsonld/v1, same kind), lists every artefact once, in the Publisher’s order, each entry naming its node and carrying only what a list row shows; check holds it to the artefact index and each node. | artifacts.html is a thin shell over that node: a jump list of categories, a filter, then every category open (nothing collapsed), anchored #artifacts-<slug>. | What a list draws: . | The IG’s own ImplementationGuide is “This guide”, drawn first (#artifacts-this-guide), never as a “Not categorised” row; the toc lists it first too. | A category that mixes resource types is sub-headed by type (#artifacts-<category>-<type>; the Publisher’s “Other”: Basic, Questionnaire, DocumentReference…), and the jump list counts each type. | A table draws only the columns its rows fill. An instance (an artefact with no canonical URL) has no description, so the index copies what the resource states: its meta.profile (dcterms:conformsTo, drawn as the last path segment, linked when it is in the same IG) and its code (dcterms:subject). A definition’s core profile (shareablevalueset) is not shown. | . | toc.html is a thin shell. The IG’s own pages (sushi-config.yaml pages:, landing page first) stay in its HTML; the artefacts under each category are drawn from the index node. | Both are written by stageIgSite when StageOptions.artifacts.index is given, which stage-ig-sites.ts does unless --full-pages. Staging thin a site whose artefact pages were generated with --full-pages (no index node) is refused. | . The narrative pages (composeIgSite) . | The IG’s prose stays in the HTML, rendered by Jekyll; composed into a host site, the page wears thinIgLayout (_layouts/ig-thin-<instance>.html) instead of the host’s layout, so none of the host’s chrome (harness bar, SVG sprite, sidebar nav, inline scripts) is written into it. | Everything around the prose is linked: assets/ig-artifact.css, assets/ig-topbar.css, assets/ig-source-links.js and the rail (folio-navbar: linked). The IG’s top bar, edit links, footer and TOC declaration stay. | The thin page has no host search box or QA badges; it has its own search box and language picker block (below). | . The footer stays in view . Every IG page ends with the Publisher’s footer (ig-footer.liquid on the Jekyll pages, ig-artifact.js on the thin pages, one igSiteFooter object for both): publisher and copyright year, package#version, FHIR version, the build day, and Links: Table of Contents | QA Report | Version History | License, each value read from the IG’s package, sushi-config.yaml or AST and left out when none holds it. Unlike the Publisher’s, it stays at the bottom of the window (owner, 2026-11-06): it is the body’s last box, after <main> on every IG page, position: sticky (ig-artifact.css), so it spans the width beside the rail, the page scrolls under it and nothing is left behind it at the end of the page. The body is a column at least the window’s height with <main> taking the free space, so on a page shorter than the window the footer lands at the window’s bottom too. In print both are off: the footer is static, once, at the end. “QA Report” is qa.html, the harness’s QA report (ig-qa-page.ts): the FHIR QA the build holds (the Publisher’s qa.json carried with the AST, the AST’s record and validity) and the knowledge graph’s (cat-harness-tools kg-qa-report.ts). The QA report is written in every locale the IG translates its pages into, as <locale>/qa.html (owner, 2026-11-14: “For this page why is there no translation?”). Its own words come from this layer’s catalogues (translations/<locale>/generated-pages/ig-qa-page.po, ig-qa-page-i18n.ts). The Publisher’s messages come from the Publisher’s own translations first: ig-publisher-i18n.ts fetches Messages_<lang>.properties from org.hl7.fhir.utilities at exactly the core version the AST recorded and translates each message by its message-id, refusing a Publisher template whose placeholders differ from the English. What the Publisher lacks comes from translations/<locale>/publisher/messages.po, an agent’s machine translation; ig-publisher-i18n.ts needs --merge --site <url> appends what a build lacks, each entry with an example and links to the rows that print it. Every row is addressable (qa.html#qa-m<group>-<row>), and assets/fhir-qa/i18n-usage.json says, per locale, where each string is used and whether it is the Publisher’s or a machine translation. A translated QA page is never reviewed by a person: it carries the machine-translation notice, “Show English” shows the Publisher’s original beside each message, and the KG half (cat-harness-tools’ English) is marked lang="en" and says it is English only. The page’s text direction is front matter text_dir, never dir: Jekyll’s own page.dir is the page’s folder, which drew dir="/" on every page. Search and the language picker . The folio rail replaces the theme’s side menu (#site-nav is dropped; IG_DROPPED in stage-local-ig.ts), and the IG’s top bar carries a search box over the IG’s pages and artefacts (ig-search.ts): . | ig-repo-site.ts compose writes the index, assets/ig-search.json (each IG page’s title and full text; each artefact’s title, id, name, key, canonical and description), and the client, assets/ig-search.js. The index is fetched on the box’s first focus, never on page load. | The box (form.ig-search, input #search-input) is in the composed pages’ .ig-topbar and the thin pages’ header.iga-top. It is not .search, so docs-ui leaves it in the top bar. A build that does not write the files (gen-ig-pages without --search, StageOptions.search unset) writes no box. | Any other built page lacking a box (for example an IG API hub page or openapi/index.html) gets one: publisher-pages puts a bar at the top of its body (header.ig-search-top: the IG’s name, the box, the picker’s slot; stampSearchBox, withSearchBar). The pass skips assets/ and runs only when the site serves a search index. | The language picker sits beside the box, in the empty <span data-fa-slot="locale"> that follows it, which docs-ui fills. A site with no IG bar keeps the picker in docs-ui’s band. | docs-ui draws the picker from a page’s fa-translation-meta block, which publisher-pages writes (cat-harness-tools lib/translation-meta.ts) into every built page lacking one, from the IG checkout’s translation declaration; set-html-lang.ts reads it afterwards. | Translated pages (fhir-harness#382). When the IG declares translations/ in contentTypes.ig.include, each catalogue translations/<locale>/pagecontent/<page>.po is injected into its page (cat-harness-tools injectMarkdown, the segmentation the catalogue was extracted with) and staged at <locale>/<page>.md, the path the picker opens. The page and its translations carry lang, available_locales and, on a translation, translation_status and translation_source; the thin layout writes the picker’s block from them, so the picker links each language that exists. A span with no translation stays in English. A locale is verified only when translations/<locale>/status.json records a sign-off; otherwise unverified, and docs-ui shows its notice. Translated pages are out of the menu, and relative links climb out of the locale folder unless they point at a page translated into the same locale (scripts/ig-page-translations.ts). | . The root parity guard (cat-harness-tools site-parity.ts) refuses to publish a build lacking the search box or language block over a root that had them. The opt-out . gen-ig-pages.ts --full-pages and stage-ig-sites.ts --full-pages build full pages (composeIgSite(…, { fullPages: true })). Pass both or neither. --thin is a no-op; --thin --full-pages is refused.

ae48d31f1b87.title: What this does not replace
ae48d31f1b87.content: Which AST the pages are drawn from. An IG repository’s site is drawn from the AST on its cache branch, cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>, which a Publisher run on a runner refreshes; the publish refuses an AST not valid for the commit. See ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle”. The Publisher still runs: validation, dependency resolution and terminology expansion are its job and are not reproducible from cached output.

d11a9f2a1167.title: index.config.json: what this checkout instantiates
d11a9f2a1167.content: Skill index-config: index.config.json at an instantiation root says which harnesses the checkout instantiates, where each one comes from (local, or a remote mount pinned to a SHA), each layer’s config INLINE in its entry (a legacy <name>.config.json is only imported until --inline retires it), and which harness / is. Covers instantiated against declared, landing resolution and its error case, index.lock.json and its legacy fallback, the reserved index stem, the generated .gitignore block and its gate, and index-config:migrate (with --inline) for separated repositories. Named by: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Remote-mount a dependency . The schema is folio-index-config/v1 in cat-harness/schemas/kg/index-config.ts. The index is the ONE config. Each layer’s config is written inline in its instances[] entry. A <name>.config.json is a legacy file: imported only as a migration step, then retired with index-config:migrate --inline --write. Never create one — not to make a tool find a recipe, not for a new layer. If a reader only finds config in the file, that reader is the bug; fix it to read the index entry first. index.config.json holds three facts about how a checkout is instantiated: which harnesses are instantiated, which one is / (a checkout has one <base>/index.html), and where each one comes from, so each is stated once rather than spread across every root config. When it exists at the root it is authoritative. When it is absent, readers fall back to the root *.config.json files, their site.landing flags, and remoteMounts on the root declaration. { "$schema": "folio-index-config/v1", "instances": [ { "name": "folio-assistant", "source": { "local": { "at": "." } } }, { "name": "cat-harness" }, { "name": "my-ig", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "owner/my-ig", "ref": "<40-char sha>", "overrides": { "my-ig": { "whole": true } }, "trust": { "consent": { "...": "..." } } } } }, { "name": "my-guide", "contentType": "document", "site": { "build": { "sourceSteps": ["site:document"] } } } ], "site": { "landing": "cat-harness" } } .

a1cd99d96c94.title: Instantiated is a different fact from declared
a1cd99d96c94.content: A declaration (<name>.json) says what a layer declares. It travels with the harness into every checkout that uses the harness. An index.config.json entry says the layer is instantiated in this checkout. Without an index, a <name>.config.json at the root says the same thing. Tiles, the landing and the hub listing are all drawn from the instantiated set, which instantiatedHarnessNames(root) returns. Never derive that set from declarations or from a directory listing. The dependencies of an instantiated harness are not instantiated just because a mount’s closure brought them in. They keep a group of their own rather than disappearing. A harness that a KG subscription chose is instantiated the same way: kg:instantiate adds its entry, with its config inline, when the checkout has an index (and only without one writes a root <name>.config.json).

699c8e87e0f7.title: Inline, over a legacy import while one remains
699c8e87e0f7.content: Each entry’s effective config is built like this: . | Start from a legacy imported file, while one remains. That is import when it is given, else <name>.config.json, and only if the file exists. The target state is that no such file exists. | Overlay every other key of the entry (everything except name, import, source and _comment) as an inline HarnessConfig field. Objects merge key by key, and arrays and scalars are replaced. Inline fields win. | . effectiveInstanceConfig(root, name) computes it. readHarnessConfig(dir) returns it for any layer that an index lists, walking outward from the layer root and stopping at the first directory that holds either the index or the layer’s own config. A layer the index does not list is read from its own config file. Readers that are handed a root and a name (the site recipe in build-instance-site.ts) use readInstanceConfig in cat-harness-tools/scripts/instance-config.ts, which reads the same way and REPORTS every legacy file it reads. Retiring the files is index-config:migrate --inline --write: each imported file is folded into its entry by exactly the overlay above, so no effective config changes, and the file is deleted. index-config:inline:check fails while one remains.

eb5e9e203660.title: Local or remote
eb5e9e203660.content: . | source absent: local, at <name>/. | source.local.at: local, at that path. Use . for the layer declared at the root. | source.remote: a remote mount. It is a remoteMounts entry minus harness, which is the entry’s name. It reuses RemoteMountSchema instead of restating it, so it has ref (not pin), overrides.<name>.whole and .path, note, trust.consent and track, and every field added to RemoteMountSchema arrives with no edit here. | . There is one read path and one write path for remote mounts: . | Read: readDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot) returns the index’s remote entries when an index exists, else the declaration’s remoteMounts. If both carry mounts it throws and names both files. It never picks one. | Write: writeDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot, mounts) always writes index.config.json, seeding the index from the checkout first if there is none. It refuses while the declaration still carries remoteMounts. Nothing writes remoteMounts on a declaration. | .

88b91571662c.title: Which harness / is
88b91571662c.content: resolveLandingInstance(root) is the only reader. It applies these rules in order: . | condition | / is | . | the index is unreadable | invalid: the gate fails. There is no fallback to the flags, because the index was written to override them | . | the index’s site.landing names a layer it lists | that layer (by: "index") | . | the index’s site.landing is "hub" | the neutral hub: the harness listing and the todo panel | . | the index’s site.landing names a layer it does not list | invalid: the gate fails, and it is never a silent fallback | . | no site.landing (or no index), one layer | that layer (sole) | . | no site.landing, several layers, exactly one config flags site.landing: true | the flagged one | . | several flagged | the hub | . | none flagged | ambiguous: check:landing-instance fails, because the answer is never guessed | . | nothing instantiated | none: a state of its own, not a default | . gen-landing-data.ts and sync-docs-harness.ts ask this resolver. They do not use their own location. check:landing-instance also checks that the index and the root *.config.json files agree: . | A root config that the index does not import fails the check: without the index it would instantiate a harness, with it it does not, and nothing picks between them silently. | An import that names a missing file also fails the check. | An entry with no config file at all is the target state, and passes. | A legacy file an entry still imports is reported every time. It passes while it is a pending migration (every key it holds is either not inline or inline with the same value). It fails when the entry overrides one of its keys with a different value: the file’s value is then dead text that a reader of the file alone takes for the config. | .

aeaeb312a89b.title: A harnessed repository runs its checks on its own pull requests
aeaeb312a89b.content: Instantiating a harness in a repository includes turning its checks on there, through one reusable workflow the harness owns, never a copy per repository, so a layer is judged on its own pull requests and not only when an index re-pins it. Switching off a repository’s builds must not switch off its gates. The workflow is the tools layer’s .github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml. A repository calls it from a workflow of about fifteen lines that runs on pull_request: . jobs: checks: uses: <owner>/<tools-layer>/.github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml@main with: mode: layer # or `index`: the repository is its own index instance: <instance> # layer mode: its directory in the folio-assistant index path-in-repo: <instance> # where the instance sits in the repository ('.' at the root) . | layer mode is for a repository that an index mounts, such as cat-harness or the DAK layer. The workflow checks out folio-assistant and puts the PR in place of the locked mount. | index mode is for a repository that is its own index: an IG repository over the DAK layer, smart-ra, or a folio. Its own index.lock.json is replayed. | The gates are the harness’s graph checks over the repository’s own layer, plus every check:* / *:check script of that layer and its whole dependency harness (its transitive needs). Each is named <owning-instance>:<script>. | A PR fails only on what it newly breaks. Each gate and test runs on main and on the PR. Anything already red on main is listed, never hidden, and never counted against the PR. | . A layer PR that declares a new directory is red on two index gates it cannot clear. The index README lists every declared directory, so the PR leaves index:render:check and readme:sync:root:check stale, and only the index re-pin that takes the PR regenerates the README. Read those two as expected when they are the only new failures, and run them green in the index re-pin instead. Disabling a repository’s automatic builds is not disabling its checks. When an IG repository’s automatic gh-pages or IG Publisher triggers are switched off (the onboarding question in the FHIR IG layer’s ig-build-pipeline), the harness caller stays on.

18a04833e85d.title: The exemptions of the index’s own workflows
18a04833e85d.content: .github/workflows/ belongs to the index, so the steps CI runs there that the local gate set does not are exempted HERE, under gateExemptions.steps, each with a kind and a reason (GateExemptionsSchema, the same shape an layer declaration carries). They land in the same change as the workflow step, never ahead of it in a layer: an exemption for a step CI does not yet run matches nothing, and gates-workflows.test.ts refuses a stale exemption as it refuses an unclassified step. "gateExemptions": { "steps": [ { "match": "bun run cat state:push -- --id health", "kind": "ci-only", "reason": "…" } ] } . A layer still exempts its OWN scripts and steps in its own declaration.

b55c67f9d1a4.title: index.lock.json, and the legacy name
b55c67f9d1a4.content: The lock records what the declared mounts resolved to. It is generated by mount:remote and kept as a separate file. The legacy name is <root-instance>.mount-lock.json. The rules for each reader and writer: . | Writers write index.lock.json. mount:remote first renames a legacy lock onto the new name, so the old file is moved, never dropped. | Readers take index.lock.json first, then fall back to the legacy *.mount-lock.json, so downstream folios and old branches still replay. The readers are: . | mount-from-lock.ts | mountedInstanceRoots | mountedUnder in git-corpus.ts | mount:remote:check | . | Both files present is an error that names both. Two locks are never merged. | . mount-from-lock.ts imports only node:*, so it restates the rule inline and its test holds it to lockFilesIn. A re-pin ends with one commit per layer, and moves pins only forward (owner ruling, 2026-11-06, card “Pin target”, A). Every layer the change needs is pinned in the same re-pin, and the re-pin PR holds the pins and nothing else: a change that needs the new pins stacks on it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). The one exception is a change mutually dependent with the re-pin, where neither passes alone. It may share the PR, and the body says why. The rules are in remote-mount §”Re-pinning”.

c76fa6b87ac1.title: The reserved index stem
c76fa6b87ac1.content: index.config.json ends in .config.json, so a scan that treats “each root *.config.json is a harness” would find a harness called index. The index stem is therefore reserved across the board: . | rootConfigStems skips every index.* file. It is the one root scan; every other reader calls it or instantiatedHarnessNames. | findDeclarationFile skips every index.* file too. | The index schema refuses a layer named index, and hub, because that is the landing keyword. | . Do not add another copy of the scan: a new copy is how the reserved name leaks back in.

c0db71098210.title: The generated .gitignore block
c0db71098210.content: # BEGIN index mounts (generated from index.config.json — do not edit) /my-ig/ # END index mounts . The block holds one /<path>/ line per remote layer in the index, where the path is overrides.<name>.path, else <name>/. After those it lists every further layer root the lock records, because a mount’s closure can land layers that the index never names. Three things write the block: . | mount:remote | writeDeclaredMounts | index-config:migrate --write | . check:index-ignores fails when the block is missing or disagrees with the index. When an index exists, mount:remote does not append to .git/info/exclude: a local exclude rule is invisible to every other clone, so a path the committed block does not cover is reported as not ignored. Without an index, it still appends there.

505dcfc1a79b.title: Converting a checkout: index-config:migrate
505dcfc1a79b.content: bun run cat index-config:migrate # print the index it would write, and its findings bun run cat index-config:migrate --write # write it; move remoteMounts; write the block; rename the lock bun run cat index-config:migrate --check # exit 1 when --write would change anything (a gate here) bun run cat index-config:migrate --inline --write # also fold each <name>.config.json into its entry, and delete it bun run cat index-config:inline:check # exit 1 while any imported <name>.config.json remains bun run cat index-config:migrate --root <clone> # a separated repository's standalone checkout . The converter reads only the files under --root, so it runs on a standalone clone of any separated repository. | Which root configs it imports: a root <name>.config.json is imported only when name is a layer the checkout declares (at the root or one level down) or mounts. Anything else becomes an unmatched-config finding and is not imported. A repository cut from a fork, for example, can carry the fork’s own <fork>.config.json; importing it would instantiate a harness the repository does not hold. | Re-runs: it is idempotent. A re-run moves only the remoteMounts entries that the declaration has gained since the last run. An entry the index already holds identically is dropped from the declaration. An entry the index holds differently throws, and you reconcile it by hand. | .

Scroll horizontally to see all columns → . | locale | catalogues / templatesQ1: availability | entriesQ2: strings | translated | fuzzy | untranslated | officialQ3: signed off | . | ar Arabic | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | es Spanish | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | fr French | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | ru Russian | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | zh Chinese | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

Ages are measured on 2026-11-21 (UTC, the day this page was built); an instance is stalled when it is running and has not moved for more than 7 days. A finished instance is marked where it ended. Beans that no instance names are listed under "Beans in no process"; the store page has every bean. A running subprocess is followed on each instance's own page.

21932897144e.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
21932897144e.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components .

21932897144e-2.content: A WHO guidance publication on digitalising one area of a health system — an L1 publication whose body is a planning method rather than recommendations. Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. 8ec3d9e5f504.content: . | All instances | smart-base | . A document kind is a named structure of sections that a document authored with a harness follows: fixed (exactly these sections) or semi-fixed (these required, others allowed). Every kind and section names its sources.

e64064f93b5e.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
e64064f93b5e.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components .

e64064f93b5e-2.title: Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) dth
e64064f93b5e-2.content: A WHO guidance publication on digitalising one area of a health system — an L1 publication whose body is a planning method rather than recommendations. It sits within the DIIG process and should use the DPI-H Reference Architecture (owner, 2026-10-01). Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. The Reference Architecture for DPI-H calls itself "A Digital Transformation Handbook for DPI-H" and is cited here as the architecture the others should reference. semi-fixed structure · 22 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dth.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Audience and how to use this handbookaudience-and-how-to-use | required | Target users/roles per chapter and the stepwise reading path through the handbook.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng, 2. 1b6c0e8cdd4b.content: folio-assistant-core · 6 declared code directories · Files open on GitHub at the commit this site was built from. pipeline/ core-pipeline . `pipeline/qa-checkers-recommendation.ts` and `pipeline/qa-checkers-acronyms.ts`, the automated checkers `qa-checkers/recommendation-strength-resolves.json` and `qa-checkers/acronym-in-glossary.json` name (`RECOMMENDATION_CHECKERS`, `ACRONYM_CHECKERS`), and `pipeline/plugin-slots.ts`, the table `pipeline-plugins/tabular-csvw.json` and `pipeline-plugins/library-entry-arms.json` name (`PIPELINE_IMPLEMENTATIONS`). Under `pipeline/` because that is where the harness's `imports` input-site looks for a contributed checker, as for every layer. 7 files . | plugin-slots.feature | plugin-slots.test.ts | plugin-slots.ts | qa-checkers-acronyms.ts | qa-checkers-recommendation.feature | qa-checkers-recommendation.test.ts | qa-checkers-recommendation.ts | . adapters/ core-adapters . The content layer's own ContentAdapters: `document/`. Its imports into `cat-harness-tools/src/`, `cat-harness/schemas/` and `cat-harness-tools/pipeline/` are DOWNWARD and therefore legal (core declares `needs: ["cat-harness"]`); nothing in the harness imports it. Its consuming tests live in `scripts/tests/`. It needs `tsconfig.json`'s `include` entry (without it `bun run typecheck` passes while covering fewer files) and the `BUILTIN_ADAPTERS` module path, which is resolved by variable specifier, so no static-import gate checks it. `paper/` is the science layer's, in that layer's own `adapters/paper/`. 17 files . | README.md | document/content.ts | document/declared-adapter.feature | document/declared-adapter.test.ts | document/index.ts | document/intake-records.feature | document/intake-records.test.ts | document/intake-records.ts | document/paths.ts | document/resolver.ts | document/tools/_pipeline.ts | document/tools/audit.ts | document/tools/bib.ts | document/tools/qa.ts | document/tools/render.ts | document/tools/transform.ts | document/tools/validate.ts | . src/ core-src . Core's own server half: the HTTP routes that act on a folio's CONTENT — `routes/feedback.ts` (its feedback items), `routes/glossary.ts` (its glossary candidates), `routes/relevance.ts` (its bibliography relevance). The harness's own minimal folio renderer (bean ohx6, owner ruling 2026-10-10): `file-list.ts`, which renders the folio as the list of files it holds into `folio/index.md`, and the skill that says when to run it. Code and a skill, not folio content: the folio reader reads only `folio/*.json`, and the renderer skips this directory. 5 files . | README.md | file-list.feature | file-list.test.ts | file-list.ts | folio-file-list.md | . upstream/ cat-harness-upstream . The pinned-upstream registry, `upstream-pins.json` (`"$schema": "folio-upstream-pins/v1"`): one row per upstream dependency the build pins — such as the just-the-docs theme and the Bun runtime — naming the file the pin is READ from (`pinnedIn`, resolved against this layer's root), the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to the dependency and the MVP that must pass before it moves. It deliberately holds no version: that lives in the file the build reads. Read by `bun run cat check:upstream-pins` (weekly, `.github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml`) and worked by the `upstream-pin-watch` / `upstream-version-adoption` processes and skill this layer owns. Moved here from the repository root on 2026-10-06 (bean `ar1s`, phase 3: tooling leaves the root before the repo split). HERE rather than in the tool layer because this layer's processes, skills and scripts name it, and a harness file naming a file in the layer above is a wrong-direction reference (`check:reference-direction`). `code`: the checker's input table, authored beside the processes that read it, not content any reader renders. 2 files . | README.md | upstream-pins.json | .

b5a564902ed6.doc: Linked data — how a coding agent emits and reviews JSON-LD
b5a564902ed6.title: Linked data — how a coding agent emits and reviews JSON-LD
b5a564902ed6.content: linked-data · shipped by folio-assistant-core · folio-assistant-core/skills/voices/linked-data · every folio-assistant-core voice . IRI: https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/voice/linked-data · JSON-LD . The voice for a coding agent writing or reviewing code that EMITS JSON-LD: what makes the output linked data a processor can follow, rather than JSON that merely carries an @context. Six rules, each read from a held W3C text. Owner, 2026-10-01: "make sure that these issues are part of the one voice for jsonld" and "it is a voice for a coding agent, in a code authoring or review task". Every rule was found broken or fragile in this repository before it was written down (beans jcet, 9y9j): the PROV-O QA/QC reports carried prov:agent, prov:hadRole and prov:hadPlan as plain strings in all 100 activities, and the content context's @base resolves only because jsonld.js applies @base from a remote context. 7 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-linked-data at major · provenance evidence · derived from JSON-LD 1.1 — A JSON-based Serialization for Linked Data (W3C Recommendation, 16 July 2020) (2020); PROV-O: The PROV Ontology (W3C Recommendation, 30 April 2013) (2013); The PROV-JSONLD Serialization (W3C Member Submission, 25 August 2024; acknowledged, not endorsed) (2024) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | ld-object-property-is-a-link | A property whose value is a node is emitted as a link, never as a stringWhen the vocabulary defines a property as an OBJECT property (its value is another node: prov:agent, prov:hadRole, prov:hadPlan, prov:used), the emitted JSON-LD must make the value an IRI — through a term whose definition says "@type": "@id", or as {"@id": …}. A bare string under an uncoerced key expands to {"@value": …}, a literal: valid JSON-LD, but a graph in which the activity was done by the TEXT "owner" and nothing joins it to the actor. Review test: expand one emitted document with a real processor and look for @value where a node was meant. | structure · critical | Alternatively, the keyword @id or @vocab may be used as value to indicate that within the body of a JSON-LD document, a string value of a term coerced to @id or @vocab is to be interpreted as an IRI.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-053-note | . | ld-know-which-properties-are-object-properties | Read the ontology for which properties take nodes; do not guess from the value's shapeWhether a value is a node or a literal is decided by the vocabulary, not by what the string looks like. PROV-O marks each property op (object) or dp (data); prov:agent, prov:hadRole and prov:hadPlan are all op, so a role id like "user" is still a node reference. Code that decides by shape ("it has a slash, so it is an IRI") gets every short id wrong. | methodology · major | The superscripts op and dp denote that a property is an OWL object property or data property, respectively.w3c-2013-prov-o#sec-016-41-starting-point-terms | . | ld-link-is-the-node-release-address | A link names the node at its dereferenceable address; when it has none, say so instead of minting oneCoercing a bare id to @id is not enough: "owner" then resolves against whatever @base is in force, naming a node that does not exist there. Emit the node's release address — <iriBase><version>/<path in its knowledge graph>[#fragment], the rule check:node-iris enforces — resolved through the OWNING layer's declaration. When the owner declares no iriBase, keep the value as a literal and record a finding naming the layer; an invented address is worse than an honest string. | structure · critical | IRIs are a fundamental concept of Linked Data, for nodes to be truly linked, dereferencing the identifier should result in a representation of that node.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-023-note | . | ld-no-base-in-a-remote-context | Do not rely on @base inside a context that documents reference by URLA context referenced by URL is an external context, and JSON-LD 1.1 ignores @base there. Measured 2026-10-01: jsonld.js applies it anyway, so this repository's relative @ids resolve today only through that processor's behaviour; a conforming processor resolves them against each document's own location. Emit absolute @ids, or put @base in the document's own (inline) context. | structure · major | Please note that the @base will be ignored if used in external contexts.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-033-413-base-iri | . | ld-no-context-fetched-at-run-time | Hold every external context locally, pinned by hash; never fetch one while processingA context needed to understand a document is part of the document. Code that expands or verifies JSON-LD resolves context URLs through a documentLoader that serves a committed copy (with its sha256 recorded), and refuses anything else — the way publish:verify's localLoader does. A context that can only be had over the network makes the meaning of our data depend on somebody else's server being up and unchanged. | methodology · major | To protect against this, publishers should consider caching remote contexts for future use, or use the documentLoader to maintain a local version of such contexts.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-133-11-security-considerations | . | ld-coercion-belongs-to-the-term | A compact-IRI key does not inherit another term's coercionType coercion lives in a TERM's definition. Writing "prov:agent" as a key uses the prov prefix and no term definition, so it is NOT coerced even when the active context defines a term agent with "@type": "@id". Either use the defined term (agent) or define the compact IRI itself as a term. Mixing the two — PROV-JSONLD's context with prov:-prefixed keys — silently yields literals. | structure · major | A compact IRI has the form of prefix:suffix and is used as a way of expressing an IRI without needing to define separate term definitions for each IRI contained within a common vocabulary identified by prefix.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-013-terms-imported-from-other-specifications | . | ld-prov-in-prov-jsonld-shape | Emit PROV in PROV-JSONLD's shape, with its termsPROV is written with the PROV-JSONLD context and its terms: an Activity node with startTime/endTime, and each qualified relation as its own typed node — an Association carrying activity, agent, role and plan — so the context's coercions and @reverse mappings apply. The context is held locally (see ld-no-context-fetched-at-run-time). PROV-JSONLD is a W3C Member Submission, acknowledged and not endorsed by W3C; it is adopted here by owner decision (2026-10-01) because W3C publishes no JSON-LD context for PROV-O. | methodology · major | The JSON properties activity and plan map to the object properties prov:qualifiedAssociation and prov:hadPlan, respectively.w3c-2024-prov-jsonld#page-037, p37 | .

9dba0daf40f5.doc: Technical Writer — SDO register with RFC 2119 requirement levels
9dba0daf40f5.title: Technical Writer — SDO register with RFC 2119 requirement levels
9dba0daf40f5.content: technical-writer · shipped by folio-assistant-core · folio-assistant-core/skills/voices/technical-writer · every folio-assistant-core voice . IRI: https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/voice/technical-writer · JSON-LD . The voice for technical documentation of standards, software and knowledge assets, written as an SDO writes (W3C, IHE). Requirement levels are RFC 2119's, read from the ingested RFC rather than from memory, and constrained by RFC 8174: only UPPERCASE usage carries the defined meaning. Applies to drafting AND to review QA. Nine rules; five cite the two ingested RFCs, three cite the `technical-documentation` skill, a node of this layer's own knowledge graph, because a rule that cites a document it was not read from is the false provenance this schema exists to prevent. 9 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-technical-writer at major · provenance assertion · derived from RFC 2119 — Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels (S. Bradner, Harvard University, BCP 14, March 1997) (1997); RFC 8174 — Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words (B. Leiba, BCP 14, May 2017) (2017) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | tw-rfc2119-absolute-requirement | MUST, REQUIRED and SHALL mean an absolute requirement — nothing weakerUse MUST, REQUIRED or SHALL only where the requirement is absolute. They are interchangeable by the RFC's own definition, so choose one per document and keep to it rather than varying for rhythm. A MUST that a reader may reasonably decline is not a MUST; it is a SHOULD, and mislabelling it teaches readers to discount every other MUST in the document. | terminology · critical | 1. MUST This word, or the terms "REQUIRED" or "SHALL", mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-001, p1 | . | tw-rfc2119-absolute-prohibition | MUST NOT and SHALL NOT mean an absolute prohibitionReserve MUST NOT and SHALL NOT for absolute prohibitions. Do not soften a prohibition into 'should not' when it is absolute, and do not inflate a discouragement into MUST NOT because it feels important. | terminology · critical | 2. MUST NOT This phrase, or the phrase "SHALL NOT", mean that the definition is an absolute prohibition of the specification.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-001, p1 | . | tw-rfc2119-should-carries-a-burden | SHOULD and RECOMMENDED admit exceptions, and the writer owes the reader the implicationsSHOULD and RECOMMENDED mean valid reasons may exist to ignore the item — but the RFC puts a burden on the reader to understand and weigh the implications, which the writer can only discharge by stating them. A bare SHOULD with no account of what departing from it costs is an instruction the reader cannot act on. | terminology · major | 3. SHOULD This word, or the adjective "RECOMMENDED", mean that there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore a particular item, but the full implications must be understood and carefully weighed before choosing a different course.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-002, p2 | . | tw-rfc2119-sparingly | Imperatives are used sparingly, and only where interoperation or harm requires themThe RFC constrains its own key words: they are for what is actually required for interoperation, or to limit behaviour that can cause harm. They are NOT for imposing a preferred method where the method is not required. A document in which every paragraph carries a MUST has not been made rigorous; it has made its genuine requirements unfindable. | register · major | Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly. In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm (e.g., limiting retransmisssions) For example, they must not be used to try to impose a particular method on implementors where the method is not required for interoperability.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-003, p3 | . | tw-rfc8174-uppercase-only | Only UPPERCASE key words carry the requirement meaningRFC 8174 updates RFC 2119: only all-capitals usage has the defined special meaning. So 'the parser must handle this' is ordinary prose and 'the parser MUST handle this' is a conformance requirement, and the difference is visible rather than inferred. A reviewer MUST read lowercase 'must' as narration, and a writer who meant a requirement MUST capitalise it. | capitalization · critical | This document updates RFC 2119 by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words#page-001, p1 | . | tw-elaborate-consequences | State what not following a requirement costsRFC 2119 asks authors to elaborate the implications of not following a requirement, on the grounds that most implementors lack the experience and discussion that produced the specification. Generalised here beyond security: a requirement whose consequence is unstated is one a reader cannot weigh, and is the single most common reason a correct instruction is ignored. | structure · major | Document authors should take the time to elaborate the security implications of not following recommendations or requirements as most implementors will not have had the benefit of the experience and discussion that produced the specification.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-003, p3 | . | tw-glossary-terms-capitalised | Glossary Terms are Capitalized throughoutA Term defined in the Glossary is Capitalized every time it is used, so a reader can tell a defined Term from the same word used loosely. Before introducing a term, ask whether it is defined; if not, whether it is defined later, whether it belongs in the Glossary, and whether it is used in several places or only here. A term used once and nowhere else does not earn a Glossary entry. | capitalization · major | Glossary Terms are Capitalized on every use, so a reader can tell a defined Term from the same word used loosely.skills/authoring/authoring-core/technical-documentation.md | . | tw-no-repetition-logical-order | After the first draft: repetition, order, defined termsThree questions the writer runs against their own draft before review. Have I repeated anything? If so, consolidate — the same fact in two places is free to drift, and the copy a reader finds first is the one with no test. Does the content flow in logical order? If not, apply the detangler rather than reordering by taste. Is each Term defined? This is a drafting rule, not a reviewer's courtesy: it is cheapest to fix while the draft is still the author's. | structure · major | Have I repeated anything? If so, consolidate. The same fact in two places is free to drift, and the copy a reader finds first is usually the one with no test behind it.skills/authoring/authoring-core/technical-documentation.md | . | tw-link-schema-and-uml | Link the schema source and its UML when the prose names a schemaNaming a schema without linking it makes the reader guess which file is meant, and the guess fails precisely when the schema has moved. Link the source, and the UML documentation where one exists. This is the resolve-do-not-compose rule applied to prose: a written-out path is a composition nothing checks, a link is a reference a checker can falsify. | citation · major | When the prose names a schema, link to the schema source and to its UML documentation where one exists. A schema named but not linked forces the reader to guess which file, and the guess is wrong exactly when the schema has moved.skills/authoring/authoring-core/technical-documentation.md | .
