93f06e5dd4eb.title: WHO Digital Transformation Handbook
93f06e5dd4eb.content: who-digital-transformation-handbook · shipped by smart-base · smart-base/skills/voices/who-digital-transformation-handbook · every smart-base voice . The register of WHO's Digital Transformation Handbooks (DTHs) — the guidance publications that take one area of a health system from paper to digital within the DIIG process: the order of digitization, digitalization and digital transformation, what a registry is against a register, what master data excludes, and how the draft DPI-H Reference Architecture names its own layers. Derived rule by rule from the three DTHs and the draft Reference Architecture ingested in smart-base/library; every rule cites the section it was read from, and a rule resting on the DRAFT says so. 10 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-who-digital-transformation-handbook at major · provenance assertion · derived from Digital transformation handbook for primary health care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems (2024); Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture (2024); Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue (2025); Reference Architecture and Guidance for Digital Public Infrastructure for the Health Sector — A Digital Transformation Handbook for Digital Public Infrastructure for Health (DPI-H), DRAFT V1.0 (2026) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | digitization-digitalization-transformation-are-three-steps | Digitization, digitalization and digital transformation are three different scopesThe handbooks define the three terms narrowly. Digitization is converting paper records into digital format; digitalization is automating and simplifying processes WITHIN individual health programmes; digital transformation is systems-level change across all programme areas. Whether they are also an ORDERED sequence is where the sources differ, and both readings are on record as alternatives (smart-base/findings/dth-terms.md; owner, 2026-10-03, #1984): the supply chain handbook adds that digitization is the initial step and digitalization the second, and the product catalogue handbook repeats it as steps 'towards' digital transformation, while the primary health care handbook defines the same terms without any order. So write the scope a term names, and do not assert the order as the handbooks' common position. In ordinary usage 'digitalization' is a loose synonym for going digital at any scale, and the draft DPI-H Reference Architecture itself quotes the World Bank calling DPI 'an approach to digitalization' — a broad, cross-sector sense the earlier handbooks would call digital transformation. The draft also writes 'digitalisation' and 'digitisation' alongside 'digitalization'; the published handbooks use -ization throughout. Because the draft may change, prefer the published handbooks' sense and spelling. | terminology · major | In the health context, the process of digitally automating and simplifying processes to streamline individual health programmes and reduce manual efforts for greater efficiency. Digitalization is the second step in digital transformation9789240101197-eng#sec-002-glossary, pvi (PDF p. 8) | . | register-is-not-registry | A register is a list of service users; a registry is a governed master systemThe primary health care handbook defines the two words separately and they are not variants. A register is a list of health service users compiled to track care, aggregate activity or find people needing an intervention — a paper ANC register is a register. A registry is a governed, authoritative, centralized information system holding the unique attributes and identifiers of facilities, health service users, products and/or the health workforce against a canonical minimum data set; the supply chain and product catalogue handbooks and the draft Reference Architecture carry the same registry definition. Note that the draft groups the terminology service, the logical information model repository and the lifelong health record under 'metadata registries and foundational components'; that heading does not make them registries in this sense. | terminology · major | In the context of health care, a list of health service users compiled for the purposes of tracking care, aggregating activities or health outcomes, or identifying health service users who need specific interventions.9789240093362-eng#sec-002-glossary, px (PDF p. 11) | . | dpi-h-is-not-dpi | DPI-H is health-specific infrastructure built on foundational DPI, not DPI itselfRests on the DRAFT Reference Architecture (V1.0, for public comment), which may change. DPI-H names digital resources built as a shared means for multiple HEALTH agency functions; it leverages and extends foundational DPI (identity, payments, data exchange — abbreviated DPI-F) and does not replicate it. The draft is explicit that DPI-H is not a collection of programme-specific tools or point-of-service applications. Write DPI-H with the hyphen. The draft is itself inconsistent on the expansion — its acronym list and definition give 'Health Digital Public Infrastructure', its cover 'Digital Public Infrastructure for Health', and one glossary entry writes 'HDPI' — so the abbreviation, not any one expansion, is the stable form. | terminology · major | Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) refers to digital resources that are built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple health agency functions.who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1#sec-001-112-understanding-digital-public-infrastructure, p20 | . | pcposs-is-a-category-of-systems | A PCPOSS is a category spanning several application types, not one productThe primary health care handbook's person-centred point of service system (PCPOSS) is an umbrella: community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical or health record systems and personal health records are all PCPOSS. It is spelled 'person-centred' and, in that handbook, 'point of service' without hyphens (POS is point of service, never point of sale). Do not equate a PCPOSS with an EMR. The DRAFT Reference Architecture uses a different label, 'point-of-service applications' (glossary entry marked [Under review]), and places them outside DPI-H. | terminology · major | PCPOSS encompass various services and application types, including community-based information systems, decision support systems, electronic medical (or health) record systems and personal health records9789240093362-eng#sec-002-glossary, pix (PDF p. 10) | . | master-data-excludes-instance-data | Product master data excludes batch numbers, serial numbers and manufacturing datesIn the product catalogue handbook, product master data is the information that stays the same for every instance of a product: description, dosage, strength, manufacturer details, shelf life. Batch or lot numbers, manufacturing dates and serial numbers vary per instance and are transactional data. They are the identifiers a traceability discussion reaches for first, which is why they get mislabelled as master data. | terminology · major | In contrast, transactional data—such as batch numbers, manufacturing dates, and serial numbers—varies with each specific instance of the product.9789240116191-eng#sec-003-introduction, p1 (PDF p. 10) | . | generic-product-means-no-manufacturer | 'Generic product' means manufacturer-independent information, not a generic medicineThe product catalogue handbook gives 'generic product', 'product' and 'product information' a handbook-specific meaning: the general identifying details of a health product, without any manufacturer-specific information. In pharmaceutical usage a 'generic' is an off-patent medicine from a non-originator manufacturer — a different idea. In catalogue prose, 'generic product' is the level above the trade item, not a market category. | terminology · minor | In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information.9789240116191-eng#sec-002-glossary, pvii (PDF p. 8) | . | hscis-can-be-paper | A health supply chain information system can be paper-basedThe supply chain handbook defines a health supply chain information system (HSCIS) as a paper-based OR software tool, and defines an order management system the same way. 'Information system' therefore does not imply software, and an inventory of current HSCISs includes the paper forms. The handbook notes that the software tools are commonly called electronic logistics management information systems (eLMIS); eLMIS is the narrower term. | terminology · minor | A paper-based or software tool that supports the management and/or operations of the health supply chain.9789240101197-eng#sec-002-glossary, pvi (PDF p. 8) | . | national-product-catalogue-spelling | 'National product catalogue' in prose; 'catalog' survives in tool names and the 2024 handbookThe product catalogue handbook's title and body use 'catalogue' together with -ize spellings such as 'standardized' (the WHO pairing). Its own abbreviation list nevertheless expands NPC as 'National product catalog', and the earlier supply chain handbook writes 'National Product Catalog', capitalized, in its abbreviations and prose. The Product Catalog Management Tool (PCMT) is a proper name and keeps its spelling. In running prose write 'national product catalogue (NPC)', lower case, as the 2025 handbook does. | spelling · minor | This handbook complements the DIIG by providing a structured approach to implementing a national product catalogue (NPC) for standardized product master data management.9789240116191-eng#sec-003-introduction, p3 (PDF p. 12) | . | integration-is-not-interoperability | Integration is bespoke; interoperability is standards-basedRests on the DRAFT Reference Architecture, whose glossary marks this entry [Under review]. The draft separates integration — a bespoke connection from one application component to another — from interoperability, which it defines as a standards-based capability of heterogeneous systems. The published handbooks define interoperability through shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, and do not define integration, so the contrast is the draft's. 'Integrated with' is not a synonym for 'interoperable with' in this register. | terminology · minor | Bespoke capability of connecting one application component to another [Under review]who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1#sec-front-matter, p9 | . | refer-by-number-and-title-not-by-id | Point the reader to another part by its number or title, never by its machine idThe published handbooks send the reader to another part of the text by section number and, where it helps, its title: 'see section 3.2.1', 'see Table 4'. They never show the identifier a file or model gives that part. In a computable DTH every block, persona, process step and decision rule has such an id (a label like pers:health-worker or freq:FR-ID-01, a BPMN or DMN id like Task_4_1_SelectSoftwareAndVendor or Rule_DT02_01, a role code, a repository path). In reader text, write the title and link it to the part; leave the id in the link target and in the model files. Ids are fine where the reader needs them as data: a requirement code in a catalogue table, or a coded value a system stores. The same applies to tool notes such as hit policies or file names, which belong in the model, not the prose. | structure · major | Each user persona (generated previously – see section 3.2.1) should have a series of user stories9789240093362-eng#sec-013-32-get-to-know-the-users, p33-35 | .

ac40935967be.title: WHO digital health terminology
ac40935967be.content: who-digital-health · shipped by smart-base · smart-base/skills/voices/who-digital-health · every smart-base voice . The controlled vocabulary WHO uses to describe digital health implementations: what a digital health intervention is against the software that delivers it, what separates a bottleneck from a health system challenge, and how the two editions of the classification name themselves — including the first edition's title, which WHO says was wrong. Derived rule by rule from the ingested publications; every rule cites the section it was read from. 8 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-who-digital-health at major · provenance assertion · derived from Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health, second edition (2023); Classification of Digital Health Interventions v1.0 (2018); Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG): integrating digital interventions into health programmes (2020) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | cdisah-is-the-current-abbreviation | The current abbreviation is CDISAHThe second edition is the *Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health*, and the abbreviation it introduces itself with is **CDISAH**, with the leading C. Use CDISAH for the current classification and CDHI only when referring specifically to the 2018 first edition. Two things make this counterintuitive. CDHI is the abbreviation in wide circulation and in most secondary literature, so the familiar term is the wrong one. And the publication is not internally consistent: page 9 writes the bare form 'DISAH' once, while page 7 and the classification's own short link (bit.ly/CDISAH) use CDISAH. WHO's implementation authority settles it — `WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base` uses CDISAH throughout its FHIR artefacts (`input/fsh/codesystems/CDHIv2.fsh`, `input/fsh/conceptmaps/CDHIv1toCDHIv2.fsh`) and the bare form appears in no FSH or prose there. That divergence inside one publication is the plainest argument for this voice existing at all. | terminology · major | The updated Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health (CDISAH) is a set of categorizations that links how digital health interventions9789240081949-eng#page-007, p7 | . | intervention-is-a-capability-not-software | A digital health intervention is a capability, not a systemA digital health intervention is a discrete technology FUNCTIONALITY — a capability — such as decision support, targeted client communications or stock notification. The software that delivers it is a digital health application, or in the classification's terms a Service or Application type, such as an LMIS or an EMR. The two are different levels and an application typically delivers several interventions. Naming a product where an intervention belongs collapses the distinction the whole classification rests on. | terminology · critical | DIGITAL HEALTH INTERVENTION: A discrete technology functionality – or capability – designed to achieve a specific objective addressing a health system challenge. Examples of digital health interventions include decision support, targeted client communications, and stock notifications9789240010567-eng#page-024, p24 (printed 12) | . | bottleneck-is-specific-challenge-is-general | A bottleneck is specific; a health system challenge is generalA bottleneck is a gap or problem in the workflow of ONE health programme area, persona or process — DIIG's own example is health workers having difficulty tracking when pregnant women are due for an antenatal care visit. A health system challenge is the general form of that problem across any programme area, such as loss to follow-up. DIIG Chapter 3 maps the first onto the second, so treating them as synonyms destroys the step. The classification groups health system challenges into nine overarching categories: information, availability, quality, acceptability, utilization, efficiency, cost, accountability and equity. | terminology · major | BOTTLENECKS: Specific gaps or problems in the workflow of delivering health services specific to a health programme area, persona or process (for example, “health workers have difficulty keeping track of when pregnant women are due for an antenatal care visit”), in contrast to a health system challenge, which is a general representation of the problem across any health programme area (for example, “loss to follow-up”).9789240010567-eng#page-023, p23 (printed 11) | . | persons-is-the-grouping-term | 'Persons' is the classification's term, not 'patients'The classification groups interventions by targeted primary user, and the group covering members of the public is *Persons* — potential or current users of health services, including prevention and wellness. The classification explicitly notes that 'patients', 'clients' and 'health service users' have been used for this group; they are prior terms, not the classification's. Use Persons when writing against the classification's groupings. Outside that context an ordinary word is fine; this rule is about the taxonomy, not about banning 'patient' from English. | terminology · minor | Interventions for Persons: Persons are members of the public who are potential or current users of health services, including health prevention and wellness activities. Other terms that have been used to describe individuals in this group include ‘patients’, ‘clients’ and ‘health service users’.9789240081949-eng#page-010, p10 | . | state-the-intervention-challenge-outcome-triple | An intervention is stated against a challenge and an outcomeThe classification's stated purpose is to let a planner express what they expect to achieve, and its worked form is a triple: one implements a digital health intervention IN ORDER TO address a health system challenge, TO ACHIEVE an outcome. Prose that names an intervention with no challenge and no outcome has described a capability and asserted nothing about why it was chosen — which is the gap DIIG Chapter 4 exists to close. | structure · major | one may implement a digital health intervention, such as “targeted communication to persons”, in order to address a health system challenge, such as “lack of service utilisation,” to achieve an overarching eHealth outcome of “improving individuals’ access to knowledge resources and support for better management of their health”9789240081949-eng#page-011, p11 | . | digital-health-supersedes-ehealth | 'Digital health' is the current term; 'eHealth' is its predecessorDIIG defines digital health as the systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science and data to support informed decision-making. Where its glossary carries the older term it marks it as an alternative — a digital health outcome 'may also be known as an eHealth outcome', a digital health strategy as an eHealth strategy. Prefer digital health; keep eHealth when quoting a source that uses it, or when naming a national strategy by its actual title. | terminology · minor | DIGITAL HEALTH OUTCOME: The desired change in the health system or services by using digital health interventions. May also be known as an eHealth outcome9789240010567-eng#page-024, p24 (printed 12) | . | implementation-investment-and-plan-are-distinct | Implementation, investment and costed plan are three thingsA digital health IMPLEMENTATION is the development and deployment of applications or platforms with its governance framework, operational plan and human resources. A digital health INVESTMENT is the financial and human resources directed towards implementations. A COSTED IMPLEMENTATION PLAN is the document describing challenges with a financially justified deployment and monitoring plan, and it is what DIIG exists to produce. Using them interchangeably makes it impossible to say whether a sentence is about work, money or a document. | terminology · major | accompanied by a governance framework, operational plan, human resources and related activities for its successful execution9789240010567-eng#page-024, p24 (printed 12) | . | first-edition-title-was-wrong-and-is-reissued | The first edition's title was incorrect and is being reissuedWHO states that the first edition was published under the wrong title. It went out as *Classification of digital health interventions v1.0* under reference WHO/RHR/18.06 — the document ingested here as `who-rhr-1806-eng` — and is being reissued under the correct title, *Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health*. So the two editions do not differ only by content: the earlier NAME is disowned by the publisher. When citing the first edition, cite it by its reference number and say which title you are using, because a reader who looks it up may find either. Do not silently modernise a v1 citation to the new title, and do not treat the v1 title as merely superseded — WHO calls it incorrect. | citation · major | The first edition of this publication was published under the following title “Classification of digital health interventions v1.0: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health” with a WHO reference number - WHO/RHR/18.06. The first edition is being reissued under the correct title9789240081949-eng#page-004, p4 | .

4d5929265715.title: Glossary
4d5929265715.content: Derived: every term this instance's swimlanes define — the role's title and description, the lane names that bind it, and whether the term has been retired. This is an index, not the documentation. It says what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a process is for, when you would be in it, and what it is not, is authored beside it and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. Filter this table | Artefact | What it declares about itself | . | Activity logglossary-ledger.json | The agent activity log. A MECHANICAL role: it is written to at task start and task end, and emptied by an actor — one entry, all of them, or on a periodic sweep — and it decides nothing. Modelled on work-plan and corpus, the two existing stores; its skill is the contract it is held to. Its entries are held in the layer's unpublished store and never reach a published graph; the activity-log skill names the location, which is deliberately not repeated here because a role description IS published.notation role/logfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Actorbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_LogMessage/lane/Lane_Actorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Adjudicatorglossary-ledger.json | Settles a criterion whose reviewer entries disagree, and records WHY. Inherits reviewer because an adjudicator is a reviewer with one added entitlement — the adjudication permission — and the separation is the point: a reviewer reports, an adjudicator settles, and a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. The KNOWLEDGE spreads (several roles carry the adjudication skill, because each has to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint); the ENTITLEMENT does not, and lives on the actor as a permission.notation role/adjudicatorfirst seen 2026-09-22status current | . | Administratorglossary-ledger.json | Administers the role graph itself: who exists, what they may act as, and what they may do. The ONE lane whose activities change the substrate every other diagram's lanes bind to — which is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit. Declared 2026-09-20 on the owner's answer that administration is a swimlane; role-model.md's rule is that a role is never invented to make a diagram drawable, so it waited for that.notation role/administratorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_HumanAgentDiscussion/lane/Lane_Agentfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | Archimateglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/archimatefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Attestation serviceglossary-ledger.json | Signs a QA report's run hashes over an API. A MECHANICAL role, and the one that DISAPPEARS when the actor performing it cannot reach out — which is why the signing process carries a second, human lane rather than a retry.notation role/attestation-servicefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Attestationsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/attestationsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Auditorglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/auditorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Authorglossary-ledger.json | Writes and revises folio content. The position, not the person: an editor and a guideline developer both act as author when they are changing a block.notation role/authorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | The session agent doing the work. The broadest skill set here, and the one whose membership most needs auditing.notation role/authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring Committeeglossary-ledger.json | The people writing a document with its editor, while it is still a working draft: contributors who give feedback through the Contributor Feedback sheet, one change set per row, in their own Blue column. They recommend; an Editor decides, through the sheet's Ready columns. Added 2026-10-31 by the owner, so the drafting sheet names a process role rather than a job title, as the public-comment sheet names the Feedback Review Committee. The lane it binds is in folio-assistant-core/processes/content/contributor-feedback.bpmn and authoring-a-document.bpmn.notation role/authoring-committeefirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Auto docsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/auto-docsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Back-translatorglossary-ledger.json | The checker of a translation round trip: renders a sample of the target-language text back into the source language from the target text alone, with no tools and without seeing the source. It rules on nothing. Its rendering is the intermediate the adjudicator reads (untainted-verification, rule 1: neither party sees what would let it shortcut).notation role/back-translatorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Basic CDN siteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Basic cdn site (node kind)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bean notesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/bean-notesfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Binary releasesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/binary-releasefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Block kindsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/block-kindsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board positionsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/board-positionsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board rendererglossary-ledger.json | Draws a board and performs what the reader has already decided: reads each kind's declared zoom threshold and the layout layer, swaps a card for its avatar, projects an open window onto the canvas, and carries out a confirmed relocation. A system lane — it runs a fixed program and exercises no judgement, which is exactly why every decision in board-open-close.bpmn and board-relocate.bpmn sits in the reader's lane instead. It is NOT the build pipeline: it runs where the reader is, once per request, and publishes nothing.notation role/board-rendererfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Boardsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/boardsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation harness/bootstrapfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapping Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/bootstrapping-agentfirst seen 2026-09-23status current | . | Build pipelineglossary-ledger.json | Validates, renders and publishes, and watches whether that actually worked. A specialisation of stakeholder — accountable sign-off — but NOT judgementOnly: the exit criteria are a table it applies, and only the decision on top of them is the judgement (owner ruling, 2026-10-01). Never the tester and never the system under test. Bean 3o5b.notation role/certifierfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | CI cachesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/cachefirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Clinical / scientific SMEglossary-ledger.json | Reviewer whose judgement is about the subject matter rather than the artefact. Entered by DESCENDING into Process_CodeReview.notation role/code-reviewerfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Compute authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/compute-authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Consent Recorderglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/consent-recorderfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Consent Registryglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/consent-registryfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Content adaptersglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/content-adaptersfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Corpusglossary-ledger.json | The versioned content store and the L1 source knowledge graph. bf30c11e4077.doc: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
bf30c11e4077.title: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
bf30c11e4077.content: This is a contract, not an implementation. It fixes what an L1 coverage report for one publication must contain and what its numbers mean, so that two tools producing one can be compared and a reviewer reading one knows what was counted. This layer implements it: the skill l1-coverage and its script scripts/l1-coverage.ts. It was written in smart-kg, beside the L1 type graph, and moved here when smart-kg was deprecated: the type graph now lives in a layer above this one, and the definition of the check belongs with the check.

1c8fe44c5906.doc: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
1c8fe44c5906.title: The question it answers
1c8fe44c5906.content: Of the normative sentences in this publication, how many does the L1 graph account for — and for each one it does not capture, who decided it did not need capturing, and why? . An L1 graph is extracted from prose by hand or by a tool, and either way the failure that matters is silent: a recommendation that never became a node. The graph cannot report what it does not contain. This report compares the graph against the publication, so a missing recommendation shows up as a count. The words must, shall and should below carry their RFC 2119 meaning.

b71747f3b429.doc: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
b71747f3b429.title: 1. What counts as a normative sentence
b71747f3b429.content: A sentence of the publication’s body text is normative when it contains at least one of these markers, matched case-insensitively on whole words: . | Group | Markers | . | Obligation | should, shall, must | . | Recommendation | recommend* — recommend, recommends, recommended, recommendation(s) | . | Negation | should not, is not a reason, are not a contraindication | . | Permission | may be followed by one of given, administered, offered, considered, used, co-administered, implemented | . Rules that make the count reproducible: . | The list is closed. A tool must not add markers of its own. A report produced with a different list is a different report and must say so in definitionVersion (§4). | A sentence counts once, however many markers it carries. should not is not also counted as should. | Bare may is not a marker. It is mostly epistemic (“may be associated with”) and counting it would bury the permissive recommendations under background prose. Only the listed may be <verb> forms count. | Body text only. Reference lists, tables of contents, running headers and footers, and figure axis labels are excluded before matching. Table cells and footnotes are body text. | Sentence boundaries are the implementation’s choice, but the report must give each counted sentence a stable location (page, and an offset or ordinal on that page) so that a reviewer can find it and two runs can be compared. | The marker list is English. A report on another language edition must state its own list and is not comparable with an English one. | .

653e6a2b3f8e.doc: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
653e6a2b3f8e.title: 2. What happens to each normative sentence
653e6a2b3f8e.content: Every counted sentence ends in exactly one of three states: . | State | Meaning | . | captured | An L1 node carries it — a recommendation’s verbatim statement, a remark’s text, or a schedule-entry — and the report names that node’s id. | . | excluded | It is deliberately not in the graph, for one of the reasons below, and a person has signed that off. | . | unaccounted | Neither. This is the finding the report exists to surface. | . An exclusion carries exactly one reason from this fixed list: . | Reason | When it applies | . | background-fact | States what is or was the case rather than what to do — a past target reported as history (“all regions should have eliminated measles by 2020”), epidemiology, a description of current practice. | . | manufacturer-statement | Restates a product label or manufacturer instruction rather than making a WHO recommendation. | . | duplicate-of:<id> | Repeats a sentence already captured; <id> is the L1 node that captures it. The id must resolve in the graph. | . | editorial | About the document itself — “this paper should be read with…”, “comments should be sent to…”. | . | research-question | A research gap or call for further study, not guidance for practice. | . A report must not invent a reason outside this list. A sentence that fits none of them is either a recommendation the graph is missing, or a reason this contract is missing. Both go to a person, not to a sixth string. Exclusions require human sign-off. An exclusion is a decision that a normative sentence does not need capturing, and it is recorded the same way the graph records every other decision: who decided, when, and the reason. A tool may propose an exclusion; until a person signs it off the sentence stays unaccounted. A report that counts tool-proposed exclusions as accounted for has measured how confident the tool is, not how much has been checked.

03d5e2b63edd.doc: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
03d5e2b63edd.title: 3. The numbers
03d5e2b63edd.content: For the whole publication and for each page: . | Field | Definition | . | normative | Count of normative sentences (§1) | . | captured | Count in state captured | . | excluded | Count in state excluded with sign-off | . | unaccounted | normative − captured − excluded | . | capturedPct | captured / normative × 100 | . | accountedForPct | (captured + excluded) / normative × 100 | . A page with normative = 0 reports both percentages as null, not 100 and not 0: an empty denominator measured nothing. The target is 100 % accounted-for, not 100 % captured. A publication legitimately contains normative-looking sentences that are not recommendations, and forcing those into the graph would make it a worse copy of the PDF. So accountedForPct is what is held to target, and capturedPct is reported beside it so that a high accounted-for figure made mostly of exclusions is visible as such. Per-page figures are required, not optional. A whole-document 97 % hides the one page — often an annex table — where every miss is concentrated, and the page is where a reviewer has to go to fix it.

96f705150476.doc: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
96f705150476.title: 4. Minimum report shape
96f705150476.content: A conforming report carries at least the following. The field names are part of the contract. The serialisation is not: JSON is expected, and anything that round-trips to this shape conforms. publication IRI of the l1:publication node the report is about source path and sha256 of the PDF or text the sentences were read from graph path and sha256 of the L1 graph document compared against definitionVersion identifies the marker list and rules of §1 — "folio-assistant-core/methodologies/l1-coverage.md@<commit>" generatedAt date-time totals { normative, captured, excluded, unaccounted, capturedPct, accountedForPct } pages[] { page, normative, captured, excluded, unaccounted, capturedPct, accountedForPct } sentences[] { location, text, markers[], state, node? -- when captured: the L1 node id reason? -- when excluded: one of the fixed list signedOffBy?, signedOffAt? -- when excluded } . text is verbatim, as everywhere else in L1. sha256 on both inputs means a report goes stale on its own when either the publication or the graph changes, rather than quietly describing one that no longer exists.

165de1e1033a.doc: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
165de1e1033a.title: 5. What this contract does not decide
165de1e1033a.content: . | How sentences are matched to nodes. Exact substring, normalised whitespace, or a person’s judgement are all acceptable, and the implementation must say which it used. A match that was not exact is a judgement, and the report should mark it the way the graph marks inferred edges. | Where the report is stored. It is derived output about a DAK’s L1 graph, so it lives with that graph’s build, not in the layer that defines this contract. | Whether below-target coverage fails a build. That is the consuming project’s policy. This contract only makes the number mean the same thing everywhere it is computed. | .

33c18b14ea39.doc: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
33c18b14ea39.title: L1 publication coverage — the report contract
33c18b14ea39.content: ← All methodologies . l1-coverage — declared by folio-assistant-core — cited, not ingested . Applies when. An L1 extraction of a publication has been made and must be shown not to have dropped anything normative. Use it to say what a coverage report must contain and what its numbers mean, so two tools’ reports compare and a reviewer knows what was counted. The skill l1-coverage runs it. Origin. The coverage contract written for folio-assistant#2406 (FR-009) as docs/COVERAGE.md in litlfred/smart-kg (main, 0e11ce1), the L1 type graph’s repository. smart-kg was deprecated on 2026-10-16 and its schema moved to the WHO SMART layer that mounts this one; this layer, which implements the check, took the contract with it (folio-assistant#3108). Substance unchanged: the marker list (§1) and the exclusion reasons (§2) are as written there. Node file: l1-coverage.md .

d93f2317fc8c.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
d93f2317fc8c.title: Doc-Researcher
d93f2317fc8c.content: Two modules, and the paper’s own claim is that the second cannot work without the first: “effective document research requires not just better retrieval, but fundamentally deep parsing that preserve multimodal integrity and support iterative research.” .

97db13915320.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
97db13915320.title: 1 — Parsing produces FOUR granularities, not one
97db13915320.content: The part worth taking, and the part this checkout is furthest from. A document is parsed once into layout elements — text, table, figure, equation — each carrying its page and bounding box. Then it is assembled at four levels: chunk (layout-aware merges within section boundaries), page (all elements of a page, or its raw screenshot), full (everything), and summary (an LLM summary of the full text). The four exist so that a later step can CHOOSE. That is the whole mechanism: a broad question is answered from summaries, a specific one from chunks, and the choice is made per query rather than fixed by the pipeline. A corpus parsed at one granularity has made that choice for every question in advance. Visual elements are converted to text once, at parse time, rather than on every retrieval — tables and figures to both a coarse summary and a fine description, equations to LaTeX. The paper’s reason is cost, and it is worth restating as a design rule: a conversion that will be needed many times is done at write time.

b3dd5b61c8e2.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
b3dd5b61c8e2.title: 2 — Research is four roles and a sufficiency threshold
b3dd5b61c8e2.content: | role | what it does | . | Planner | filters the corpus against document summaries, picks the granularity, and decomposes the question into sub-queries | . | Searcher | retrieves for one sub-query at the chosen granularity | . | Refiner | deduplicates and filters what came back to what is actually relevant | . | Reporter | synthesises the accumulated evidence, with citations to page and bounding box | . The loop is Search → Refine → Evaluate, and it is the evaluation that makes it a method rather than a habit: a sufficiency measure σ over everything accumulated so far, against the original question, with the loop continuing until σ ≥ τ or t = T_max. Sub-queries are re-derived each iteration rather than fixed at the start. Both stopping conditions are load-bearing. Threshold alone never terminates on a question the corpus cannot answer; iteration cap alone stops an answerable question early. A loop with only one of them is a different and worse method.

77455c71f647.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
77455c71f647.title: What the paper measured, and what it did not
77455c71f647.content: Measured, on M4DocBench — 158 expert-annotated questions over 304 documents, built by the same authors: 50.6% accuracy, which they report as 3.4× the best baseline they tried. Planner filtering reduced the search space by 60–80% “while maintaining high recall”. Not measured, and it matters for adoption here: the benchmark is the authors’ own, so the headline ratio compares their system against baselines on ground they chose. 50.6% is also the absolute number — on a benchmark built to be answerable, roughly half the questions are not answered correctly. Neither observation makes the METHOD wrong; both make “3.4×” the wrong thing to quote, and this node quotes the structure instead.

a071d813a6ed.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
a071d813a6ed.title: What this checkout already does, and where it differs
a071d813a6ed.content: methodology-adoption §”Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools” requires this comparison before any tool is proposed. Read from the pipeline, not assumed: . | the method asks for | this checkout has | gap | . | layout-aware parse with page + bbox provenance | pdf-structure.py → structure.json, images placed with page ids | none of substance | . | visual elements described once at parse time | pdf-images.py + the image-verdict and narrative state machine, where an agent drafts and only a person confirms | stricter here, deliberately — see below | . | four granularities {chunk, page, full, summary} | l1-blocks.ts produces blocks; sections exist; no summary level and no per-query granularity choice | the real gap | . | retrieve text-only / vision-only / hybrid | not modelled | open | . | Planner / Searcher / Refiner / Reporter with a sufficiency threshold | not modelled as a process | the second real gap | . Where this checkout is STRICTER, and should stay so. The paper generates figure descriptions with a VLM and uses them. Here, a description an agent wrote is a draft and only a person may confirm it, because — in apply-image-verdicts.ts’s words — “an uncited narrative is indistinguishable from a transcription of the source, and the two have very different standing.” Adopting the method must not quietly adopt machine descriptions as fact. The four-granularity idea is separable from that and is what is worth taking.

c2fcbdee259a.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
c2fcbdee259a.title: What this checkout holds, and what it does not
c2fcbdee259a.content: The paper is at library/arxiv-2510.21603v1 and promoted, L1 complete: 24 chapters read from the embedded outline, and fifty images each carrying a description drafted from inspection. evidence: points at it. It took a day and a correction to get there, and the correction is the part worth reading.

735282670bd9.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
735282670bd9.title: CORRECTED 2026-09-24 — the first reading of those 383 was wrong
735282670bd9.content: This section said the 383 were “fragments of one composite architecture figure”, “many byte-identical in size”, and that writing 383 descriptions “would be the fabrication document-image.ts’s inspection basis exists to refuse.” All three claims were wrong, and they were wrong in the way that matters: they were inferred from counts and file sizes rather than from looking at the images. Looking at them: . | They are clip-art icons — a newspaper, a picture placeholder, and so on: the icons the paper’s Figure 1 uses to depict document types flowing through its pipeline. Distinct, meaningful, individually describable. | 383 placements are 50 DISTINCT images by content hash. Page 3’s 335 are 22 distinct, each placed about fifteen times. | . So the defect is not fragmentation of a composite. It is that the extractor emits one entry per placement rather than per distinct image. And the conclusion that followed from the wrong reading does not hold: describing 50 images is ordinary work, not fabrication. This document is promotable once the duplicates are collapsed. Bean j820 carries the measurement across all 29 ingested documents, including the same ratio in three other entries (9789241509510-eng 161→102, 9789241511766-eng 99→44, arxiv-2312.07755v1 84→28). It was a general extractor defect with a mechanical fix, and issue #1234 shipped it: pdf-images.py now emits one entry per distinct image, keyed on the PDF’s own xref, with every placement recorded in placements[]. Each of the fifty was then opened and described. Four are logo — the Word, PowerPoint, Excel and Wikipedia marks, stock glyphs rather than content the authors drew. Every narrative is a draft: only a person may confirm one, which is the rule this node argues for two sections above. Why the wrong reading is left on the record rather than deleted. It is the exact failure this node warns about two sections above, committed by the node itself: a description asserted from measurement rather than from inspection. Two file reads falsified it. That is worth more as a worked example than as a clean paragraph.

55cb3c3e72f9.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
55cb3c3e72f9.title: Where this rendering stops
55cb3c3e72f9.content: . | No implementation is adopted. MinerU, Qwen2.5-VL and UniMERNet are the paper’s tools, not obligations; methodology-adoption is explicit that the process is extracted and the tools chosen separately. | M4DocBench is not adopted. A benchmark of 158 questions over somebody else’s 304 documents measures their corpus, not this one. | The retrieval paradigms are recorded, not chosen. Text-only, vision-only and hybrid are a real trade-off, and nothing here has measured which suits a folio corpus. Choosing one from the paper’s numbers would be adopting a result obtained on other documents. | σ is not defined here. The paper gives sufficiency a symbol and a threshold and does not say how it is computed. That is the load-bearing quantity in the whole loop, and this node will not invent one. | .

996c70c23406.doc: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
996c70c23406.title: Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold
996c70c23406.content: ← All methodologies . doc-researcher — declared by folio-assistant-core — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A question must be answered from documents this folio has ingested, and one retrieval pass will not do it. Use it when the answer is spread across several documents, or across text and figures within one, or when the asker will follow up. It answers how to search a corpus you already hold, never what to hold — library-ingestion and the L1 completeness gate answer that, and this method assumes their output. Do NOT reach for it for a single lookup in a known document. The loop below costs iterations, and a method whose cheapest path is more expensive than reading the page is the wrong method. Origin. Kuicai Dong, Shurui Huang, Fangda Ye, Wei Han, Zhi Zhang, Dexun Li, Wenjun Li, Qu Yang, Gang Wang, Yichao Wang, Chen Zhang and Yong Liu, “Doc-Researcher: A Unified System for Multimodal Document Parsing and Deep Research” (arXiv:2510.21603v1, Huawei Technologies, 24 October 2025). Open access. THE PRIMARY IS HELD AND PROMOTED, at library/arxiv-2510.21603v1, which is what evidence: below points at. It was staged and unpromotable for a day: the extractor reported 383 images, 335 of them on page 3, and its image-descriptions requirement could not be met. It holds fifty. See §”What this checkout holds” — the first reading of those 383 was wrong, and the correction is kept there rather than tidied away. It is a SYSTEM paper reporting one implementation against a benchmark its own authors built, so what is adopted below is the METHOD, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2510.21603v1 | . Node file: doc-researcher.md .

c5d6491155e1.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
c5d6491155e1.title: Skill-pipeline subject indexing: decompose the cataloguer’s stages and validate each
c5d6491155e1.content: Adopted 2026-09-26 (work item 0js9). All three sources were ingested through the library pipeline, and the primary was read whole before this node was written.

f9c079689741.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
f9c079689741.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
f9c079689741.content: Prior systems found the right topics and still got the headings wrong. The failures were in applying the rules, and a single prompt gives rule application nowhere to happen. The source reviews the earlier LLM studies and states the diagnosis directly (its section “Present Contribution”): the documented accuracy failures “are not primarily failures of topic identification — they are failures of rule application”. The models “produce unauthorized heading forms, omit required subdivisions, use deprecated subfield practices, and fail to verify headings against authority files”, and every prior study “treats subject assignment as a single-step task”. The remedy is structural. A professional cataloguer works through distinct stages, so the pipeline gives each stage its own skill, and each skill passes a structured intermediate output to the next. The source’s own framing is “an externalized, architecturally enforced form of chain-of-thought reasoning”: the intermediate outputs are “inspectable and correctable at each step before proceeding to the next”, and that is what a single prompt “cannot” provide.

31212c86326b.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
31212c86326b.title: The four stages, as the source defines them
31212c86326b.content: Section “The Four-Skill Pipeline” and its Figure 1. Each stage names the policy it encodes, which is the point: every stage is small enough to be checked against its own source document. | # | stage | receives → emits | what it encodes | . | 1 | Conceptual analysis | title, abstract, table of contents → an aboutness statement and a flat list of candidate concepts, each justified | Wilson’s four methods of subject determination (purposive, figure-ground, objective, cohesion), Langridge’s three questions, the Joudrey–Taylor framework, via Holley & Joudrey’s review | . | 2 | Quantitative filtering | concept list → an ordered list of candidate headings, each with its intended MARC field | SHM H 180: the 20 % rule, the rule of three, specificity, depth of indexing; H 80: order by predominance; the 2026 LC genre/form policy | . | 3 | Authority validation | candidates → authorised forms, with variants redirected through their UF references | a local index over the LCSH and LCGFT authority files; a live query against LCNAF for names; H 830 for geographic subdivision | . | 4 | Field synthesis | validated headings → MARC 21 6xx fields | H 1075 subdivision order, H 830 indirect geographic subdivision, H 405 and H 430 for name headings, J 105 and J 110 for genre/form | . Two design choices inside the stages are part of the method, not details: . | Stage 1 over-generates on purpose. The source: “The skill intentionally over-generates at this stage — filtering is deferred to Skill 2.” Recall is one stage’s job and precision is the next stage’s. A stage 1 that filtered as it went would be doing stage 2’s job with none of stage 2’s rules. | Authority validation is a lookup, not a judgement. Stage 3 asks whether each candidate exists as an authorised form in the file. It does not ask the model whether the candidate looks authorised. That makes it the one stage whose output is deterministic given its input. | .

d575af30fbe8.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
d575af30fbe8.title: How the skills were made: the construction discipline is part of the method
d575af30fbe8.content: Section “Source Material and Skill Construction”: each of eleven LC policy documents and one review article was “read in full and its normative content — rules, exceptions, decision criteria, and worked examples — was translated into structured instructions”. The resulting skills “are not simply prompts; they are multi-section documents that define terminology, enumerate decision steps, specify output formats, and include validation checks.” . This is what makes the method survive a change of vocabulary. The pipeline shape stays fixed, and moving to another vocabulary means re-reading that vocabulary’s policy manual into the same four stages. The source names MeSH, AAT and FAST as the next candidates. A stage whose instructions cannot be traced back to a clause in the vocabulary’s own policy is not this method.

300b548d5cc3.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
300b548d5cc3.title: What it refuses
300b548d5cc3.content: . | Never go from the work to the finished fields in one pass. That is the failure the method exists to correct. | Never rely on the model’s internalised knowledge of the vocabulary. The source contrasts itself with single-prompt approaches on exactly this point: it “explicitly encodes SHM rules at each stage rather than relying on the model’s internalized knowledge of LCSH conventions”. | Never emit a heading that stage 3 did not find in the authority file. If a validator is never allowed to say no, the stage is only there for show. | Never ship the output as final. The source’s conclusion: the output “would serve as a draft for review by a subject cataloger rather than as a final product, consistent with the human-in-the-loop workflow advocated throughout the literature”. | Never read a difference from an existing record as an error. The source’s baseline records “may reflect subject indexing decisions made years or decades ago — potentially under different LC policies”. Its largest systematic difference, genre/form in 655 fields rather than as $v subdivisions, is the pipeline applying the current policy correctly. | .

4e64078a064b.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
4e64078a064b.title: The parallel tracks, and why they are not this node
4e64078a064b.content: methodology-adoption: parallel tracks are recorded, not blended. Two ingested sources take a different route to the same task. Each is recorded here as it presents itself. Trained extreme multi-label classification, with LLMs in support (Annif, arXiv:2504.19675v2). A toolkit of XMTC backends is trained on catalogued records, and its suggestions are merged by ensemble. Omikuji uses partitioned label trees; MLLM does lexical matching; XTransformer is a fine-tuned transformer. Language models are used around the classifier and do no classifying themselves: they translate records between languages and generate synthetic training records. It placed first in the task’s all-subjects quantitative ranking. It needs a large body of already catalogued records to train on. Chow names this as the line: the skill pipeline “does not require training data or corpus-level pattern learning”. Use Annif’s track where that corpus exists and the vocabulary’s policy is not written down in a form a stage could encode. Retrieve, then let a model judge each candidate (Homa / OntoAligner, arXiv:2504.21474v1). Subject indexing is recast as ontology alignment: embed the record, retrieve the top 30 subjects by cosine similarity, and ask a small fine-tuned model whether each one matches. The authors report that recall held up and precision did not: “the system retrieves a broad set of candidate subjects, but many are not relevant”. The retrieval step does real work. What this track lacks is any stage that applies the vocabulary’s rules: nothing in it filters by policy, orders by predominance, or constructs a subdivided heading. For a flat vocabulary that may not matter. For LCSH, it is exactly the gap Chow diagnoses. Neither is refused as wrong. They answer the same question under different conditions, and which one applies depends on the context. Composing them into “Annif’s candidates, filtered by Chow’s stage 2” would be a house method that cites nobody.

e2ea7ab532f7.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
e2ea7ab532f7.title: Against hybrid-llm-deterministic
e2ea7ab532f7.content: These are parallel nodes, and the difference is worth stating because the two look alike. hybrid-llm-deterministic has the model emit a rule that machinery then executes. The model never touches the data at scale, because a generated result would have to be checked item by item. This method has the model emit results, the headings themselves, and checks each one. That is sound here, and it is sound for a reason the other node does not cover: checking a result costs one authority-file lookup when the answer must come from a closed, enumerable vocabulary. The expensive per-item verification that the rule/result inversion avoids becomes a membership test here. Where results come from an open space, that argument fails and hybrid-llm-deterministic is the node to reach for.

8df5f9942f61.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
8df5f9942f61.title: Where this rendering stops
8df5f9942f61.content: methodology-adoption step 2 requires both halves, so both are given here. Adopted: the diagnosis (rule application, not topic identification); the decomposition into four stages, each with a structured output; the over-generate-then-filter split; authority validation as a lookup; the construction discipline of reading each policy document into a stage; and the refusals above. Not adopted, and deliberately: every tool in the paper. Claude Code, its skill file format, the local TF-IDF index over NDJSON dumps from id.loc.gov, the LC suggest2 API, and MARC 21 as the output encoding are one instantiation. The owner’s instruction on ingesting a tool paper, 2026-09-23: “do not need to match tools in paper, start with process, determine most appropriate tools (known or which can be added).” The same holds for the specific LCSH rules: they are the content of stages 2–4 for LCSH, and another vocabulary’s policy supplies its own. Not assessed: the source’s evaluation is ten titles, one or two per discipline, compared with existing Harvard records along four dimensions. The source calls the comparison “interpretive rather than strictly quantitative” and says ten comparisons “are insufficient for statistical generalization”. No claim about how well this method performs rests on this node. It also cites a 26–35 % alignment figure for single-prompt approaches from Tang & Jiang (2025). That paper is not ingested here, so the figure is second-hand and is not repeated as a finding. Named by the source as open, and left open here: under-subdivision (geographic $z and chronological $y), choosing among overlapping authorised headings, the missing step of consulting peer records for the same ISBN, and overlapping population groups in conceptual analysis. These are the source’s own stated limitations (section “Limitations and Areas for Improvement”). They are listed so that a skill built on this node does not rediscover them.

de3818824997.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
de3818824997.title: How this platform applies it
de3818824997.content: It does not apply it yet, and says so. No skill here assigns controlled vocabulary terms. Library entries produced by the L1 ingest (epic slw1) carry structure, sections, images and labels, but no subject field. This node exists so that the day one is added, the method is chosen by adoption and not improvised. A skill that implements it names this node and does not restate it.

e2449268ea7e.doc: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
e2449268ea7e.title: Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectable
e2449268ea7e.content: ← All methodologies . skill-pipeline-subject-indexing — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Assigning terms from a closed, rule-governed controlled vocabulary to a work: deciding what it is about and saying so in the vocabulary’s own authorised form. Use it when the vocabulary comes with a written policy manual (LCSH has the Subject Headings Manual; MeSH, AAT and FAST are the source’s own named candidates) and an authority file that can be queried, and a wrong but plausible term would be acted on in cataloguing, retrieval or linking. It answers how to produce the assignment. It does not answer how to tell whether an assignment is good: that is consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation, which is a parallel node and is not folded into this one. Not for choosing between options (kepner-tregoe), a recurring decision rule (dmn), or making a model emit a rule instead of a result (hybrid-llm-deterministic); §”Against hybrid-llm-deterministic” explains why the last is a separate method and not this one’s parent. Not for free keywording with no vocabulary to validate against, because the authority step is what the method rests on. Origin. Eric H. C. Chow, “A Skill-Based Agentic Pipeline for Library of Congress Subject Indexing” (arXiv:2605.03537v1), School of Humanities, The University of Hong Kong. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. The method is rendered from that paper alone. Two parallel tracks, both entrants in SemEval-2025 Task 5, were ingested beside it and read so that §”The parallel tracks, and why they are not this node” rests on the papers and not on how Chow summarises them: Suominen, Inkinen & Lehtinen, “Annif at SemEval-2025 Task 5: Traditional XMTC augmented by LLMs” (arXiv:2504.19675v2), National Library of Finland; and Bayrami Asl Tekanlou et al., “Homa at SemEval-2025 Task 5: Aligning Librarian Records with OntoAligner for Subject Tagging” (arXiv:2504.21474v1).
