87e2725b3098.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
87e2725b3098.title: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
87e2725b3098.content: ← All methodologies . hybrid-llm-deterministic — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. An agent must produce an artefact that something downstream will act on. Use it when a language model is in the loop and a wrong output would be acted on rather than merely read — a schema, a mapping, a classification, a branch, a judgement. It answers how to get the output safely, never which option to choose: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, who is involved is raci, and situation analysis is swot. Those pick an answer; this one constrains how an answer is produced. Not applicable where no model is involved, and unnecessary where the output is only ever read by a person who will notice it is wrong. Origin. Felix Neubauer, Jürgen Pleiss and Benjamin Uekermann, “AI-assisted JSON Schema Creation and Mapping” (arXiv:2508.05192v2), University of Stuttgart. The authors’ own word for it is a “hybrid approach that combines large language models (LLMs) with deterministic techniques”. Open access, read whole and ingested here — unlike most nodes in this graph, the primary IS held. It is a tool paper reporting one implementation (MetaConfigurator), so what is adopted below is the METHOD it generalises, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2508.05192v2 | . Applied by skills: . | deterministic-and-agentic | . Node file: hybrid-llm-deterministic.md .

24bb51c6187e.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
24bb51c6187e.title: RACI — involvement, in four kinds
24bb51c6187e.content: Adopted on the owner’s ruling, 2026-09-22 (work item 2xfl): RACI is a methodology, not a house practice, so it has a node here. Until that ruling it existed only as a skill, and the methodology graph reported five nodes where a reader might reasonably expect it to report this one too.

de8af9899bd8.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
de8af9899bd8.title: ⚠ The cited source backs ONE sentence of this node, and nothing else
de8af9899bd8.content: evidence points at Dusengumuremyi (2026), ingested 2026-09-23. It earns its place only as a secondary rendering of the four roles — its §2.1, verbatim from sections/page-002.md: . a classic project management instrument delineating four roles: Responsible (doer), Accountable (owner), Consulted (input provider), and Informed (notified). Everything else in that paper is rejected, and the rejection is load-bearing rather than fastidious. Its own Data Availability statement reads “No new datasets were generated or analyzed during this study” while its abstract claims 1,247 decision events and its §4.1 reports t(1245)=47.3, p<.001; its abstract’s headline 92.4 % detection rate appears nowhere in its findings, which say 78.4 %; and its running head claims Journal of International Business Studies “Vol. 1, 2026” while its own reference list cites that journal at vol. 53 in 2022. Work item thb1 holds the full assessment with every item checkable against the ingested pages. So: cite this source for the four letters. Never cite it for a claim about what RACI achieves. No efficacy, latency, error-rate or risk-detection statement anywhere in this repository may rest on it. That split is why evidence here is not the same kind of backing swot has. swot rests on two sources that survive reading whole; this rests on one paragraph of one paper that does not. check:methodology-evidence counts nodes with a resolvable source and will now count this one — the axis measures whether a citation resolves, not whether a reader would accept it, and conflating those is what this box exists to prevent.

09d4d8499523.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
09d4d8499523.title: The four letters
09d4d8499523.content: | letter | means | direction | . | Responsible | does the work | may be several | . | Accountable | carries the decision; answers for the outcome | exactly one | . | Consulted | asked for input before | two-way | . | Informed | told after | one-way | . The axis that makes it a method rather than a list is time and direction: C happens before and is a conversation; I happens after and is a broadcast. Collapsing them turns consultation into notification, which is the failure the letters exist to keep apart.

4f4b63219fb5.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
4f4b63219fb5.title: Exactly one Accountable
4f4b63219fb5.content: The method’s central constraint, and the one most often broken in practice. A chart with two A’s does not record a shared decision — it records that nobody established who answers for the outcome, and it reads as complete while doing so. Zero is also a breach, once a row claims anything at all. A half-filled row is worse than an empty one for the same reason: the chart looks answered. A row where the same party is both Accountable and Consulted is not a row with two facts in it. Asking yourself is not consultation, and that pairing is how consulted becomes a formality while the chart still reads complete.

f899328cbd28.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
f899328cbd28.title: What RACI is not
f899328cbd28.content: . | Not a decision method. A is who answers for a decision, not how it is reached. Reaching it is kepner-tregoe or dmn; recording it is madr. | Not an approval gate. Answering for an outcome and signing off on one are different acts, and a method that conflated them would let a chart stand in for a gate. | Not a permission model. What a party may do in general is a different question from who is involved in this activity, and the two cross-cut. | Not a party registry. RACI names roles in rows; it does not establish who exists. Something else has to say that first. | .

9b71c4d9884d.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
9b71c4d9884d.title: The primary is still not held
9b71c4d9884d.content: A secondary rendering is cited above; the primary is not, and the gap has narrowed rather than closed. literature-search’s outcome 3, recorded so the next agent does not repeat the search: nothing was found because nothing could be fetched. Measured 2026-09-22 — doi.org, pmi.org and every open-access aggregator fail through this container’s proxy; only raw.githubusercontent.com answers. Candidates worth fetching, unverified and listed as leads rather than as provenance: . | candidate | why it is a candidate | access | . | PMI, PMBOK Guide — the responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) | the most commonly cited formal treatment | not open access | . | The Linear Responsibility Chart literature (Cleland & King and successors) | commonly named as the earlier form RACI descends from | books, not open access | . For both, the commonly cited sources are books and paid standards, so no open-access primary exists to fetch, and closing the gap needed either a copy or a decision to render from an open secondary — the route swot took. The owner made that decision for RACI on 2026-09-23. kepner-tregoe is still in the bucket, and the same two exits are still open to it.

400040ca9841.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
400040ca9841.title: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways

e994059828cc.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
e994059828cc.title: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM)
e994059828cc.content: Adapted from the Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII) and PATH. The harness’s CRDM requirements workflow (crdm-requirements-workflow (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) and specification template (crdm-requirements-template) adapt PHII’s Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) and PATH’s 2012 application of CRDM to health information systems, combining their process-centric requirements method with the platform’s own agentic facilitation, codebase impact analysis, work-plan decomposition, and pull-request sign-off gates. | Canonical SKOS glossary concept: https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/glossary/platform/collaborative-requirements-development-methodology (docs/assets/glossary/cat-harness--platform.skos.jsonld) | . | Ingested source | What it establishes | Library entry | . | PHII (2021/2023), Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems (https://phii.org/crdm/, 10 pp.) | The three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, and swimlane Task Flow Diagrams | library/phii-2023-crdm | . | PHII (2016/2021), 5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (EHR Toolkit, 6 pp.) | Functional vs. non-functional requirement grammar (“The system must or should…”), the three-level priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have), nine requirement quality criteria, and three validation techniques (Desk checking, Walkthrough, Peer review) | library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide | . | PATH & PHII (2012), Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (36 pp.) | Domain-scale application of CRDM: a four-column Process Framework (Table 1), swimlane Task Flow Diagrams across facility and community pools with numbered activity narratives (Appendix 1), Activity-Linked Functional User Requirements (Appendix 2), and General System Requirements (Appendix 3) | library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm | . | IETF BCP 14 — RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017) | Normative conformance keywords (MUST / SHALL, MUST NOT / SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY) in uppercase | library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels, library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | .

0d393a6e9ea1.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
0d393a6e9ea1.title: 1. The PHII and PATH CRDM method
0d393a6e9ea1.content: PHII developed CRDM as a process-centric methodology grounded in business process management that brings multi-disciplinary subject matter experts (SMEs) together to document how work is performed, redesign how it should be performed, and derive what an information system must do to support that work (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 1–3; path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, pp. 4–7). 1.1 The three concentration areas . PHII organises CRDM around three sequential concentration areas (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 2–9): . | Concentration area | Guiding prompt | Core artefacts | What happens | . | 1. Business Process Analysis (BPA) | Think: How do we do our work now? | Business Process Matrix (process goal, inputs, activities, outputs, actors/roles, business rules, issues/opportunities) and Task Flow Diagrams (swimlane diagrams showing the sequence of tasks across pools and actors) | SMEs map current-state operations end to end, making implicit workflows, hand-offs, and decision points explicit (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 3–6). | . | 2. Business Process Redesign (BPR) | Rethink: How should we do our work? | Redesigned Business Process Matrix and updated Task Flow Diagrams | Before automating anything, participants examine the current-state model to eliminate bottlenecks, redundancies, policy barriers, and information gaps (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 7–8). | . | 3. Requirements Definition | Describe: How can an information system support our work? | Functional User Requirements (anchored to numbered task-flow activities) and Non-Functional / General System Requirements | Every activity in the redesigned task flow is examined to state the information system capabilities needed to support it, followed by structured SME validation (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 8–9; phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, pp. 1–5). | . 1.2 PATH (2012): domain-scale health information system artefacts . PATH & PHII (2012) demonstrate how CRDM scales across a clinical and public health domain (path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm): . | Process Framework (Table 1, PDF p. 8): Inventories all domain business processes across functional columns (Patient Administration, Patient Care, Patient Fees and Accounting, Planning, Management & Surveillance) and selects priority processes for deep modeling (sec-009-outputs-of-the-crdm-process.md). | Task Flow Diagrams with Activity Narratives (Appendix 1, PDF pp. 11–20): Draws each priority process using a ten-element notation (Pools, Swim Lanes, Start Event, End Event, Sequence Flow, Activity, Subprocess, Decision, Multi-Page Connector, Annotation) paired with numbered activity details and narratives (sec-013-appendix-1-business-process-flows.md). | Activity-Linked Functional User Requirements vs. General System Requirements (Appendices 2–3, PDF pp. 21–36): Groups functional requirements by process and numbered activity ID, and separates cross-cutting system requirements (security, audit logging, reporting, interoperability, offline operation) into a dedicated general system requirements catalogue (sec-014-appendix-2-requirements.md, which also holds the general and nonfunctional requirements). | . 1.3 Quality criteria and validation techniques . PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, pp. 3–5) checks every requirement against nine quality criteria — Correct, Unambiguous, Complete, Consistent, Ranked for importance and/or stability, Verifiable, Modifiable, Traceable, and Comprehensible — using three validation methods: . | Desk checking: Individual review of the specification against the business process models and quality criteria. | Walkthrough: Facilitated step-by-step group traversal of task flows and requirements with the SMEs who perform the work. | Peer review: Independent structured inspection by peers to catch ambiguities, omissions, and conflicts before sign-off. | .

f2b34d2ee5c9.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
f2b34d2ee5c9.title: 2. How the harness adapts PHII and PATH CRDM
f2b34d2ee5c9.content: The relation between crdm-requirements-workflow and PHII/PATH CRDM is adapts: Phases 1–3 and the SME validation walkthrough follow PHII/PATH CRDM directly, while the facilitation channel, Phase 4/4b codebase impact and dependency analysis, Phase 5 work-item and filing decomposition, and Phase 6 pull-request sign-off are the platform’s own extensions. | Workflow phase / mechanism | Relation to PHII & PATH CRDM | What follows PHII/PATH CRDM vs. what is the platform’s own | . | Facilitated elicitation channel (crdm-requirements-workflow § Core Principle) | Platform adaptation of CRDM workshop facilitation | PHII/PATH run multi-stakeholder SME workshops facilitated by a human business analyst. The harness adapts this into an LLM agent acting in the Business Analyst role (Role_BusinessAnalyst) conversing with the human SME (Role_SME) over an issue/PR thread before any code is modified. | . | Phase 1: Needs Assessment & Problem Framing | Follows PHII CRDM (Business Process Analysis — context & scope) | Establishes the business problem, actors/personas (Role_*), scope boundaries (in-scope vs. out-of-scope), and information inputs/outputs, matching PHII’s Business Process Matrix header and PATH’s process framework scoping. | . | Phase 2: Business Process Analysis & Redesign | Follows PHII & PATH CRDM (Concentration Areas 1 & 2: BPA + BPR) | Models current-state (“as-is”) and redesigned (“to-be”) workflows using swimlane task-flow diagrams (BPMN 2.0 / Mermaid) across pools and actor lanes, paired with a gap analysis table (bottlenecks, redundancies, missing rules). | . | Phase 3: Requirements Definition (Functional, Non-Functional & Data Model) | Follows PHII & PATH CRDM (Concentration Area 3) + BCP 14 keywords | Derives atomic Functional Requirements (FR-001, …) linked to redesigned process steps, Non-Functional / General System Requirements (NFR-001, …), business rules/decision tables, and domain data entities with cardinalities and validation criteria. | . | Phase 4: Impact Analysis & Effort Estimation | Platform’s own extension | Inspects the repository’s existing schemas, skills, BPMN/DMN models, UI components, pipelines, tests, and downstream consumers across 7 impact dimensions to identify breaking changes and t-shirt effort estimates. PHII/PATH CRDM is technology- and codebase-agnostic and has no code impact phase. | . | Phase 4b: Capability Area Grouping, Dependency Ordering & Formalize-First Rule | Platform’s own extension | Groups requirements into capability areas (CA-1, CA-2, …), orders them by a dependency DAG, and enforces the platform’s formalize-first rule (formalizing existing implicit behavior before adding net-new capabilities). | . | Phase 5: Work Breakdown, Work Items & Specification Filing | Platform’s own extension (+ PHII Walkthrough / Peer review) | Writes the specification to docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and upon filing to docs/requirements/<slug>.md per requirements-filing-and-organisation), decomposes work into agent work items (beans/) and human todos (todos/), and conducts the SME walkthrough on the proposal PR. | . | Phase 6: Implementation & Merge Sign-Off | Platform’s own extension | Implements approved requirements on a feature branch, publishes a branches/<branch-slug>/ preview, verifies every acceptance criterion against automated gates, and requires explicit human owner sign-off before merging. | .

981e192efbb1.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
981e192efbb1.title: 3. Priority scale and normative conformance keywords
981e192efbb1.content: In CRDM and in the harness’s requirement template (crdm-requirements-template), implementation priority and normative conformance level are two distinct fields with different semantics and different standards origins: . 3.1 Priority weighting (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) . PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 2) and PATH (2012) (path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, p. 1 / Appendix 2) rank requirements by relative implementation importance using a three-tier priority scale. The harness aligns its three priority labels one-to-one with PHII’s scale: . | PHII / PATH priority rank | Harness template label | Meaning when sequencing or trading off scope | . | High | Must-have (High / Must-have) | Essential to the core business process; the system cannot satisfy the process goal without this capability. | . | Medium | Should-have (Medium / Should-have) | Important for operational efficiency or completeness; expected in standard operation, though a temporary workaround may exist. | . | Low | Nice-to-have (Low / Nice-to-have) | Desirable enhancement that improves convenience or secondary workflows when resources permit. | . 3.2 Normative conformance keywords (SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT) . While PHII’s informal prose grammar phrases requirement statements as “The system must or should…” (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 1), the harness’s separate Conformance field (SHALL / MUST, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT / MUST NOT) uses uppercase normative keywords governed by IETF BCP 14: . | RFC 2119 (Bradner 1997, library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels): Defines MUST / SHALL (absolute requirement of the specification), MUST NOT / SHALL NOT (absolute prohibition), SHOULD (recommended; valid reasons may exist in particular circumstances to ignore, but full implications must be understood and weighed), SHOULD NOT (not recommended), and MAY (truly optional). | RFC 8174 (Leiba 2017, library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words): Clarifies that only UPPERCASE words carry the RFC 2119 normative meanings; lowercase “must”, “should”, and “may” in surrounding prose carry only their normal English meaning. | . Keeping Priority (High / Must-have, Medium / Should-have, Low / Nice-to-have) separate from Conformance (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT) avoids conflating when a capability is scheduled for delivery (priority) with how strictly an implementation must behave once it claims conformance to that requirement (BCP 14 modality).

f4cf7fe8c553.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
f4cf7fe8c553.title: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
f4cf7fe8c553.content: ← All methodologies . crdm — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Eliciting, structuring, prioritising, and validating functional and non-functional requirements from current-state and redesigned business processes before implementation begins. Use it when a capability, specification, or workflow spans actors and tasks that must be analysed and redesigned first so every requirement traces to a concrete business activity. Not a replacement for filing and lifecycle governance (requirements-filing-and-organisation), interchange standards mapping (requirements-standards-assessment), one-off option trade-offs (kepner-tregoe), recurring decision logic (dmn), or architecture decision records (madr). Origin. Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII, a program of The Task Force for Global Health), “Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems” (2021, updated 2023-08-29, https://phii.org/crdm/) and companion EHR Toolkit guide “5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide” (2016/2021, https://phii.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Defining-and-Validating-Requirements-Guide_0.pdf); applied to health information systems in PATH & PHII, “Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology” (December 2012, https://media.path.org/documents/MCHN_mhis_crdm.pdf); combined in the harness’s requirement statement template with IETF BCP 14 / RFC 2119 (Bradner 1997) and RFC 8174 (Leiba 2017) for normative conformance keywords.
