d5d658c032a0.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
d5d658c032a0.title: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
d5d658c032a0.content: The method behind classify-and-code-content, recommendation-extraction, and recommendation-scenarios. It joins the platform’s generic ontology and glossary rules — ontologist, glossary-terms, vocabulary-authority, and code-lists — with the WHO Family of International Classifications (WHO-FIC) and SMART Guidelines DAK component conventions.

82faccde661b.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
82faccde661b.title: 1. The scheme for each slot
82faccde661b.content: Every classifiable slot in an L1 extraction or L2 DAK component has an authoritative primary scheme and a local fallback or code list. Coding a slot means resolving a concept in the scheme designated for that slot, never picking an arbitrary string or borrowing a code from an unrelated axis. | Slot | Where it sits | Authoritative scheme(s) | Local representation in this stack | . | Condition / disease / health problem | L1 recommendation.population / condition; L2 data dictionary (C5) & DMN inputs (C6) | ICD-11 (WHO International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision; MMS & foundation URI) | KGTerminologySystem (#ICD11, http://id.who.int/icd/release/11/mms); DAK C5 ICD-11 binding column | . | Intervention (clinical, public-health or digital) | L1 recommendation.intervention; L2 user scenarios (C3), business processes (C4), data dictionary (C5), indicators (C8) | ICHI (International Classification of Health Interventions) for clinical and public-health interventions; CDISAH / CDHI v2.0 (library/9789240081949-eng, input/fsh/codesystems/CDHIv2.fsh, CDSCv2.fsh) and CDHI v1.0 (library/who-rhr-1806-eng, CDHIv1.fsh) for digital health interventions and system categories; WHO UHC Intervention Compendium for service packages | input/fsh/codesystems/CDHIv2.fsh, CDHIv1.fsh, CDSCv2.fsh, CDSCv1.fsh; KGTerminologySystem (#ICHI, #SNOMEDCT, #LOINC) | . | Persona / actor / occupational role | L2 generic personas (C2), user-scenario involves edges (C3), BPMN swimlanes (C4) | ISCO-08 (ILO International Standard Classification of Occupations) and CDISAH / CDHI health-workforce categories | Target guide’s personas.md (l1-scenario-vocabulary/v1), then smart-base generic personas (input/fsh/actors/*.fsh, DAK.Persona.*, input/fsh/codesystems/ISCO08.fsh), then local glossary-terms candidate | . | Medicine / vaccine / health product | L1 recommendation.intervention; L2 data dictionary (C5), scheduling logic (C7), product catalogues (library/9789240116191-eng) | WHO ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification) and ICD-11 medicaments/vaccines extension | KGTerminologySystem (#ATC, http://www.whocc.no/atc); product-catalogue attributes per library/9789240116191-eng | . | Guideline / scenario domain | L1 intake classification; L2 user-scenario domain property | SMART Guideline domain scheme (clinical | public-health | health-system-strengthening) | folio-assistant-core/glossary/guideline-domain.glossary.json (folio-glossary/v1, SKOS ConceptScheme guideline-domain) | . | Business process | L2 business processes (C4); business-process realises user-scenario edge | Target SMART Guideline’s C4 business process catalogue (business-processes.md); domain process catalogue where published | l1-scenario-vocabulary/v1 processes[]; could-not-determine with a structured warning when absent | . | Normative statement strength, direction & certainty | L1 recommendation (strength, direction, certaintyOfEvidence); EtD frameworks | GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) and RFC 2119 / BCP 14 requirement levels | smart-base/code-lists/grade-*.json (grade-recommendation-strength, grade-recommendation-direction, grade-certainty, grade-etd-criterion, grade-rating-down, grade-rating-up) and folio-assistant-core/code-lists/rfc2119-requirement-level.json | .

342d91292742.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
342d91292742.title: 2. The reuse-first precedence
342d91292742.content: An agent or terminologist coding any slot walks the four-rung ladder and stops at the first rung that yields an exact or well-scoped match: . | Rung 1 — Target guide’s own declared vocabulary (exactMatch in guide). The target guide’s own personas (personas.md), business processes (business-processes.md), data dictionary (C5) and local code lists. If one defines the concept and its scope covers the statement, reuse its identifier verbatim. | Rung 2 — Layer base vocabulary (smart-base generic personas, FSH CodeSystems, and shared code lists). When the target guide does not declare the concept, or declares it more narrowly than the statement needs (an immunization guide’s health worker cannot be stretched to cover inpatient clinical management): . | smart-base generic personas (DAK.Persona.* in input/fsh/actors/, extracted in smart-base-generic-personas.json); | smart-base FSH CodeSystems (ISCO08, CDHIv2, CDHIv1, CDSCv2, CDSCv1, KGTerminologySystem and KG*); | shared folio-code-list/v1 lists (smart-base/code-lists/*.json, folio-assistant-core/code-lists/*.json) and SKOS glossaries (folio-assistant-core/glossary/guideline-domain.glossary.json). | . | Rung 3 — External authoritative standard (WHO-FIC / ILO / HL7 / W3C). A standard clinical, occupational or ontological term not in Rungs 1–2 is resolved against the external authority in vocabulary-authority and §1 above (ICD-11, ICHI, CDHI, ISCO-08, ATC, SNOMED CT, LOINC), recording the mapping predicate (skos:exactMatch or skos:closeMatch) per ontologist. | Rung 4 — Local candidate or explicit third state (citing glossary-terms). When Rungs 1–3 hold no match: . | For a persona or domain concept: mint a local glossary entry in <instance>/glossary/<scheme>.glossary.json following glossary-terms with status: "candidate", source: "extracted" (citing the doc_id and section / quote), and emit WARNING <slot>-glossary-candidate. An agent writes only status: "candidate"; promotion to status: "authored" is a person’s, in the terminologist/ontologist lane. | For a business process: never invent a process. Record could-not-determine with WARNING process-not-determined and the basis quoting the statement. That warning is the work list for the guide or domain process catalogue. | . | .

eab9e1ffda31.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
eab9e1ffda31.title: 3. Provenance and review status on every coding
eab9e1ffda31.content: Every classification or coding link records two independent facts: . | How the coding was obtained (source): . | declared — a person acting in an authorised role explicitly stated the code or link (must carry by); | context — the printed section heading, table header, or structural container in the source document settles the classification without inference; | inferred — an agent or author read the statement text and matched it against the scheme’s definitions. | . | Where it sits in review (status): . | candidate — proposed by the authoring-agent (using terminology-lookup and classify-and-code-content); | reviewed / authored — checked and signed off by a person acting in the terminologist (or l1-extraction-reviewer) role in classify-and-code-content.bpmn. | . | .

c190751151a1.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
c190751151a1.title: 4. Adjudicating L1 coverage exclusions (l1-extraction-reviewer)
c190751151a1.content: When l1-recommendation-candidates scans an L1 source, every sentence carrying a normative marker (should, shall, must, recommend*, may be …) must either become an L1 node (recommendation, implementation-practice, remark, or part-of) or be excluded with one of the five closed reasons (background-fact, manufacturer-statement, editorial, research-question, duplicate-of:<id>). An agent may propose an exclusion in exclusions.proposed.json ("signerRole": {"role": "l1-extraction-reviewer"}) and never signs it. A person acting as l1-extraction-reviewer, in classify-and-code-content.bpmn, reads each candidate sentence in place on the printed page (sections/page-NNN.md), checks that it is non-normative under the stated reason, and either signs it (signedOffBy) or rejects it back to extraction curation, so no guidance is silently dropped.

e2e58ae792ad.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
e2e58ae792ad.title: 5. Refusals
e2e58ae792ad.content: . | Never invent a business process to make coverage look complete. When no process in the target guide or a published domain catalogue realises a scenario, the only valid value is could-not-determine with a warning. | Never stretch a narrower code as exactMatch. If a guide’s persona or a code list entry covers only part of the concept, use skos:closeMatch (or skos:broadMatch / skos:narrowMatch per ontologist) or fall through to the next rung. | Never self-approve a candidate term or an L1 exclusion. An agent writes status: "candidate" on glossary terms and leaves signedOffBy absent on exclusions; only a person in the reviewer lane records sign-off. | .

b64dca8cca00.doc: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
b64dca8cca00.title: WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding
b64dca8cca00.content: ← All methodologies . terminology-coding — declared by smart-base — source held . Applies when. Classifying and coding L1 narrative content (guideline recommendations, implementation practices, remarks) and L2 Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) artefacts (personas, user scenarios, business processes, data-dictionary elements, decision-table concepts and indicators) against authoritative vocabularies and local code lists. Reach for it whenever a slot requires a code or SKOS concept (condition, intervention, persona/role, medicine, guideline domain, business process, or GRADE rating), or when deciding whether to reuse an existing term, fall back to a generic base concept, or propose a local glossary candidate. It does NOT grade evidence (that is grade), does NOT model BPMN/DMN control flow (bpmn-authoring, dmn-authoring), and does NOT plan programme investment (diig). Origin. World Health Organization, SMART Guidelines: Digital Adaptation Kits (DAKs) (Mehl et al., BMJ Global Health 2021;6:e004908, ingested at smart-base/library/mehl-2021-who-smart-guidelines/); Classification of digital health interventions, services and applications in health (CDISAH) v2.0 (WHO, 2023, ISBN 978-92-4-008194-9, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240081949-eng/, superseding CDHI v1.0 at who-iris/library/who-rhr-1806-eng/); Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture (WHO, 2024, ISBN 978-92-4-010119-7, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/); and Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue (WHO, 2025, ISBN 978-92-4-011619-1, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/). 581a14b4f5c1.title: DIIG — the investment path from a health system bottleneck to a costed plan

c9c7a24d077e.title: What it is, in one sentence
c9c7a24d077e.content: A nine-chapter sequence taking a health programme from we have a problem to we have a budgeted, governed, monitorable digital implementation, in which each chapter’s output is the next chapter’s input.

f7a67a57c8d2.title: The nine chapters, as the Guide numbers them
f7a67a57c8d2.content: |   | chapter | what it produces | . | 1 | Introduction | scope, key terms, and when the Guide applies | . | 2 | Form the team and establish goals | roles and responsibilities; a shared statement of the programme’s needs and goals; an understanding of operations across levels of the health system | . | 3 | Identify health system challenges and needs | a map of the current state, bottlenecks confirmed and prioritized, and those bottlenecks mapped to generic health system challenges | . | 4 | Determine appropriate digital health interventions | selected interventions, an enabling-environment assessment, functional requirements and user stories, a future-state workflow | . | 5 | Plan the implementation | infrastructure; legislation, policy and compliance; leadership and governance; workforce and training; services and applications | . | 6 | Link the digital health implementation to the enterprise architecture | an assessment of the architecture, the common and enabling components (the digital health platform), and the investment linked to both | . | 7 | Develop a budget | phases of implementation, cost drivers, a budget matrix | . | 8 | Monitor the implementation and use data effectively | a logic model, an M&E plan, a culture of data use, adaptive management | . | 9 | Value proposition and next steps | the case made to whoever pays | . Chapters 4 and 8 close with a progress check, the Guide’s own gate.

599e7793e406.title: It builds on CRDM, and this platform already carries CRDM
599e7793e406.content: Chapter 3 says so in its own words: . This process builds on the Public Health Informatics Institute’s Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM), a commonly used approach for defining the problem, identifying how it could be improved, and describing how the improved process would need to function (50). — library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-043.md (PDF page 43, printed page 31), introducing Fig. 3.1. Adaptation of CRDM approach for defining health system challenges . CRDM’s three areas of concentration, verbatim from the same page: . | Business process analysis | Business process redesign | Requirements definition | . cat-harness runs CRDM (skills in cat-harness/sdlc/skills/crdm/, processes including cat-harness/processes/process/crdm-needs.bpmn and crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn), so DIIG Chapter 3 and the platform’s requirements process descend from one published method. DIIG adapts CRDM for health system challenges; it does not restate it. Where the two disagree, neither overrides the other and they are not merged (methodology-adoption: never blend two methodologies). Pick one per decision, name it, follow it.

6d36a40e4421.title: Where this adoption stops
6d36a40e4421.content: . | The annexes are named, not rendered. DIIG’s fourteen worksheets and templates (the planning and implementation charter, the persona worksheet, the process matrix, the budget template, the logic model template, the adaptive management checklist, and more) are instruments a programme fills in, not steps an agent performs. They are cited to the ingested sections. | Figures are cited, not described. The Guide’s figures are in the ingested entry as figures/vfig-p<PDF page>.png (Fig. 3.1 is vfig-p043; Fig. 1.1.1 also as SVG, by smart-base:diig-figure); where this file mentions a figure it quotes the text around it. | Chapter 5’s country-specific and intervention-specific considerations (Annexes 5.3, 5.4) are a reference table of scale, not a method. Left in the library. | .

c3d6fbe9597f.title: Refusals
c3d6fbe9597f.content: methodology-adoption’s refusals bind. The first has a concrete target in this method. Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. DIIG Table 3.3.1, Formula for scoring and ranking bottlenecks (sections/page-050.md, PDF page 50, printed page 38), scores each bottleneck on three criteria, each 1–3: . | How much impact does this bottleneck have on the process? | What is the likelihood of overcoming this bottleneck? | Is this important to a wide range of stakeholders? | . — and combines them into a Score and a Prioritized Ranking. This platform adopts the three criteria and refuses the arithmetic. Three ordinal judgements on incommensurable scales, summed with equal weight, give a number whose precision is invented. An agent applying DIIG Chapter 3 records each criterion’s answer and its reason, and orders the bottlenecks by argument; it does not print a score. The summed score is kept as an alternative: the DTH for health supply chain architecture repeats the tally in its Annex 3 (9789240101197-eng, sections/page-068.md: “Adding the scores yields the prioritized ranking.”), and DIIG Table 3.3.1 and SC Annex 3 are both recorded beside this refusal in smart-base/findings/dth-terms.md. The refusal still governs what an agent applying this method does. Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. DIIG Chapter 4 selects interventions against prioritized challenges. The interventions considered and not chosen are part of the output, with why. Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A DIIG citation with no rendered step is an appeal to authority no reader can check. Never blend DIIG with CRDM, MAPS or the M&E guide. All touch digital health implementation; they are parallel tracks selected by context, not a toolkit to assemble from.

e95bbfbeebfa.title: Its neighbours in this library, and what each is for instead

78a86a1da9cd.title: Choosing one
78a86a1da9cd.content: applies-when is what a selection question matches against, so it is the column to read first. A methodology whose applicability is unstated is one an agent picks by resemblance, which is why the schema requires the field. Scroll horizontally to see all columns → . | methodology | applies when | origin held? | declared by | . | Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against realityadequacy-for-purpose-modelling | A formal model is being built, and somebody will later ask whether it is right. Use it when the artefact is a mathematical model of a process — agents, action and reward spaces, update rules — and the question is what the model is allowed to claim. It answers what would count as this model succeeding, and nothing else. Reach for it BEFORE the model is written, because its whole force is that the purpose is declared first and the evaluation follows from it. Reaching for it afterwards turns it into a defence of whatever the model happens to do. Do NOT reach for it to choose between options (kepner-tregoe), to grade evidence, to settle a recurring rule (dmn), or to pick an algorithm (probabilistic-decision-analysis, mcdm-aggregation). It is not a decision method at all: it is a rule for judging a model, and it is filed here because methodology-adoption routes “how do we evaluate X” to a methodology node. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decideautomatic-term-extraction | Finding which words and phrases in a body of prose are the TERMS of its domain, so that a glossary can be proposed from the text rather than typed from memory. It answers which strings are candidate terms, ranked. Every output is a candidate: a person decides what is a term and writes its definition (glossary-terms: an extractor writes candidate, only a person moves one to authored). Not for assigning terms from a closed controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), not for keywords that summarise one document against the others (lsi, correspondence-analysis, the keyword graph), and not for reading definitions a source already states in its own glossary section, which are copied verbatim and need no extraction. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one scoreconsensus-grounded-subject-evaluation | Judging how good a set of controlled-vocabulary assignments is, when qualified people would themselves disagree about the exact answer. Use it to evaluate a subject-indexing system, compare two of them, or decide whether one is good enough to draft for a human reviewer. It is also for any labelling task whose gold standard is expert judgement with a subjective surface. It answers how to measure. It does not answer how to produce the assignment, which is skill-pipeline-subject-indexing, a parallel node. Not for certainty of evidence behind a recommendation (grade), and not for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe). Not applicable where the answer is decidable, meaning a single correct output a checker can verify, because then there is no disagreement for a consensus to absorb. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the countscorrespondence-analysis | The same question as lsi — which units of a prose graph are close in what they are about — when the answer must not be dominated by how LONG a unit is or how COMMON a term is. CA removes those margins by construction, so it is the method to reach for when LSI’s first dimensions are margins (a first dimension with no negative pole) or when the question is which units are UNUSUAL — outlier pages, specimen text, a list among prose. It answers which units have similar term profiles, relative to independence. Like lsi, every output is a PROPOSAL. Not for choosing between the two methods by blending them (methodology-adoption §”Parallel, not composable”), not for a controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), and not for any decision. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptationcrdm | Eliciting, structuring, prioritising, and validating functional and non-functional requirements from current-state and redesigned business processes before implementation begins. Use it when a capability, specification, or workflow spans actors and tasks that must be analysed and redesigned first so every requirement traces to a concrete business activity. Not a replacement for filing and lifecycle governance (requirements-filing-and-organisation), interchange standards mapping (requirements-standards-assessment), one-off option trade-offs (kepner-tregoe), recurring decision logic (dmn), or architecture decision records (madr). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | DIIG — Digital Implementation Investment Guidediig | Planning, costing and monitoring a DIGITAL HEALTH IMPLEMENTATION inside a health programme — from forming the team through to the budget and the monitoring plan. It is a programme-investment method, not a judgement method: it does not grade evidence (that is grade), does not choose between design options (kepner-tregoe), and does not constrain how a decision is recorded (madr). Reach for it when the question is what shall we build, with whom, at what cost, and how will we know it worked — and specifically when the answer has to survive a funder. | source held | smart-base | . | DMN — Decision Model and Notationdmn | The criteria RECUR and the inputs are data. A gateway that must branch the same way on the same facts every time. Not for a one-off judgement — that is kepner-tregoe, recorded per madr. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency thresholddoc-researcher | A question must be answered from documents this folio has ingested, and one retrieval pass will not do it. Use it when the answer is spread across several documents, or across text and figures within one, or when the asker will follow up. It answers how to search a corpus you already hold, never what to hold — library-ingestion and the L1 completeness gate answer that, and this method assumes their output. Do NOT reach for it for a single lookup in a known document. The loop below costs iterations, and a method whose cheapest path is more expensive than reading the page is the wrong method. | citation does not resolve | folio-assistant-core | . | Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs ithybrid-llm-deterministic | An agent must produce an artefact that something downstream will act on. Use it when a language model is in the loop and a wrong output would be acted on rather than merely read — a schema, a mapping, a classification, a branch, a judgement. It answers how to get the output safely, never which option to choose: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, who is involved is raci, and situation analysis is swot. Those pick an answer; this one constrains how an answer is produced. Not applicable where no model is involved, and unnecessary where the output is only ever read by a person who will notice it is wrong. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | JSON-LD 1.1 — the knowledge graph serialised as Linked Data in plain JSONjson-ld-serialisation | Choosing how a node of the knowledge graph is written to disk or published, so that it is ordinary JSON to a reader with no RDF tooling and RDF to one with it. Use it when adding a generated .jsonld sibling, a term to a published @context, a prefix, or a new exported document. It answers how a node is identified, typed and linked in the serialisation. It does NOT answer what a node means (that is the vocabulary and the schemas), whether a relation is true (uses-editorial-review), or how a table is modelled (CSVW, bound as a vocabulary, not a serialisation). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Kepner-Tregoe Decision Analysiskepner-tregoe | A decision with several candidate options and no recurring rule — a platform choice, an architecture question, which of three fixes to take. Contextual, not default: if the criteria recur, use dmn; if the question is certainty of evidence for a recommendation, use grade. | cited, not ingested | cat-harness | . | L1 publication coverage — the report contractl1-coverage | An L1 extraction of a publication has been made and must be shown not to have dropped anything normative. Use it to say what a coverage report must contain and what its numbers mean, so two tools’ reports compare and a reviewer knows what was counted. The skill l1-coverage runs it. | cited, not ingested | folio-assistant-core | . | Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared wordslsi | Finding or relating units of text that discuss the same thing in different words, across a corpus too large to read whole, where no controlled vocabulary has been assigned. Use it to ask “what else in this graph is about this?”, to propose a home for an unfiled item among existing groups, to find near-duplicates, and to surface clusters nobody named. It answers which units are close in co-occurrence structure. It does NOT answer whether a unit is relevant, correct, or a dependency: every output is a PROPOSAL a person or an agent confirms. Not for assigning terms from a controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), not for judging an assignment (consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation), and not for any decision (kepner-tregoe, dmn). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | MADR — Markdown Architectural Decision Recordsmadr | Bean context — the owner’s binding, 2026-09-20. When a bean records a decision, this is the form. Not for the decision METHOD (see kepner-tregoe) and not for a recurring rule (see dmn). | cited, not ingested | cat-harness | . | Aggregation-type MCDM — an alternatives-criteria matrix collapsed to one score per alternativemcdm-aggregation | A FIXED, FINITE set of alternatives is to be ranked against several explicit criteria, all known up front. The input is an alternatives-criteria matrix: every alternative scored on every criterion, with weights obtainable. The output is a ranking. Use it when the decision is made ONCE, from data already in hand. Choose within the family by what you can supply. SAW and MEW need only weights and normalised scores. AHP needs pairwise comparisons, which grow as the square of the criteria count, and gives a consistency ratio in return. ANP needs those plus the interdependence structure, and is the only member that admits feedback between criteria. COPRAS, MOORA, FUCA and WASPAS sit between SAW and AHP in what they ask for. Do NOT reach for it when the alternatives are explored REPEATEDLY and information accrues as you go — that is probabilistic-decision-analysis. Do not use it for a recurring rule (dmn), for a decision whose criteria are MUSTs and WANTs rather than weighted scores (kepner-tregoe), or for grading evidence. It also assumes the criteria set is complete: a criterion nobody wrote down is weighted zero, silently. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actionsodrl-policies | What an actor may DO — may this party perform this action, here? Use it when a grant or a refusal has to be written down so a machine can evaluate it: who holds an action, scoped to a process, a task or a role, and which broader action it falls under. It answers permit, deny or nobody has said. It does NOT answer who is involved in an activity (raci), which lane an actor may act in (role-model), or how a decision is reached (kepner-tregoe, dmn). It is not used here for source licences, which are recorded as SPDX ids in each library entry’s licence.json. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Probabilistic decision-making algorithms — and what their regret bounds are claims ABOUTprobabilistic-decision-analysis | The alternatives can be TRIED, repeatedly, and what you learn from one try changes what you should try next. Bandits, Bayesian optimisation and tree search all live here. The defining features are that the alternative set is sampled rather than scored, that information is gathered adaptively, and that each trial costs something — the monograph’s motivating setting is scientific discovery, “where experiments are costly”. Reach for it also when the question is not which algorithm to run but what an existing bound entitles anyone to say: the monograph is an analysis text first, so it is the right source for reading a regret guarantee rather than quoting one. Do NOT reach for it for a one-shot choice from a fixed matrix — that is mcdm-aggregation — nor for a recurring rule (dmn), a MUST/WANT decision (kepner-tregoe), or grading evidence. And do not reach for it when you cannot actually run the alternatives: adaptivity is the whole premise, and without it every guarantee in the book is vacuous. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Process model quality — what the comprehension and error research supports for BPMNprocess-model-quality | A BPMN diagram is being written, reviewed or checked, and the question is which readability rules rest on evidence and how strong it is. It is the source behind the rules in the bpmn-authoring skill and the diagram-quality checks. Not for layout geometry the owner set as house style (fixed task size, text size, right-angle edges, loop-backs below the lane): those are policy, and this methodology does not claim evidence for them. Not for DMN tables (dmn). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | PROV-O — the record of who did what, in which role, under which planprov-o-provenance | Recording, after or as it happens, what was done — which activity ran, which agent was responsible for it, in which role, following which plan, and what it read and wrote — in a form another system can read without knowing this one. Here that is the log of every BPMN task run, which the QA/QC after-check grades against policy, and the derivation and alternate-of links on the published knowledge graph. It answers what happened and who answers for it. It does NOT answer whether the action was permitted (that is the ODRL policy the record points at), how to decide anything (kepner-tregoe, dmn), or who should be involved in a task before it runs (raci). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four waysraci | Who is involved in an activity, and how. Use it when a process or a breakdown exists and the question is participation — who answers for this, who must be asked first, who is told afterwards. Not a decision method: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, and situation analysis before any of them is swot. RACI answers who, never what or whether. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apartrasci | Who is involved, when a role does the work without owning the deliverable. Use it where a separate Supportive party is real — someone who contributes effort or resources to an activity that another role answers for. If no such party exists, use raci instead: a fifth letter nobody fills is a column that makes the chart look more considered than it is. Like raci it answers who, never what or whether — a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, situation analysis is swot. | cited, not ingested | cat-harness | . | Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing processrequirements-filing-and-organisation | Filing a requirement from docs/proposals/.md into docs/requirements/.md, organising filed requirements by concern group, assigning collision-free identifiers (req: and req:#), recording bidirectional traceability (derivedFrom, dependsOn, verification), and governing requirement change, supersession, or retirement | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirementrequirements-standards-assessment | Evaluating how requirements authored or verified in the harness map to or from open industry standards, interchange formats, statement grammars, and quality models — and deciding which transformations belong in higher harness layers (cat-harness, and content layers above it) while keeping the bootstrap Requirement schema strictly self-contained and free of external dependencies. It answers how bootstrap requirements translate to ReqIF, OSLC-RM, EARS, ISO 29148, and ISO 25010, what each standard costs in serialization and semantic complexity, and where mapping adapters must live. It does NOT govern runtime execution logs (prov-o-provenance), decision table structures (dmn), software package bills of materials (spdx-3), or access policy enforcement (odrl-policies). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectableskill-pipeline-subject-indexing | Assigning terms from a closed, rule-governed controlled vocabulary to a work: deciding what it is about and saying so in the vocabulary’s own authorised form. Use it when the vocabulary comes with a written policy manual (LCSH has the Subject Headings Manual; MeSH, AAT and FAST are the source’s own named candidates) and an authority file that can be queried, and a wrong but plausible term would be acted on in cataloguing, retrieval or linking. It answers how to produce the assignment. It does not answer how to tell whether an assignment is good: that is consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation, which is a parallel node and is not folded into this one. Not for choosing between options (kepner-tregoe), a recurring decision rule (dmn), or making a model emit a rule instead of a result (hybrid-llm-deterministic); §”Against hybrid-llm-deterministic” explains why the last is a separate method and not this one’s parent. Not for free keywording with no vocabulary to validate against, because the authority step is what the method rests on. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundaryspdx-3 | Describing an artefact that LEAVES this repository so that a party who does not run our tooling can check what is in it, what it depends on, under which licences, and that it arrived intact — a release, a signed package, a published layer’s dependency set, the licences of what we redistribute. It answers what is this, what is it made of, who supplied it, under what licence, with what known vulnerabilities. It does NOT answer what happened inside the repository or who answers for it (prov-o-provenance), what an actor may do (odrl-policies), how a node is serialised internally (json-ld-serialisation), or whether a block passed its QA criteria (the house QA schemas; see §”What it refuses”). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model’s planspecification-compiled-agents | A process is already written down as a diagram, and something must now EXECUTE it. Use it when the control flow is external and authored — a BPMN process, a DMN table, a pipeline someone drew — and the question is how an LLM should act inside it. It answers where the plan comes from, never what the plan should be: authoring the diagram is bpmn-authoring, deciding a branch from a table is dmn, and choosing between options is kepner-tregoe. Its companion is hybrid-llm-deterministic, and the two are the same shape at different grains: that one has the model emit a RULE that machinery validates and runs; this one has the model act inside a CONTROL GRAPH that machinery derived from a specification. Reach for this one when the artefact that constrains the model already exists as a diagram. Do NOT reach for it where no specification exists, or where the process is genuinely open-ended. The paper’s own evaluation is scoped to deterministic workflows and says so; a setting with ambiguity, stochasticity or open-ended human decision-making is outside what it measured, and outside what this node claims. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factorsswot | Situation analysis, before a decision — never instead of one. Use it to assemble what is true about a subject’s internal attributes and its external environment, when the point is to see the field whole rather than to choose between candidate options. Not for choosing: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence behind a health recommendation is grade, and the record of whatever is decided is madr. SWOT produces the INPUT to those; it is not a substitute for any of them. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Codingterminology-coding | Classifying and coding L1 narrative content (guideline recommendations, implementation practices, remarks) and L2 Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) artefacts (personas, user scenarios, business processes, data-dictionary elements, decision-table concepts and indicators) against authoritative vocabularies and local code lists. Reach for it whenever a slot requires a code or SKOS concept (condition, intervention, persona/role, medicine, guideline domain, business process, or GRADE rating), or when deciding whether to reuse an existing term, fall back to a generic base concept, or propose a local glossary candidate. It does NOT grade evidence (that is grade), does NOT model BPMN/DMN control flow (bpmn-authoring, dmn-authoring), and does NOT plan programme investment (diig). | source held | smart-base | . | WireGen: wireframing from a written design intentwiregen | Designing a USER INTERFACE, for example a page layout, a navigation scheme or a visualiser, where the choice between candidate designs has to be reviewed and, when reviewers disagree, adjudicated. It is a design-generation and design-evaluation method. It does not choose between non-UI options (use the decision-analysis methodology) or grade evidence. It does not by itself settle a disagreement: that is adjudication. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision pointzero-trust-architecture | A participant is about to act on something another participant gave it, and the question is whether to trust it. That covers an access decision at a boundary, a hand-over between agents, a tool or a dependency graph reaching this platform, and the design of a check that decides any of these. It answers how trust is decided: never by location, per request, by policy, at a named decision and enforcement point. It is NOT a method for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe), for recording a decision (madr), for a recurring business rule (dmn), or for who is involved (raci). It is also not a threat-modelling or risk-scoring method: it says where trust is decided, not how likely an attack is. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | .

e58ca410b689.title: Where each one came from
e58ca410b689.content: The three states are different facts and are kept apart deliberately. Source held means an evidence: reference resolves to a document in a declared library — you can open it from this checkout. Cited, not ingested means the node names an origin and nobody has fetched it; that is an open question, reported by check:methodology-evidence and gated by nothing. Citation does not resolve is neither: the node claims a source and the slug names nothing, which reads as evidence in every listing and is strictly worse than declaring none. Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality . adequacy-for-purpose-modelling — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A formal model is being built, and somebody will later ask whether it is right. Use it when the artefact is a mathematical model of a process — agents, action and reward spaces, update rules — and the question is what the model is allowed to claim. It answers what would count as this model succeeding, and nothing else. Reach for it BEFORE the model is written, because its whole force is that the purpose is declared first and the evaluation follows from it. Reaching for it afterwards turns it into a defence of whatever the model happens to do. Do NOT reach for it to choose between options (kepner-tregoe), to grade evidence, to settle a recurring rule (dmn), or to pick an algorithm (probabilistic-decision-analysis, mcdm-aggregation). It is not a decision method at all: it is a rule for judging a model, and it is filed here because methodology-adoption routes “how do we evaluate X” to a methodology node. Origin. Kavya Ravichandran, “Algorithmic Approaches to Sequential Decision-Making and Social Epistemology”, PhD thesis, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago, August 2026; arXiv:2607.20636v1 [cs.DS], 22 July 2026. Chapter 5, “Why Algorithmic Approaches” — an essay inside the thesis rather than a result of it. Open access, ingested whole. The view it builds on is Wendy Parker’s (2020) “adequacy-for-purpose”, quoted directly in that chapter; the how-possibly / how-actually distinction is from the philosophy-of-explanation literature the chapter cites, and the confirmatory / applied prediction split is Elliott-Graves’. Ravichandran’s contribution adopted here is the ORDERED three-purpose taxonomy and the evaluation rule that follows from it. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2607.20636v1 | . Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide . automatic-term-extraction — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Finding which words and phrases in a body of prose are the TERMS of its domain, so that a glossary can be proposed from the text rather than typed from memory. It answers which strings are candidate terms, ranked. Every output is a candidate: a person decides what is a term and writes its definition (glossary-terms: an extractor writes candidate, only a person moves one to authored). Origin. Automatic term extraction (ATE) as surveyed by Hanh Thi Hong Tran, Matej Martinc, Jaya Caporusso, Antoine Doucet and Senja Pollak, “The Recent Advances in Automatic Term Extraction: A survey” (arXiv:2301.06767v1, CC BY 4.0), ingested whole and read. The C-value measure for nested multi-word units is Katerina T. Frantzi and Sophia Ananiadou, “Extracting Nested Collocations”, COLING 1996 (ACL Anthology C96-1009, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0), ingested whole and read; its equations were checked against the printed page, because the Anthology’s own text layer is a poor OCR. The later C-value/NC-value papers that apply the measure to terms (Frantzi, Ananiadou & Tsujii 1998; Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima 2000) are not open access and are not held. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2301.06767v1 | library/frantzi-ananiadou-1996-c-value | . Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score . consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Judging how good a set of controlled-vocabulary assignments is, when qualified people would themselves disagree about the exact answer. Use it to evaluate a subject-indexing system, compare two of them, or decide whether one is good enough to draft for a human reviewer. It is also for any labelling task whose gold standard is expert judgement with a subjective surface. It answers how to measure. It does not answer how to produce the assignment, which is skill-pipeline-subject-indexing, a parallel node. Kwok Leong Tang, “LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment” (arXiv:2606.04382v1), 2026. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. The method is rendered from that paper. The parallel design it is contrasted with is the one used by the shared task the other ingested subject-indexing papers were entered in: D’Souza, Sadruddin, Israel, Begoin & Slawig, “SemEval-2025 Task 5: LLMs4Subjects — LLM-based Automated Subject Tagging for a National Technical Library’s Open-Access Catalog” (arXiv:2504.07199v3), TIB Hannover. It was ingested and read too, so that design is described from its own text. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2606.04382v1 | library/arxiv-2504.07199v3 | . Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts . correspondence-analysis — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. The same question as lsi — which units of a prose graph are close in what they are about — when the answer must not be dominated by how LONG a unit is or how COMMON a term is. CA removes those margins by construction, so it is the method to reach for when LSI’s first dimensions are margins (a first dimension with no negative pole) or when the question is which units are UNUSUAL — outlier pages, specimen text, a list among prose. It answers which units have similar term profiles, relative to independence. Like lsi, every output is a PROPOSAL. Not for choosing between the two methods by blending them (methodology-adoption §”Parallel, not composable”), not for a controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), and not for any decision. Origin. Correspondence analysis is Jean-Paul Benzécri’s (L’Analyse des Données, 1973) and is set out in Michael Greenacre, Theory and Applications of Correspondence Analysis (Academic Press, 1984) and Correspondence Analysis in Practice (3rd ed., 2017). The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2605.03537v1 | library/arxiv-2504.19675v2 | library/arxiv-2504.21474v1 | . SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary . spdx-3 — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Describing an artefact that LEAVES this repository so that a party who does not run our tooling can check what is in it, what it depends on, under which licences, and that it arrived intact — a release, a signed package, a published layer’s dependency set, the licences of what we redistribute. It answers what is this, what is it made of, who supplied it, under what licence, with what known vulnerabilities. It does NOT answer what happened inside the repository or who answers for it (prov-o-provenance), what an actor may do (odrl-policies), how a node is serialised internally (json-ld-serialisation), or whether a block passed its QA criteria (the house QA schemas; see §”What it refuses”). Origin. The Linux Foundation and its Contributors, with SPDX Model contributions from OMG, “System Package Data Exchange (SPDX) Specification Version 3.0”, OMG formal/24-11-01, March 2025 (https://www.omg.org/spec/SPDX); its model is the SPDX 3.0.1 model (Annex A points at https://spdx.org/rdf/3.0.1/spdx-model.ttl). Licensed Community-Spec-1.0, with pre-existing portions CC-BY-3.0. SPDX® is a registered trademark of The Linux Foundation. SPDX 3.1, a release candidate since 2026-01-26, is held only as a secondary source (a 2025 conference deck, CC-BY-SA-3.0) and as its RC1 machine-readable schema queued in uploads/, NOT as a specification. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/omg-2024-spdx-3-0 | library/strauch-carbno-2025-spdx-3-1-supply-chain | . Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model’s plan . specification-compiled-agents — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A process is already written down as a diagram, and something must now EXECUTE it. Use it when the control flow is external and authored — a BPMN process, a DMN table, a pipeline someone drew — and the question is how an LLM should act inside it. It answers where the plan comes from, never what the plan should be: authoring the diagram is bpmn-authoring, deciding a branch from a table is dmn, and choosing between options is kepner-tregoe. Its companion is hybrid-llm-deterministic, and the two are the same shape at different grains: that one has the model emit a RULE that machinery validates and runs; this one has the model act inside a CONTROL GRAPH that machinery derived from a specification. Reach for this one when the artefact that constrains the model already exists as a diagram. Do NOT reach for it where no specification exists, or where the process is genuinely open-ended. The paper’s own evaluation is scoped to deterministic workflows and says so; a setting with ambiguity, stochasticity or open-ended human decision-making is outside what it measured, and outside what this node claims. Origin. Harris Borman, Herman Wandabwa, Fusun Yu, Sandeepa Kannangara, Justin Liu, Anna Leontjeva and Ritchie Ng, “Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution”, Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Published as a workshop paper at SCALE, ICML 2026 (PMLR 306); arXiv:2607.14456v1 [cs.SE], 16 July 2026. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. It is a SYSTEM paper reporting one implementation against a benchmark its own authors built, so what is adopted below is the METHOD, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. §”What the figures say that the prose does not” carries a reading of the paper’s own charts that changes how its headline numbers should be used, and it is the reason this node quotes almost none of them. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2607.14456v1 | library/kg-folio-asst-2026-09-30 | library/omg-2013-bpmn-2-0-2 | . SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factors . swot — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Situation analysis, before a decision — never instead of one. Use it to assemble what is true about a subject’s internal attributes and its external environment, when the point is to see the field whole rather than to choose between candidate options. Not for choosing: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence behind a health recommendation is grade, and the record of whatever is decided is madr. SWOT produces the INPUT to those; it is not a substitute for any of them. Origin. Rendered from two ingested sources. Gürel, E. & Tat, M. (2017), “SWOT Analysis: A Theoretical Review”, The Journal of International Social Research 10(51), pp. 994–1006, doi:10.17719/jisr.2017.1832 — a theoretical review, carrying the history, the variants and the criticism. And Sammut-Bonnici, T. & Galea, D. (2015), “SWOT Analysis”, Wiley Encyclopedia of Management vol. 12 (Strategic Management), doi:10.1002/9781118785317.weom120103 — a reference chapter, carrying the conceptual framework and the practical discipline. The METHOD’s own origin is contested and neither source settles it — see §”Where the method came from, and why that is not a settled question”. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/gurel-tat-2017-swot-analysis | library/sammut-bonnici-galea-2015-swot-analysis | . WHO SMART Guidelines Terminology Classification and Reuse-First Coding . terminology-coding — declared by smart-base — source held . Applies when. Classifying and coding L1 narrative content (guideline recommendations, implementation practices, remarks) and L2 Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) artefacts (personas, user scenarios, business processes, data-dictionary elements, decision-table concepts and indicators) against authoritative vocabularies and local code lists. Reach for it whenever a slot requires a code or SKOS concept (condition, intervention, persona/role, medicine, guideline domain, business process, or GRADE rating), or when deciding whether to reuse an existing term, fall back to a generic base concept, or propose a local glossary candidate. It does NOT grade evidence (that is grade), does NOT model BPMN/DMN control flow (bpmn-authoring, dmn-authoring), and does NOT plan programme investment (diig). Origin. World Health Organization, SMART Guidelines: Digital Adaptation Kits (DAKs) (Mehl et al., BMJ Global Health 2021;6:e004908, ingested at smart-base/library/mehl-2021-who-smart-guidelines/); Classification of digital health interventions, services and applications in health (CDISAH) v2.0 (WHO, 2023, ISBN 978-92-4-008194-9, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240081949-eng/, superseding CDHI v1.0 at who-iris/library/who-rhr-1806-eng/); Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture (WHO, 2024, ISBN 978-92-4-010119-7, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/); and Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue (WHO, 2025, ISBN 978-92-4-011619-1, ingested at who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/). WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent . wiregen — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Designing a USER INTERFACE, for example a page layout, a navigation scheme or a visualiser, where the choice between candidate designs has to be reviewed and, when reviewers disagree, adjudicated. It is a design-generation and design-evaluation method. It does not choose between non-UI options (use the decision-analysis methodology) or grade evidence. It does not by itself settle a disagreement: that is adjudication. Origin. Sidong Feng, Mingyue Yuan, Jieshan Chen, Zhenchang Xing and Chunyang Chen, “Designing with Language: Wireframing UI Design Intent with Generative Large Language Models”, arXiv:2312.07755v1 [cs.HC], 12 Dec 2023. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2312.07755v1 | . Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point . zero-trust-architecture — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A participant is about to act on something another participant gave it, and the question is whether to trust it. That covers an access decision at a boundary, a hand-over between agents, a tool or a dependency graph reaching this platform, and the design of a check that decides any of these. It answers how trust is decided: never by location, per request, by policy, at a named decision and enforcement point. It is NOT a method for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe), for recording a decision (madr), for a recurring business rule (dmn), or for who is involved (raci). It is also not a threat-modelling or risk-scoring method: it says where trust is decided, not how likely an attack is. Origin. NIST Special Publication 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, by Scott Rose, Oliver Borchert, Stu Mitchell and Sean Connelly, August 2020, doi:10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207. The primary is held, in full, at library/nist-sp-800-207: 59 pages, 55 sections and all 12 figures described. The owner supplied it on 2026-10-07 after this container’s network policy denied both NIST hosts. It is a US-government work: the PDF states it “is not subject to copyright in the United States” (p. i). Every quotation below is from that copy, cited by section id. 79662773814e.title: Skills it satisfies
79662773814e.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. review-comments . Reviewer comments on a folio’s edit-set, from a tagged pull-request comment to a structured todo on the review page. Covers the tag a reviewer types, how the comments are ingested into review-comment/1.0.0 todos, where the published review-comments.json comes from and when it refreshes, how a comment follows a renamed block and survives a removed one, who may change a comment’s status, and how to change this process. d26a7f8c8e8d.content: Read a workbook into a folio-tabular-csvw/v1 record, one CSVW table per rectangular block of cells. Dates are read through the number formats in styles.xml, not misread as integer serials. A malformed part is refused rather than half-read. 30456d2c6d95.title: Build the review sheet’s Apps Script and a document’s Config tab
30456d2c6d95.content: Builds Code.gs (--script), the one Google Apps Script every review sheet runs (from review-sheet.gs), and one document’s Config tab rows (--config), filled from the folio’s review/public-comment/sheet-sync.json, its review anchors and the draft’s pdf-line-map.json. The script keeps a public-comment review sheet’s links and joins current: each comment No. links to its comment page; Sections, Page and Line no(s) link to the page of the frozen review draft; Review Change Sets joins its comments, suggested revisions, feedback and dispositions, each No. n linking to its row; and on both tabs Agentic status lists each pull request of the change-set, linked, with its status and what it changed, from the Agent tab. It reads the document’s URLs, tab and column names and data from the sheet’s Config tab (visible, locked to the owner), which the agent writes from these rows. A person pastes the script (one file) into the sheet once (Extensions > Apps Script) and runs installTriggers; from then on the sheet rebuilds itself within about a minute of an edit, with no agent. With "mode": "drafting" in the config it builds the drafting sheet instead: one Contributor Feedback tab where each row is a change set (ids assigned by the script), Sections picked from the document’s table of contents and linked to it, and Issue and Agentic status from the Agent tab. |   |   | . | Tool | review-sheet-sync | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/tools/review-sheet-sync.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/folio-assistant-core.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | folio-assistant-core | . | source | folio-assistant-core/tools/review-sheet-sync/review-sheet-sync.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

bd6ede2f253c.title: Rank candidate glossary terms in prose by C-value
bd6ede2f253c.content: The scoring step of the automatic-term-extraction method: count the word n-grams of one or more Markdown or text files (not across punctuation, front matter or code), and rank them by C-value as Frantzi & Ananiadou 1996 define it, so nested multi-word terms are not swamped by the longer phrases that contain them. Tested against the paper’s own worked example (Table 2). Every row is a candidate; it writes nothing and promotes nothing. |   |   | . | Tool | c-value-terms | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/tools/c-value-terms.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/folio-assistant-core.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | folio-assistant-core | . | source | folio-assistant-core/tools/c-value-terms/c-value-terms.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

Check that an L1 extraction accounted for every normative sentence in its source publication — captured as a node, or excluded for a fixed-list reason a person signed off. Per-page counts, captured %, accounted-for %, and a non-zero exit below 100 % accounted-for. Generic: three input files, nothing folio-specific. Implements the methodology l1-coverage, the report contract. Source: folio-assistant-core/skills/library/ingestion/l1-coverage.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/l1-coverage/{input,output}.schema.json).

2928454aad31.title: Skills it satisfies
2928454aad31.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. figure-rebuild . Turn a figure into a computable diagram: every figure of a source publication when a folio is built from its L1 entry, and any hand-drawn figure in a folio, an IG or a demonstrator that is redrawn from a source. Every declared figure gets a block, and each one is rebuilt in the form its type calls for: an ArchiMate view, BPMN, DMN, a FHIR logical model, or an SVG generated from data, always from one schema-backed source. The PDF crop stays beside the rebuild as the cited source, and the rebuild keeps the original’s layout. The figure-coverage check counts what is missing and what is still only a picture. Source: folio-assistant-core/skills/library/ingestion/figure-rebuild.md. Also satisfied by: as-drawn-svg, figure-coverage, smart-approach-svg. 895df29e6cd8.title: Validate draft MeSH headings against NLM’s authority
895df29e6cd8.content: Stage three of skill-pipeline-subject-indexing for MeSH: look up every candidate heading of a draft (a preferred heading, an entry term, or a descriptor id, with an optional qualifier) in NLM’s MeSH authority at id.nlm.nih.gov, current year. Each candidate comes back resolved (in the preferred form), qualifier-not-allowed (descriptor kept, qualifier dropped), ambiguous (options listed for a person) or not-found (dropped). It never adds a heading the draft did not propose and never emits one the authority lacks. |   |   | . | Tool | mesh-authority | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/tools/mesh-authority.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/folio-assistant-core.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | folio-assistant-core | . | source | folio-assistant-core/tools/mesh-authority/mesh-authority.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

8db4e5cdb59f.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. mesh-subject-indexing . Assign Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) to a work as a DRAFT for a person to review, in the four stages of skill-pipeline-subject-indexing: over-generate concepts, filter them by NLM’s own rules, validate every heading against NLM’s MeSH authority with Tool mesh-authority, and write the reviewed list. c76119f22e28.title: Skills it satisfies
c76119f22e28.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. review-comments . Reviewer comments on a folio’s edit-set, from a tagged pull-request comment to a structured todo on the review page. Covers the tag a reviewer types, how the comments are ingested into review-comment/1.0.0 todos, where the published review-comments.json comes from and when it refreshes, how a comment follows a renamed block and survives a removed one, who may change a comment’s status, and how to change this process. Use when a reviewer asks how to comment on a block, when the review page shows no comments or a wrong one, when editing the ingestion, or when a folio’s staging workflow is set up. Source: folio-assistant-core/skills/content/content-lifecycle-ext/review-comments.md. Also satisfied by: folio-review-comment-move, folio-review-coverage. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/review-comments/{input,output}.schema.json).

21ad8fcfc106.title: Check a review log and its repository’s issues for changes
21ad8fcfc106.content: The mechanical check a review-log watcher runs on every poll. Given a drafting sheet’s Contributor Feedback values and the folio repository, it reads the repository’s open and closed issues (leaving out pull requests, issues labelled no-sheet and, with --author, issues someone else opened) and compares a digest of them and of the cells people set (Title, Selected Sections, Contributor Feedback, Disposition, Ready for agent, Ready for merge, Dispositions confirmed; on a public-comment log also Committee Feedback, TWG (CS), TWG (human) and Change Set (human)) with the last check’s. Unchanged: it prints {"status":"unchanged"} and exits 0. Changed: it exits 10 and lists what changed (issue opened, updated or closed; a cell’s old and new text), the Contributor Feedback rows to append, one per issue that no row’s Issue cell links yet (Title the issue’s title, the first Contributor Feedback column @login (#N): first paragraph, Issue the issue’s URL; a closed issue’s row marked closed), and closedRows, the rows linking a closed issue, which the watcher hides with their text struck through. A read with no Issue column (a public-comment log’s Review Change Sets) tracks only issues labelled change-set unless --label says otherwise, and appends no rows: each open issue is reported as an issue-unlinked change instead. It writes no sheet and no issue: the watcher appends the rows and does the agent pass. With --accept it stores the new state for the next poll to compare against. |   |   | . | Tool | review-log-watch | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/tools/review-log-watch.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/folio-assistant-core.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | folio-assistant-core | . | source | folio-assistant-core/tools/review-log-watch/review-log-watch.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

e9f344459d8f.title: Skills it satisfies
e9f344459d8f.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. dublin-core-renderings . Render a catalogue’s Dublin Core records in the two standard forms an outside reader can use: Dublin Core XML, which a harvester reads, and JSON-LD bound to DCMI Metadata Terms. Each rendering is published beside the item’s page. Covers which records get one, which XML form is used and why, how every field maps from the record’s own data (never composed), what cannot be expressed and how that is reported, and the gate. Read this before changing the mapping, adding a catalogue layer, or linking a rendering from a page. Source: folio-assistant-core/skills/library/catalogue/dublin-core-renderings.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/dublin-core-renderings/{input,output}.schema.json).

468ac9911247.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. figure-rebuild . Turn a figure into a computable diagram: every figure of a source publication when a folio is built from its L1 entry, and any hand-drawn figure in a folio, an IG or a demonstrator that is redrawn from a source. Every declared figure gets a block, and each one is rebuilt in the form its type calls for: an ArchiMate view, BPMN, DMN, a FHIR logical model, or an SVG generated from data, always from one schema-backed source. The PDF crop stays beside the rebuild as the cited source, and the rebuild keeps the original’s layout. The figure-coverage check counts what is missing and what is still only a picture. Source: folio-assistant-core/skills/library/ingestion/figure-rebuild.md. Also satisfied by: diig-phases-svg, figure-coverage, smart-approach-svg. b96a54378f5b.title: Tools — folio-assistant-core
b96a54378f5b.content: The Tool nodes folio-assistant-core declares in its tools graph — one instance’s slice of every instance’s tools. As an API: OpenAPI document · MCP tool list · API reference. A skill states a capability generically: what an actor needs to know to perform a task. A Tool is one concrete way to exercise it, with an installation, an invocation and typed inputs and outputs. One skill may be satisfied by several tools, and one tool may satisfy several skills. They are separate graphs and this is the tools one. The relation between them is satisfies, and it runs from a tool to a skill — this tool is one way to do that, never this skill is a tool. 30Tool nodes 21skills satisfied 30invoked as a shell command 0reachable over MCP

b71249203330.title: Refer to HL7’s published FHIR core definitions by canonical URL, and derive their UML class model
b71249203330.content: Read HL7’s own core package for each stable FHIR release (https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/hl7.fhir.r4.core.tgz, R4B, R5) at the sha1 and sha512 fhir-core/pins.json pins, and keep, under fhir-core/<release>/, only what refers to it or is derived from it: index writes the manifest (each resource, complex, primitive and root type by canonical URL, with HL7’s published JSON for it, its kind, base and the sha256 of its bytes in HL7’s package); uml derives the UML class model HL7 publishes only as pictures, citing the definition and element of every class and attribute; materialise fills a labelled local cache, never committed; check holds all of it to the pins offline; resolve answers with HL7’s URL for a canonical (--cache for the cached copy); diagram prints a type’s Mermaid class diagram. HL7’s publication is the authority: a mirror may only fill the cache. A package that cannot be fetched or verified is recorded as unread with the reason, never as an empty graph. |   |   | . | Tool | fhir-core | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/tools/fhir-core.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/fhir-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | fhir-harness | . | source | fhir-harness/tools/fhir-core/fhir-core.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

7badfb946b6a.title: Skills it satisfies
7badfb946b6a.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. Source: fhir-harness/skills/fhir-ig-base/ig-build-pipeline.md. Also satisfied by: build-ig-site, ig-artifact-jsonld, ig-ast-refresh, ig-index-build, ig-page-render-qa, ig-pages, ig-publisher-i18n, ig-repo-site, ig-site-data, ingest-ig-menu, jsonld-vocabularies, logical-model-schemas, stage-ig-sites, strip-library-binaries, strip-library-content, terminology-index, valueset-schemas. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/ig-build-pipeline/{input,output}.schema.json).

19282cb5892f.title: How it is deployed and reached
19282cb5892f.content: . | Command line. From the repository root: bun run fhir-harness/scripts/fhir-core.ts <index|uml|materialise|check|resolve <url>|diagram <Type>>. | GitHub Actions. No workflow in this checkout runs its command. | . As an API: its operation in the OpenAPI document and the MCP tool list of its layer. |   |   | . | install | none | . | runtime | bun | . | network | yes | . When a host it reaches is refused: . | host / error | remedy | . | hl7.org | none: Pass --tgz-dir with HL7’s package fetched elsewhere: the bytes are still checked against HL7’s hashes. Without it, index writes the release unread and uml cannot determine the class model; materialise may still fill the cache from a pinned mirror, file by file against the manifest. | . | when to choose it |   | . | when | Before a reader resolves a FHIR core type by canonical URL or draws a class diagram of core types (an IG’s logical models or profiles over them), or when a pin changes. | . | limits | Stable releases only. Constraint profiles, extension definitions and logical models in the core package are left out and counted. The class model copies no constraint, binding or description: the cited HL7 definition holds them. | . | cost | One 4-17 MB download per release from hl7.org, then seconds; check, resolve and diagram are offline. | .

54396fd36a6e.title: Skills it satisfies
54396fd36a6e.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. 1111e00507ca.title: Skills it satisfies
1111e00507ca.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. Source: fhir-harness/skills/fhir-ig-base/ig-build-pipeline.md. Also satisfied by: build-ig-site, fhir-core, ig-artifact-jsonld, ig-ast-refresh, ig-index-build, ig-page-render-qa, ig-pages, ig-publisher-i18n, ig-repo-site, ingest-ig-menu, jsonld-vocabularies, logical-model-schemas, stage-ig-sites, strip-library-binaries, strip-library-content, terminology-index, valueset-schemas. 96c2fb88961c.title: Cut an IG release as a GitHub draft that carries its packages and AST, and report a version left untagged or unreleased
96c2fb88961c.content: Gather a release’s files from a full Publisher build (package.tgz and its R4/R4B variants, and ast-data.zip, the IG’s AST with the Libraries’ ELM), say from sushi-config.yaml whether it is a pre-release, and make or refresh the GitHub DRAFT release for the tag with the files uploaded. The owner publishes the draft; a published release is never changed. check is the catch-up the AST refresh of the default branch runs (advisory): it reports a current version with no v<version> tag, naming the commit that set it for the owner to tag, and a tag with no release, for the owner to run ig-release.yml by hand. It never tags and never releases: the tag is the owner’s governance step (ig-release.bpmn). |   |   | . | Tool | ig-release | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/tools/ig-release.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/fhir-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | fhir-harness | . | source | fhir-harness/tools/ig-release/ig-release.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

b2308a44890f.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site.
