573a0ae5d26e.title: KG export — publishing the graph as linked data, not as a page
573a0ae5d26e.content: Skill kg-export: Serialize a layer’s knowledge graph to one JSON document, for publication and inspection. Read when asked to visualize, audit or share the KG, before adding a node type to the export, and before minting or authoring any subject IRI — subjects are <doc dir>/<kind>/<id>, never #fragments. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . The export is data, not a page. One JSON document describes the graph; drawing it is somebody else’s job — a static viewer, an external tool, or nothing at all. The export makes the harness inspectable. Per skills-and-tools: . |   |   | . | this skill | produce the serialization — generic, no host named | . | the Tool | publish it somewhere — today pages-publish (GitHub Pages) | . A GitLab Pages or object-store Tool would satisfy the same skill. Nothing in this skill names a host.

8f7881c8f0f8.title: It is JSON-LD, and the @type: @id coercion is the whole point
8f7881c8f0f8.content: Modelled on WHO’s SMART Base repository’s input/scripts/generate_jsonld_vocabularies.py. Five rules carry the weight; the first is cheap to lose and invisible when you do: . 1. Every edge term is declared {"@type": "@id"}. Without that coercion, requires, performedBy and partOf are string literals to any JSON-LD processor, and the document is a list of records that merely looks linked to a human reading the JSON. The coercion is the difference between a list of records and a traversable graph, and a test asserts it. 2. The document’s @id is the URL it is served from, with @type: prov:Entity and a generatedAt typed xsd:dateTime. Fetch the @id, get the document. WHO SMART Base’s type-usage note is explicit about this and it is what makes the graph mergeable with anyone else’s. 3. A subject’s IRI is a path under its layer, never a #fragment of the document — <doc dir>/<kind>/<id>, each served as its own file. This is the rule for every IRI an agent mints or authors; the reasons and the exceptions are in §”Subject IRIs — a path, not a #fragment” below. 4. No @vocab, and id/type are aliased. Every term carries its full namespace IRI, so an undeclared key stays undeclared instead of silently minting an IRI nobody chose. The aliases keep the published JSON readable as ordinary records for someone who does not know JSON-LD. 5. Every property name in @graph is declared in @context, and the export FAILS if one is not. A name that is neither declared nor an absolute IRI is not a property: a processor drops it, although it stays visible when the file is read as plain JSON — which is why it goes unnoticed until the document has a consumer.

7b83f3db7c48.title: Subject IRIs — a path, not a #fragment
7b83f3db7c48.content: This section owns the rule. Every other skill that names a subject’s IRI points here rather than restating it. The rule . A knowledge-graph subject (a skill, a process, a global task, a role, an actor, a decision, a directory, a package, a capability, an asset) is named . <doc dir>/<kind>/<id> . where <doc dir> is the directory the layer’s own document is served from. That is the URL-space rule: <baseurl>/<instantiated harness>/<path to rendered content>. §”Which base an @id is minted against” in instance-publication says which base applies to a layer on this site and to a layer with its own canonicalUrl. It is the form Tools use, <doc dir>/tools/<id>.jsonld. The host has no special case: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document. So <doc dir> is <site>/<instance>/ for every layer this site publishes, the host included: . |   | IRI | . | the host’s document | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | a host subject | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/skill/kg-export | . | a host Tool | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/beans-cli.jsonld | . | ❌ never | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness.jsonld, …/folio-assistant/tools/<id>.jsonld: the host at the site root | . Do not mint, link or write anything at a root-level host path; nothing answers there (instance-publication §”An @id that moved is not forwarded”). |   | IRI | . | ✅ right | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/<instance>/globalTask/GT_SeedWorkPlan | . | ❌ fragment | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/<instance>/<instance>.jsonld#globalTask/GT_SeedWorkPlan | . | ❌ unservable | …/<instance>/<instance>.jsonld/globalTask/GT_SeedWorkPlan: a static host cannot hold a file and a directory under one name | . A process’s parts. Steps and lanes get pages; flows stay fragments of the process page, because only their diagram cites them: . | part | IRI |   | . | a step (any flow node) | <doc dir>/process/P/node/T | a subject: its own page and .jsonld | . | a lane | <doc dir>/process/P/lane/L | a subject: its own page and .jsonld | . | a sequence flow | <doc dir>/process/P#flow/F | a fragment of the process’s page | . A flow is the one # this rule allows for instance data; the other is the vocabulary exception below. It is allowed because nothing cites an arrow on its own. Any other part of a subject that people cite is itself a subject and takes a path. Why . | A #fragment never reaches the server. Dereferencing the subject fetches the whole layer graph, and the subject cannot have a page or a document of its own. | A subject is a real resource: its own page, its own JSON-LD, its own history and cache, linkable on its own. | # already means “a place on this HTML page”. Using it for identity mixes identity with navigation. | Slash paths nest (…/process/P/node/T); fragments do not. | It is the FHIR convention: <base>/<Type>/<id>. | . The other exception: vocabulary terms keep # . # stays right for vocabulary and namespace terms (…/ns#Term): one small document holds every term, and fetching it is what a consumer wants. That covers classes, properties, graph-typology individuals, and the SKOS glossary’s concepts, which live in the layer’s namespace. If a thing has instances, a page or a history of its own, it is a subject and takes a path. Every @id still has to load . An @id that looks dereferenceable and is not is worse than one that is obviously local. GitHub Pages has no redirects, no 303 and no content negotiation. So a path IRI is served by a file of its own: a small page at <doc dir>/<kind>/<id> carrying the node as JSON-LD, plus <id>.jsonld beside it, as Tools are served. Whoever mints the path also publishes the file, in the same change. Every rendered link to a subject uses its subject IRI, meaning its page, and never a fragment of the layer document. That covers the ⓘ panel and the icons on a rendered BPMN diagram, step tables and role links. bootstrap states the same rule for its own graph, in its own terms, in bootstrap-graph-publication §”Each subject’s own address”. Today, and what is still a fragment . The tools layer mints paths. makeIri in scripts/kg-export.ts calls subjectIri (scripts/lib/subject-iri.ts), which mints <doc dir>/<kind>/<id>, and a process flow as <doc dir>/process/P#flow/F. The glossary export and the directory-container @id (subgraphIri) go through the same function. Two things still mint fragments: . | bootstrap’s own graph. bootstrap-tools scripts/export-graph.ts publishes it, so subjectIri keeps bootstrap.jsonld#<kind>/<id> for a link into that document (FRAGMENT_DOCUMENT_STUBS). The entry goes in the PR that moves that publisher to paths. | own-canonical layers (the SMART IGs and others), whose subject IRIs do not load yet. | . So: . | mint through subjectIri (or makeIri, which calls it), never by hand. | do not add a new hash-IRI minter for subjects, and do not hand-write a ….jsonld#<kind>/<id> IRI in new content. | remove this subsection when bootstrap’s publisher mints paths and own-canonical subject IRIs load. | .

6e371ae93094.title: Declaring a term is a decision, not a line of context
6e371ae93094.content: Five questions, in this order. The worked call for each term is in buildContext(), beside the term it justifies. | Does the fact belong in the graph at all? A denormalised copy of a link already present (a name beside the link that reaches it) is a second answer that can go stale: remove it rather than declare it, once the link resolves for every node. A consumer must never have to recover a fact by splitting an IRI. | Is it a LINK or a literal? Wrong here is worse than undeclared — confidently wrong rather than absent. Under {"@type": "@id"} the value must already BE an IRI: a bare git-push resolves against the document base to <base>/git-push, which nobody minted and nothing serves. So hasCapability mints its values with makeIri, and a repo-relative path (instructionsPath, sourcePath, maintainsFrom) stays a literal for the reverse reason. | Does the referent exist in this graph? roleName, permissionName and decisionRef stayed names: the role registry, the permission vocabulary and the DMN tables are not collected, so coerced IRIs would resolve to nothing. Each becomes a link the day its referent becomes a node. | Is one name carrying two relations? Then it is two terms: source was a .bpmn path on a Process and a kind marker elsewhere, so it is sourcePath and sourceKind. Heterogeneous SHAPE under one relation is a different case — install is a command string from a Capability and a dispatch object from a Tool, and stays one term typed @json, because declaring a container term alone keeps the outer key and drops every inner one. | Does a published standard already say it? Then the term IS the standard’s property, and nothing is minted. title and description are Dublin Core’s; partOf/inSubgraph are dcterms:isPartOf, holdsGraph is dcterms:type, conformsTo is dcterms:conformsTo; a sequence flow’s from/to are BPMN’s own sourceRef/targetRef and a node’s incoming/outgoing BPMN’s attributes of those names; a task’s skill is requires, which is dcterms:requires (the task, the dependent node, requires the skill), and a lane’s role (bindsRole) is BPMN’s own partitionElementRef. bootstrap’s own graph (bootstrap-tools’ export-graph.ts) uses the same IRIs, so the two graphs agree. How, so it cannot drift: a term that restated a standard keeps its gloss in schemas/content/vocabulary.ts and gains replacedBy, a CURIE. buildContext() maps each such key through propertyIri() (schemas/kg/namespaces.ts), which reads that field, so the exporter cannot name one IRI while the vocabulary names another. The published vocabulary keeps the old term, owl:deprecated and dcterms:isReplacedBy the standard property: data already holding the old IRI still dereferences to a definition that says where to go. The JSON keys are unchanged, so a reader of plain JSON sees no difference. What stays minted is what no standard says: performedBy, inLane, hasSkill, startNode, and the rest. BPMN spells a lane’s members as flowNodeRef on the LANE; inLane is the inverse, on the node, and no standard names that direction. | . No canonicalUrl and no --base-url → no absolute IRIs, reported in problems[] rather than papered over. A fabricated absolute base is the same failure as a fabricated link.

3c5494645c3a.title: Every key is a declared term — in content documents too
3c5494645c3a.content: Rule 5 above, applied to CONTENT: in every document on the published content context, a plain key must be a declared term, or a JSON-LD processor drops it without a word. bun run cat check:content-keys fails on one (it judges documents on the content context and on a layer’s own context). It does not descend into a value typed @json. Such a value is a JSON literal by declaration: its inner keys are data, not properties. That is the right home for a nested structure that is ours rather than linked data, and the only way its nulls survive — the three-state rule lives in them. A path is a literal, never an @id. A document-relative path coerced to @id resolves against the context’s @base, not against the document, and so names a location the file is not at (../sections/x.md becomes a well-formed link to nowhere). So text, leanSource and file are literals, and check:content-keys fails if a file path sits under any @id term. The upgrade rule: a path term becomes a link — @type: @id with ABSOLUTE IRIs minted by the one function that mints block IRIs — when, and only when, the files it names are SERVED at a URL a layer declares. Until then a link is a promise nothing keeps, and a literal is the honest record: one reading, resolved by our tools against the file that carries it.

06abe82887de.title: A prefix is the stub — and a prefix that is spoken must be bound
06abe82887de.content: Each of our namespaces is <canonical>/<stub>/ns#, so the prefix bound to it is that same word as the stub: . | namespace | prefix | . | https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/ns/ | bootstrap | . | …/folio-assistant/cat-harness/ns# | cat-harness | . | …/folio-assistant/<content-core>/ns# | the content core | . bootstrap’s row is the exception to the <canonical>/<stub>/ shape, and says so: its namespace sits under bootstrap’s own iriBase and carries the release’s MAJOR, because bootstrap is published from its own repository; the exact release an agent reads is its pin’s. The prefix is still the stub. The address is written once, in cat-harness/code-lists/own-namespaces.json (read as CAT_BOOTSTRAP_NS), and iri:sync keeps every literal copy — this table’s included — at bootstrap’s declared major. One word in three places — path segment, stub, prefix — instead of three words that must agree. Naming a namespace document — ns, and why . A namespace document is published where its identifiers point, so its file name IS its address: bootstrap/ns.jsonld is what makes …/bootstrap/v0/ns#Node resolve, and check:node-iris fails the day they differ. Renaming the file renames every term. Keep ns; do not rename it to something friendlier (vocabulary.jsonld, schemas/terms.jsonld): . | It is the house rule and the common practice. This project’s namespaces end in /ns#, and <canonical>/<stub>/ns# is what “the prefix is the stub” rests on. W3C publishes PROV, DCAT, ORG and SHACL under w3.org/ns/. | Renaming is not local. Changing the pattern means renaming published namespaces (a MAJOR version each under instance-versioning) and every BPMN file binding the process namespaces. | schemas/ would misclassify it. Here a schema is what a Node is checked against; a vocabulary defines words. | Findability is solved without renaming: the file’s own label (“bootstrap vocabulary”) is what the generated README file table shows beside it. | . One source per layer — and no all-layers union . Each layer’s vocabulary is ONE document, and every term’s rdfs:isDefinedBy names that document. bootstrap’s is bootstrap/ns.jsonld, written by bootstrap-tools from bootstrap’s own terms and committed; the site copies it, and the harness’s full build reads it rather than rebuilding it, so nothing can say a thing about a bootstrap term that bootstrap’s file does not (ns-export-skos.test.ts holds them equal, node for node). There is no all-layers union document. A program follows a term’s IRI to its layer document; a person looking for terms goes to the Glossary, which lists every term and publishes SKOS for every scheme. NS_PREFIXES in schemas/kg/namespaces.ts is the one list; stubOfNamespace() reads the stub back off an IRI. Do not bind abbreviated prefixes (bs, cat, fac). Why an abbreviation is a defect waiting to happen. An unbound prefix is not an error to a JSON-LD processor: if a context binds fac while terms are still written folio:…, the processor reads folio as a URI SCHEME, and folio:Definition expands to an absolute IRI that is well-formed, means nothing, and joins with nothing. A --check drift gate does not catch it, because the source is wrong the same way — a drift gate proves agreement, never correctness. The two rules, and what enforces them. Every emitted document names its own layer’s generated context, <iriBase>ns/context/v1.jsonld. jsonld:contexts --check (cat-harness-tools scripts/gen-instance-contexts.ts) enforces rule 1 over every .jsonld in the checkout, failing on a prefix used in an IRI position that nothing binds; a context generated from use binds nothing unused. Rule 2 is upheld by construction — own prefixes are spelt from the declarations: . | Spoken ⇒ bound. A compact IRI used as a KEY or an @type value must have its prefix bound in that document’s context — inline, or the published one by URL, or an array of both. The published context’s own term targets are checked too, whether or not a document uses them. Plain string VALUES are not read as CURIEs: label: "def:foo" is an authored label, which is exactly the hazard schemas/kg/jsonld.ts opens with. | Own namespace ⇒ stub spelling. A binding onto a …/<stub>/ns# namespace of ours must be spelt <stub>, and <stub> must be declared by a layer (<stub>/<stub>.json). | . A context URL the check cannot resolve is “could not determine”, counted and listed — never read as clean. Checking a fix: expand, don’t read. A compact IRI looks right to a human whether or not it is bound. The evidence that closes a prefix defect is a document run through a JSON-LD processor, with zero expanded IRIs outside http(s):. Where a prefix cannot be bound at all, a different spelling is never the answer. CSVW metadata allows only @language and @base in its local context, so prefixed keys there dangle under ANY prefix. The two real answers are absolute IRIs, or not being JSON-LD at all; tabular-metadata takes the second: the record is plain JSON and the CSVW document is derived from it. A file whose extension says .jsonld is making a claim — a processor will read every colon-key in it as an IRI.

f0fc40a38af9.title: fsh-guts NEVER reaches a published graph
f0fc40a38af9.content: fsh-guts, and every reference to it, is stripped from the KG before publication. Keeping the CONTENT out of the render pipeline is a different property from keeping the REFERENCE out of the graph. A layer’s declared directories become nodes in <stub>.jsonld, and fsh-guts/ must be declared (or no tool can find it and the never-delete rule has no destination), so its id, path and description must be stripped from the published document. UNPUBLISHED_GRAPH_TYPOLOGIES in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts is the one list, read by every emitter, so two filters cannot disagree about what is excluded. Three emitters are filtered: . | emitter | what would leak | . | graph typologies | the fsh-guts GraphTypology node | . | declared directories | the Directory node — id, path, description — and its holdsGraph edge | . | skills | skill/fsh-guts, plus the declaresSkill edge from package/folio-core | . The skill is excluded on the merits as well as the letter: its subject IS where SDLC churn goes, so publishing it advertises the trashcan to every consumer of the graph. An edge to a stripped node is not a compromise — it is a dangling reference that still spells the name it was meant to remove. A directory is excluded when ANY graph it holds is excluded, not when all of them are. graphs is an array and schemas/ already holds two; an “all” test would publish a directory holding both cat-harness and fsh-guts, naming the path on the way past. This is not a contradiction of <base>/fsh-guts.jsonld . Different documents. That one IS the trashcan’s graph and is fetched by name; every other published artefact must carry no path to it. A consumer may go there deliberately and must never arrive by following an edge. Strip where the document is built . Not at upload. A strip on the happy path only leaves a graph that looks clean and is not, and the test must read the built artefact rather than the inputs. scripts/tests/fsh-guts-unpublished.test.ts serialises the whole export and asserts the substring is absent — a structural check would have to know every field that could carry it, and the one it forgets is the one that leaks. It also asserts the node list is non-empty before filtering it, so a wrong key cannot make it pass vacuously.

4220e7a45da5.title: Staging must not claim to be canonical
4220e7a45da5.content: CI passes --base-url for a branch preview. Without it every staged export mints @ids pointing at main’s published document, and two different graphs assert the same IRIs — the preview would claim to be the canonical graph. That is not cosmetic: an @id is an assertion of identity, and duplicating one is how a merged graph acquires contradictory statements about the same node.

5f58c4eea7fe.title: The graph carries its own vocabulary
5f58c4eea7fe.content: Graph typologies are nodes, not just TypeScript. Follow holdsGraph from a directory and you arrive at a node saying what that kind holds and whether it renders. Without them the vocabulary needed to interpret the document lives only in code the consumer cannot fetch — which is the difference between a self-describing graph and a graph with documentation. The schema half is scripts/harness-schema-export.ts: the declaration’s JSON Schema, published at the URL its own $id names, so a consumer holding an a declaration it does not understand has somewhere to go. It is a third rendering of CatHarnessDeclarationSchema beside the JSON-LD — not a second authority; the Zod is authoritative, per directory-conventions.

5bc172f40fcc.title: A preview says what it is, and links back — explicitly
5bc172f40fcc.content: Passing --base-url gives a preview’s nodes preview IRIs, so the two graphs cannot contradict each other. To keep them relatable (“this PR changes skill X”), three things are stated in the artefact rather than left to a convention: . |   |   | . | @type | [prov:Entity, folio:PreviewGraph] — “am I the real one?” is answerable from the document’s own type | . | canonicalDocument | the canonical document’s IRI, at document level | . | alternateOf | per node, prov:alternateOf → that node’s canonical IRI | . prov:alternateOf, never owl:sameAs. sameAs entails identity, so a reasoner merges every statement about both nodes — and if the preview changed a skill’s description, the merged graph would assert two conflicting descriptions of one thing. That is exactly the contradiction distinct IRIs were introduced to avoid. alternateOf says “same underlying thing, different presentation” and merges nothing. The per-node links are derivable, and are emitted anyway, because a downstream consumer must never have to string-manipulate or infer a rule to follow a link: a rule a consumer has to know is a rule a consumer can get wrong. See crdm-requirements-workflow (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Consumer burden is a requirement”. Vocabulary nodes get no alternateOf. Graph typologies are minted under the namespace, not the document, so they are byte-identical in both graphs; an alternateOf on them would point at a node that does not exist. A test pins it.

e55211009f60.title: Naming — artefacts take the repository’s name, the config does not
e55211009f60.content: The stub (<name>.json → stub, defaulting to name) is the filename stem of everything this layer publishes: <stub>.jsonld, <stub>.schema.json. One helper, artefactStub(), computes it, so the two exporters cannot disagree about what this layer is called. WHO SMART Base does the same and derives its stub by stripping a prefix (smart-<stub> → <stub> → https://smart.who.int/<stub>), so stub, directory and published path are one word. The declaration file is named for the layer’s name, not its stub: <name>.json. A consumer finds it without being told its filename: findDeclarationFile() scans a directory for a *.json carrying a name whose stem EQUALS that name — the file agrees with itself — and two such files in one directory throw rather than one being picked silently. It never derives the name from the DIRECTORY, which would find nothing in a repository cloned under a different name. Everything the declaration describes is free to be named: by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration naming them.

6f620afc7d88.title: The edges are the reason to publish
6f620afc7d88.content: What makes the export worth having is the relations that already exist on disk and that no other tool surfaces: . | activity → skill. Every BPMN activity may carry <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="…"/>, so the export can say which process step is implemented by which skill. | activity → role. A BPMN lane is the role that performs the step. | skill → package, and a skill’s two facets: its instruction body (<name>.md) and the I/O contract it names in its front matter (input:/output:, usually schemas/skills/<name>/). | . That last one is the one to understand before editing the exporter. A name may have an instruction body, an I/O contract, or both — they are facets of one skill, not two kinds of skill. So the graph is keyed by name, which is also what a BPMN ref uses. Keying by file instead produces two disconnected node sets and loses the relation entirely. It is also what makes “declared somewhere, written nowhere” visible: which skills have prose only, an I/O contract only, or both.

194e3701cd79.title: A partial graph must never pass for a whole one
194e3701cd79.content: A consumer of the JSON cannot distinguish a skill that is absent from one that was never collected: both are simply not in @graph, counts look plausible, and nothing fails — a clean run over a corpus the tool could not read. So: . | A source that cannot be read goes in problems[] and the export exits non-zero. Publishing is blocked, rather than a truncated file being deployed. | counts by type ships with the graph, so a consumer can see at a glance that a corpus it expected is missing, without re-deriving it. | The invariant is asserted against something outside the exporter’s own view. scripts/tests/kg-export.test.ts requires every skill a diagram names to appear — and check:workflow-refs independently guarantees those refs resolve against the real skill locations. So if the exporter’s notion of where skills live narrows, the test fails. An invariant checked only against the exporter’s own collection would not catch it. | .

5a32db9a182c.title: Whose nodes — a layer publishes its own
5a32db9a182c.content: The policy is instance-publication §”What each layer publishes — graph, address, schema, and what is stripped”: which layer publishes which document where. This section is the exporter’s side of it. buildExport takes scope, and the CLI --scope <instance|checkout>: . | scope | reads | for | . | instance (default) | this layer’s declaration alone | the published document, its locale variants, its QA sidecar | . | checkout | this layer plus every layer stacked on it | a corpus-wide consumer that says so — the kg search slice | . An @id the checkout-scope document mints and the instance-scope one does not is held by its owner’s own document, and this one says nothing about it: no forwarding node. A link to a node that left reads as dangling until it is re-homed.

5b4574bc8d9f.title: Named subgraphs — one IRI, two files, framed from one graph
5b4574bc8d9f.content: A named subgraph is a directory of a declared graph, read as a set of KG nodes: skills/ is one, and so is sdlc/skills/. Asking for “every node of cat-harness/sdlc/skills” takes one fetch. Identity . | The subgraph IRI is a directory IRI in its own namespace: <BASE_URL>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/<PATH>/, for example …/subgraph/cat-harness/sdlc/skills/. | It is kept apart from content-node IRIs on purpose. A subgraph is a view of nodes, not one of them, so renaming a file never renames the subgraph, and re-homing a node never re-mints the subgraph. | Not /hydrated-graph/: the pointer-only file would then live under a path that says “hydrated”. | The repository’s level is <BASE_URL>/subgraph/. It has index.jsonld only, and its hasSubgraph are the harness roots this build frames. It is the one file a consumer needs to find every root. The workflow page starts there. | . Two files under the IRI . Both files have root @id = the directory IRI. | file | what is in it | who it is for | . | index.jsonld | referenced: each direct member as a pointer (@id, @type, label), and each child subgraph by its IRI | search, navigation, skeleton loading | . | index.hydrated.jsonld | dereferenced: every node in the subgraph’s transitive membership, inline and fully hydrated | “give me all of sdlc/skills” in one fetch | . Rules for the pair: . | The hydrated file carries KG metadata, never heavy content. Markdown bodies, images and binaries are payloads, reached by a payload link (§”Payloads — heavy content by content address”, below). | The root has index.jsonld only. A harness layer is itself a named subgraph of the repo KG, and the repo KG is the level above it. A deep hydrated file at the root would be the whole graph in one document — a monolith. Hydration is deep, but not at the root. | The GitHub Pages caveat. Pages does no content negotiation, so the directory IRI is documented as resolving to index.jsonld by explicit path. A consumer that dereferences the bare IRI gets whatever Pages serves for the directory; index.jsonld and index.hydrated.jsonld are always addressable by name. | . Building the files . | One source, two frames. Both files come out of one build step, from the same in-memory graph, by JSON-LD framing: a pointer frame (@embed: @never) and an embed frame (@embed: @always). | Never two hand-synced properties. No authorUri beside author. Two properties carrying one fact is the drift data-modelling §3 exists to stop. | @context is never inlined. Every file declares the one shared, cached context URL, the way content documents already use ns/content/v1.jsonld. | Where it is built. bun run cat subgraph:jsonld (scripts/gen-subgraph-jsonld.ts) frames kg-export’s in-memory graphs — one per framed layer, each from its OWN export, never a stacked layer’s node under this document’s name — and writes docs/subgraph/<HARNESS>/<PATH>/index[.hydrated].jsonld, which Pages serves at the subgraph IRI, plus the context at ns/subgraph/v1.jsonld. subgraph:jsonld:check is the gate. The file shape is schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts. | . Published per pin, in a package . The files are built at publish (builtAtPublish: docs/subgraph/), so no commit holds them. For a consumer that reads them at a PIN rather than from the Pages site, each pin’s index files are published in a package: an npm package, <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>, holding every index.jsonld and index.hydrated.jsonld under <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/ at the paths above and a subgraph-index.json manifest (folio-subgraph-index/v1: repository, pin, harness, each file’s sha256). It is attached, with its folio-binary-release/v1 record, to the GitHub release subgraph-index-<sha>. | Not committed: a committed copy of a build over other layers is stale on the next re-pin. | Not generated at mount: reading one file of metadata must not need the build toolchain, and one pin must have one set of files. | Every name is computed from repository, pin and harness (subgraphIndexPackage, schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts), so a consumer never lists releases. | Who builds it: layer-publish-subgraph-index.yml (the tools layer), on each push to main: subgraph:jsonld, then the subgraph-index-package Tool. A release that already exists for a pin is never replaced. | Who reads it: a hydrated mount (remote-mount), when the pin’s tree holds no file. remote-mount §”Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package” has the checks. | . Membership is declared, not inferred . | A subgraph’s members are what its declared membership rule selects. | For a directory of a declared graph, the rule is containment: a node is in the deepest subgraph directory that contains its source path, and in every ancestor of that one, transitively. | An overlaid layer heads its own tree. kg-export reads the corpus of every layer stacked on this one, so the content core’s processes and skills are nodes of this graph. A directory belongs to the layer that declares it, so those nodes sit under <BASE_URL>/subgraph/<that layer>/…, framed by this build because this graph publishes them. Their @ids do not change. | Bootstrap gets no tree here. bootstrap and bootstrap-tools sit below this layer, and their processes are kept out of its graph; they publish their own subgraphs, and a tree framed for them here would re-carry what was excluded. | A harness’s own rule, saying which directories are its graph, is its <instance>.json declaration. Harness and Subgraph therefore share one base, GraphNodeDirectoryShape. They do not get two parallel “directory with members” types. | A node whose subgraph cannot be determined goes in problems[]. It is never silently left out (§”A partial graph must never pass for a whole one”). | . Consumers . | Remote materialization reads these same files. bun run cat kg:materialize --nodes <subscription> <subgraph-path> fetches one subgraph’s index.hydrated.jsonld at the subscription’s pin. It never does a sparse checkout of the subgraph’s directory. The file is validated against SubgraphHydratedSchema, its root @id must be the subgraph asked for, and it is held with a sha256 record. A request for the root is refused, with a pointer to index.jsonld. This is a metadata mode. The byte copy (kg:materialize <subscription> <subgraph>) keeps its five gates. See kg-subscription §”metadata mode”. | A subgraph manifest that lists a child IRI but whose child file is missing is a dangling link. It is reported, never skipped. | .

ab800fce7be8.title: Payloads — heavy content by content address
ab800fce7be8.content: The subgraph files are the skeleton: topology and the metadata a search needs. Heavy content is the muscle, and it lives outside the graph, one file per distinct body. No generator emits a monolithic graph file that inlines bodies. Addressing . | A payload’s IRI is <BASE_URL>/payload/sha256/<hex>, where <hex> is the lower-case hex SHA-256 of its bytes. Nothing else names it: no extension, no source path, no node id. | It is immutable. The bytes at an IRI never change, because a change to the bytes is a change to the name. A consumer may cache a payload forever. | Immutable is not “kept forever”. A payload no node links to is an orphan: the gate fails on it and the generator removes it on write. An old IRI may therefore stop resolving once nothing references it; while it resolves, it resolves to the same bytes. | Identical bodies are one file, linked from every node that has them. | The bytes are the source file verbatim. A Markdown body keeps its front matter, and its relative links resolve against the node’s own source path (instructionsPath), not against the payload IRI. | . The link . Every node with a payload carries one payload link, in both subgraph files. In the index it sits on the pointer; in the hydrated file it sits on the whole node, in place of the body: . "payload": { "@id": "<BASE_URL>/payload/sha256/<hex>", "sha256": "<hex>", "bytes": 12653 } . sha256 and bytes let a consumer verify a fetch, and decide whether to make it, without a second request. sha256 is the IRI’s last segment by construction, and the schema checks it. The media type is in a sidecar . <hex>.json beside <hex> carries $schema: cat-harness-payload/v1, sha256, bytes and mediaType. It is a sidecar rather than an extension for two reasons: . | the ruled IRI has no extension, and <hex>.md would be a second address for one payload; | GitHub Pages types a file by its extension, so an extensionless payload is served as application/octet-stream whatever it holds. | . A consumer holding only the IRI appends .json. The media type is not also on the link, because one fact gets one place. It comes from the source file’s extension through a declared table; an undeclared extension is a problem, never a guess. What is heavy . The graph inlines no body, so “heavy” means what its pointers name: . | node | field | heavy? | . | Skill | instructionsPath (.md) | yes — the instruction body | . | Asset | path (.md; an image would be too) | yes | . | Process / Decision | sourcePath (.bpmn / .dmn) | not yet — the topology is already graph nodes, and the XML is its own graph’s source | . | Schema | module (.ts) | no — code, not content | . The table that decides this is HEAVY_POINTERS in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts, and adding a row there is the whole change to make a field heavy. Building and checking . | bun run cat subgraph:jsonld writes the payloads to docs/payload/sha256/ in the same run as the subgraph files, from the same graph. | The docs workflows copy that directory into the site verbatim. It is excluded from Jekyll, which would render a body’s front matter and Liquid, and then the served bytes would not hash to their name. | subgraph:jsonld:check is the gate. It fails on any of these: . | a stale or stray file; | a payload no node references; | a node whose payload is missing; | bytes that do not hash to their name; | a payload without its sidecar, or a sidecar without its payload. | . | The schema is PayloadLinkSchema and PayloadSidecarSchema in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts. | .

acf8ea2345c7.title: Per-slice SQLite — a named subgraph as one file a browser mounts
acf8ea2345c7.content: A large graph needs search on the client, and a static host cannot run a query. So CI flattens one slice into a relational schema and publishes it as <slice>.<sha256>.sqlite3, and the browser opens it with the official SQLite WASM build and an OPFS VFS. There is nothing to parse, because SQLite reads its B-tree pages on demand. This is the skeleton in a second encoding. It never replaces the JSON-LD files above; it sits beside them for the consumer that has to search. One builder, one definition per slice. scripts/gen-slice-sqlite.ts is the slice-sqlite Tool; its procedure is the slice-sqlite-publish process. Each slice is one SliceDef in its SLICES table: the DDL, each stored table’s columns and row order, the one FTS5 index and the rows it covers, where the payloads live, the search block the page reads, and a load that turns the source into rows. The engine (build, VACUUM INTO, digest, manifest, --check) names no slice. Adding a slice is adding a definition, never a copy of the builder. The four slices . | slice | source | payloads | . | beans | beans/defs/ | work item files, at deploy | . | todos | assets/todos/index.json | todo files, at deploy | . | library | assets/library/index.json + entries/<id>.json | entry files, at deploy | . | kg | the whole-repo KG export | already committed | . Run bun run cat slice:sqlite -- --out <scratch> for current sizes. The whole-repo slice is the no-body variant: nodes, edges, and an FTS5 over names, titles, summaries and descriptions, with bodies as payload pointers. It stores IRIs relative to the document (skill/todo-manager, with the base in meta.base) to stay small. The ~5 MB budget is SIZE_BUDGET_BYTES, reported in the manifest as overBudget and not gated (the work items slice grows every session, and a gate would turn every open PR red for a change nobody made). Over budget means stop and report (the process’s budget gateway), not ship. What a slice file holds . | One table per node type, one row per node. Columns are the fields a search filters or sorts on. Each has a B-tree index where a query needs one. A JSON-valued field stays a JSON column and is read through JSON1 (json_each), rather than becoming another stored table. | One stored table per relation, never two. When a relation can be declared from either side, as a work item’s blocking: and blocked_by: can, the table has a declared_on column saying which side declared each edge, and the two directions are views over it. Two tables for one relation are two answers that can disagree. When a relation is declared on one side only, a declared_on column could hold one value, so it is left out (todos, library). When the relations are many and share one shape, they share ONE table keyed by rel: the kg slice’s 36 @id-typed terms are rows of edges (src, rel, dst), with incoming and dangling as views, because 36 tables of one shape would be 36 places to change it. | An FTS5 index over the searchable text. It is CONTENTLESS (content=''), so it indexes text without storing it. It keeps full detail, because positions are what make a phrase query work. Both the official WASM build and bun:sqlite compile with ENABLE_FTS5. | No heavy content. A row carries payload_sha256, a pointer to the payload at <BASE_URL>/payload/sha256/<hex> (§”Payloads”). The client fetches the payload when a result is opened. What the payload is, is a per-slice decision: a work item’s or a todo’s source file verbatim; for the library, the PUBLISHED entries/<id>.json, one payload per entry that every one of its blocks points at, never the section files under library/, because a withheld entry publishes no verbatim text and the published entry is what already applied that rule; for kg, the KG’s own committed payloads, from the same planPayloads call the subgraph files use. A row with nothing heavy has a NULL pointer, never an invented one. | A meta table and PRAGMA user_version carry the schema version. No timestamp and no commit go in the file. | . The manifest beside it . <slice>.sqlite3.json, $schema: folio-slice-sqlite/v1, carries: . | file, the database’s content-addressed name (§”Content-addressed file, fixed-name manifest”); | sha256 and bytes of the file; | contentDigest, a sha256 over the canonical row dump; | the row count of each table; | schemaVersion, sqliteVersion and pageSize; | fts5: the index’s table, the table whose rows it covers, and its columns; | payloadPath, and payloads: whether they are written at deploy or already published, how many, how many bytes; | any duplicateIds the source holds, and any other source findings in words (a todo with no source file, an entry file the index does not list), so a gap is reported rather than silently dropped; | overBudget; | search: the query, the alias, the column a typed query degrades to, and what a payload is, which the one search page reads (§”The search page”). | . assets/slices/index.json (folio-slice-index/v1) lists every slice built into a directory. There are two digests because there are two questions. sha256 asks whether these are the bytes that were promised; it is what the client verifies a download against and keys its cache by. contentDigest asks whether this is the same data, and it stays equal across a SQLite upgrade that changes the file’s bytes. The header records the writing library’s version at offset 96. Content-addressed file, fixed-name manifest . The database is published at assets/slices/<slice>.<sha256>.sqlite3, the full lower-case hex of its bytes, and the manifest’s file names it. At one fixed path, a client behind a CDN could fetch a fresh manifest and a stale database, fail the sha256 check and fall back: safe for correctness, unsafe for availability. A fresh manifest names a file no cache has seen. A stale manifest names an older file whose bytes still hash to what that manifest promises, so the worst case is an older but self-consistent database, or a 404 the page reports. Why not payload/sha256/<hex>. §”Payloads” is the muscle: a node’s body, the source file verbatim, linked from a node’s payload and kept only while something links to it. A slice file is the skeleton in a second encoding. It is derived and SQLite-version dependent, and no node links to it, so under the payload tree’s own orphan rule it would be an orphan. It would also need a <hex>.json sidecar for a media type that its extension already gives. What the scheme does take from §”Payloads” is the property that matters, immutable, not kept forever. It also takes the full hex rather than a prefix, so the name’s hash segment is sha256 by construction and can be checked against it. Beside its manifest, file stays a sibling name that the client resolves against the manifest’s URL. The manifest stays at the fixed <slice>.sqlite3.json because it is the one file that says which build is current, and the page finds it by slice name. It needs a short TTL. The client’s no-store bypasses only the browser cache; a CDN keeps the manifest for the host’s TTL, and GitHub Pages sends max-age=600, which a repository cannot change. With content addressing that TTL bounds availability, not correctness. Rotation. A build writes only the current file and removes any other <slice>.<hex>.sqlite3 of the same slice from --out, along with the legacy <slice>.sqlite3 (rotateSliceFiles). Nothing else in the directory is touched. On gh-pages nothing piles up. docs-site.yml publishes as a full replace and restores each branches/ preview as it was. feature-staging.yml empties branches/<slug>/ before copying the build in, and staging-rotate.ts caps the number of previews. What a CDN can still hold: . | for one TTL, a stale manifest together with the older file it names; | an older file that nothing now names, until it expires; | a stale manifest whose file the origin no longer serves. The client reports this case as a 404 with “reload”, never as an empty result. | . The branch’s git history keeps old blobs, as it always did when one path changed bytes. Deterministic, proved . Rows go in sorted by key, the page size is fixed, and the published file is VACUUM INTO a fresh path, so no free page or insertion history leaks in. The gate builds twice and requires one sha256 on every run. Built at deploy, not committed — when the source moves on most merges . A slice of a corpus that every session writes, which beans/ is, is not committed. A committed binary would be stale against every merge ref, so a content gate would be red on every open PR. It would also grow the clone on every edit. This is the same reasoning that checks assets/beans/index.json only for existence. The deploy builds each slice from the tree it publishes, one line per slice in docs-site.yml and feature-staging.yml, straight into _site/assets/slices/, and writes the deploy payloads into _site/payload/sha256/. The other three are built at deploy too, although their sources are committed generated files that a session does not write by hand. The todo index, the library index and entries, and the KG export are regenerated on most merges, so the same staleness applies one step removed. And a committed binary’s sha256 is stable for one SQLite version only, so a content gate over it would go red on a Bun upgrade that changed no data. A slice whose source truly does not move may still be committed and gated like any generated file; none of the four pilots is that slice. Deploy payloads never go into the committed docs/payload/. Its orphan audit admits KG nodes only, and work items, todos and library entries are not KG nodes (§”Adding a node type”). The gate (bun run cat slice:sqlite:check, or --check --slice <name> for one) therefore checks, for every slice: . | the builder runs, and a source it cannot read is could-not-determine, red; | two builds give one sha256; | the row digest read back from the file equals the one computed independently from the source, so a dropped or truncated row fails; | an FTS5 phrase query finds a known row, and a slice with no row to probe is red rather than an empty green; | the payloads pass auditPayloadTree; for kg, every pointer names a payload the committed tree holds; | the manifest’s file is the content-addressed name of the file the build wrote. | . The client — download, OPFS, mount, with a fallback . docs/assets/js/slice-sqlite.js gives openSlice(manifestUrl) → { mode, info, query(sql, params) }: . | Fetch the manifest with no-store. | Look in OPFS for /<slice>-<sha256>.sqlite3. A hit opens with no download. A new build has a new name, which is the whole invalidation story. | On a miss, download the file by the manifest’s file as an ArrayBuffer. Refuse it if its sha256 is not the manifest’s. That is a SliceIntegrityError, which no fallback retries: the same URL would give the same answer. The page shows it (“the manifest and the database disagree … Refused”) and marks data-slice-error="integrity". Import it into the pool and unlink older builds of that slice. | Open it. info.contentAddressed is false only for a legacy manifest that names a fixed path. | . The VFS is opfs-sahpool, in a Worker (slice-sqlite-worker.js), not the opfs VFS. That one needs SharedArrayBuffer, which needs COOP/COEP headers, and GitHub Pages cannot send them. When there is no Worker or no OPFS, the verified bytes are opened in memory with sqlite3_deserialize. That is no parse either, but nothing is persisted. The mode actually used is reported, never assumed. The WASM build is vendored from the pinned @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm devDependency, at 1.51 MB (bun run cat slice:sqlite:vendor, gated by :vendor:check), because jsDelivr is unreachable from some builders and a reader’s search should depend on no host but the site’s own. The search page — one page, the slice is a parameter . docs/slices/search.html?slice=<name>; with no slice, it lists what assets/slices/index.json says was built. One page rather than one per slice, because every per-slice fact the page needs is already in the manifest’s search block, which the builder writes from the same definition that built the tables. A page per slice would be a second copy of those facts for each slice, free to drift from the schema it queries; this page has no slice-specific code that could. A payload is shown by what the manifest says it is: markdown (front matter stripped), or library-entry (the block of the published entry whose id the row names). The parameter is checked against a name pattern before it becomes part of a path. beans/search.html forwards to ?slice=beans. Adding a slice . Follow the slice-sqlite-publish process. In short: . | Add one SliceDef to SLICES in scripts/gen-slice-sqlite.ts. Never copy the builder. | Choose its heavy fields by the table in §”What is heavy”. A heavy field is a payload_sha256 column, never a stored column. Choose what the payload IS by what the site already publishes, and never publish through a payload what a withheld or private source keeps back. | Measure before wiring. Build it to a scratch directory and read bytes. Over the ~5 MB budget, try the no-body variant first, then stop and report the measurement rather than ship it. | Decide committed or built at deploy by the question above. | Wire it: one deploy line per workflow, a unit test over a fixture and over the real source, and a search in slice-sqlite.e2e.ts. The manifest, the gate and the page come from the definition. A slice whose rows do not match its source must fail. It must never pass as whole (§”A partial graph must never pass for a whole one”). | .

e5a0d832bcb6.title: Adding a node type
e5a0d832bcb6.content: . | Decide it is in this graph. The kg graph holds skills, processes, roles, capabilities and the directory declaration. Work items are not in it — beans/ is its own graph typology with its own nodes (defs, workflows), and folding the work plan into the KG re-merges what was separated. | Mint its @id with makeIri, and give it an @type. Both are asserted by test. Never hand-build an IRI: makeIri is the one place every node’s IRI is decided (§”Subject IRIs — a path, not a #fragment”), so a change to the IRI scheme changes them all at once. | Report what you could not read, in problems[]. Never continue silently past a parse failure. | Say which edges it carries, and declare each one in the context with {"@type": "@id"}. A node type that relates to nothing is a list and belongs in a list; an edge that is not declared is a string and might as well be one. | Emit the nodes your edges point at. An edge type without its target node type (performedBy without Role nodes, incoming/outgoing without SequenceFlow nodes) leaves every edge dangling. The export reports danglingLinks for exactly this. | .

64271e1f39a1.title: Running it
64271e1f39a1.content: bun run cat kg:export # → _kg/<stub>.jsonld (gitignored) bun run cat kg:schema # → _kg/<stub>.schema.json bun run cat kg:export -- --base-url https://… --out path.jsonld . --base-url (or KG_BASE_URL) overrides the declaration’s canonicalUrl. --scope instance|checkout picks whose directories are read (see “Whose nodes” above); the deploy says instance aloud. The output is a build artifact, deliberately not committed: it is a snapshot of a tree that changes every commit, so a committed copy is stale by construction. CI regenerates it on every publish. Do not read .claude/skills/registry.json for this. It is a runtime manifest, not the graph: it reads only .claude/skills/local/*.json. Package skills appear in it as bare name lists with no instruction body, and processes, the graph-typology registry and the declaration are absent entirely. It is also uncommitted and published nowhere. The two coexist; only one is the graph.

0a50458bca96.doc: Move the graph into its repositories
0a50458bca96.title: Steps
0a50458bca96.content: Every one of the 8 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Create the repositoriesTask_Create | Administrator | kg-separation | The owner creates the content and tools repositories and their Pages. Nothing is committed to them before this. | . | Drain: land, close or re-target the open PRsTask_Drain | Authoring agent | shared step GT_Drainkg-separation | Work the PRs seed:ready named until the source settles: land or close the heavy movers and the next layer’s PRs, bring the layer’s open PRs to five or fewer, and finish any move in flight. Fix a red rehearsal or a discovery miss where it is. Nothing is seeded from here; it goes back to the gateway, which re-asks. | . | Seed both repositoriesTask_Seed | Authoring agent | kg-separation | Seed main, then bring the content and the tools in as reviewed pull requests with their history, so neither repository’s first commit is unreviewable. The seed includes every publisher the declaration promises (sub-kg-lifecycle stage 10): a qa directory with storage needs .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml, the caller of the tools layer’s layer-qa-publish.yml, and test/results/ ignored. Without it the declared store is never written, and once the layer stops committing its results no reader finds them. Once main is on each new repository, create the state branches its declaration names (bun run cat state:seed --init from a checkout of that repository, the same step state:mount and folio_init run): the layer that declares a state branch creates it, and a layer that mounts it never does. | . | Re-point: livesAt, seam, mount or subscriptionTask_Repoint | Platform authoring agent | sub-kg-lifecycleupstream-version-adoption | In the new repository livesAt goes (absent means it sits at the root of repository) and platform.ts points at where the platform now is. The host consumes it as a remote mount (a source.remote instance in its root index.config.json) if it imports its code, or a subscription if it only reads its content, pinned to a commit while staging. Additive: the host keeps its copy. | . | Verify on a fresh cloneTask_FreshClone | Build pipeline | sub-kg-lifecycle | bun run cat sub-kg:verify-clone --repo <owner>/<name> --ref <branch> (Tool sub-kg-verify-clone): clone into an empty scratch directory with submodules and any sibling it needs, install, and run its own gates. Green, red or unknown, and unknown is never green. Nothing in a seed runs standalone until the seam is re-pointed, so a missing module shows here. | . | Parent consumes, additivelyTask_Consume | Platform authoring agent | upstream-version-adoption | The parent pins the pair (a commit while staging, a version once released) — a code dependency as a source.remote instance in its root index.config.json (remote-mount skill), never a submodule — repoints its imports, and keeps its own copy until it is green with the dependency declared. Where cat-harness.sdlc is switched on, this step is the opt-in process upstream-version-adoption (Process_UpstreamAdoption, sdlc/processes/upstream-version-adoption.bpmn); it is not called from here, because a layer without that sub-graph does not have it (owner card Q-OPTIN-CALLS A, 2026-11-12). | . | First releaseTask_Release | Publication manager | — | Tag each repository, publish /v<major>/. From here the two are versioned independently; a tools release lists the content majors it supports. | . | Every identifier dereferencesTask_Verify | Build pipeline | — | After the release is live, every published identifier resolves to the file it names. Where cat-harness.sdlc is switched on, this step is the opt-in process publish-verification (Process_PublishVerification, sdlc/processes/publish-verification.bpmn); it is not called from here, because a layer without that sub-graph does not have it (owner card Q-OPTIN-CALLS A, 2026-11-12). | .
