9dd3cb9e7d7a.title: pcf-consent
9dd3cb9e7d7a.content: | Skill pcf-consent: Model IHE Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF 1.1.0, Trial Implementation) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use) resources referenced by canonical URL only, translate PCF Basic and Additional PurposeOfUse Consents plus the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets into W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policies (consentToOdrl()), and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown) across decide() / permits(), odrl:obtainConsent duties, IHE ITI-108 Consent Registry reads, and PROV-O decision records citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . Named by: Questionnaire wireframe review, L2 DAK to L3 FHIR IG . Skill id: pcf-consent · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Layer: fhir-harness · Modules: schemas/pcf-consent.ts (consentToOdrl, decide, evaluatePcfPolicy, PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS), schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts (findAccessConsents, Iti108ConsentClient), schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts. Model patient privacy consent directives in FHIR Implementation Guides, translate them into W3C ODRL 2.2 policies, and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown). Standards and scope: . | Specifications: IHE IT Infrastructure Technical Framework Supplement — Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) 1.1.0 (Trial Implementation, 2023-08-04) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use, FMG maturity level 2). | Profiles: IHE PCF Basic (IHE.PCF.consentBasic) and Additional PurposeOfUse (IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate: extended HL7 PurposeOfUse codes and nested provision exceptions). The translator also handles IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced security-label sensitivity tags when declared. | Referenced by canonical URL only: never copy or re-author IHE PCF StructureDefinitions or ValueSets in an IG; pin the upstream packages in sushi-config.yaml and reference IHE profiles and value sets by their canonical URLs. | No IUA claim: do not claim conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA), and do not profile ITI-71 / ITI-103 OAuth token exchange; HTTP Authorization headers on ITI-108 reads are passed through opaque to the transport. | Trust-anchor neutral: any consent-bearing workflow or verifiable link depends on an abstract trust anchor (a national PKI, a regional federation, did:web, the Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN), …); none is hardcoded. | .

ef8771b993b6.title: 1. Model — Authoring IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent in a FHIR IG
ef8771b993b6.content: 1.1 Package dependencies in sushi-config.yaml . An IG that profiles, instantiates, or references IHE PCF consent directives or Verifiable Health Links pins the upstream IHE packages in sushi-config.yaml and references their artefacts by canonical URL only: . dependencies: ihe.iti.pcf: id: ihe_iti_pcf uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.pcf version: 1.1.0 ihe.iti.vhl: id: ihe_iti_vhl uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.vhl version: 1.0.0-comment . FHIR R4 Consent in an R5 IG (could-not-determine): ihe.iti.pcf@1.1.0 is an R4 (4.0.1) package. When an R5 (fhirVersion: 5.0.0) IG compiles against it and SUSHI or the IG Publisher rejects cross-version R4-in-R5 profile resolution, report that cross-version outcome explicitly as could-not-determine with the exact tool diagnostic rather than silently dropping the dependency or hand-copying the profile. 1.2 Canonical URLs (never re-declared locally) . Reference the IHE PCF profiles, value sets, and HL7 code systems by their canonical URLs exported in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts: . | Artefact | Canonical URL | Constant in schemas/pcf-consent.ts | . | PCF Implementation Guide | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF | PCF_IG_CANONICAL | . | PCF Basic Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic | PCF_CONSENT_BASIC_PROFILE | . | PCF Intermediate Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate | PCF_CONSENT_INTERMEDIATE_PROFILE | . | PCF Advanced Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced | PCF_CONSENT_ADVANCED_PROFILE | . | PCF Basic Purpose ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/BasicPurposeVS | PCF_BASIC_PURPOSE_VS | . | PCF Advanced Security Tag ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/AdvancedSecurityTagVS | PCF_ADVANCED_SECURITY_TAG_VS | . | HL7 v3 ActReason (PurposeOfUse) | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason | HL7_ACT_REASON_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 Confidentiality | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-Confidentiality | HL7_CONFIDENTIALITY_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ActCode | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActCode | HL7_ACT_CODE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ParticipationType | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ParticipationType | HL7_PARTICIPATION_TYPE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 ConsentScope | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope | HL7_CONSENT_SCOPE_SYSTEM | . | LOINC Privacy policy / Consent | http://loinc.org (59284-0) | LOINC_SYSTEM / LOINC_CONSENT_CODE | . 1.3 Required structure of a PCF Consent instance . Every conformant IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent resource carries: . | meta.profile: one of IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, or IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced (detectPcfProfile(consent) inspects meta.profile and falls back to structural inspection). | status: "active" for an enforceable consent directive ("draft", "proposed", "rejected", "inactive", and "entered-in-error" carry no active permissions or prohibitions). | scope: http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope#patient-privacy. | category: includes http://loinc.org#59284-0 (Consent). | patient: reference to the Patient subject (Patient/<id>). | dateTime and performer (the consenting patient or authorized representative, which becomes the ODRL assigner) and organization (the custodian organization). | sourceReference or sourceAttachment: the signed paper/electronic consent artifact or questionnaire response. | policy: policy[].uri naming the overarching privacy policy (such as one of the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit policy URIs). | provision: root provision (type: "permit" or "deny"), purpose codings from http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason (TREAT, HPAYMT, HOPERAT in BasicPurposeVS, or extended PurposeOfUse codes such as HRESCH, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, PUBHLTH, ETREAT, BTG, PATRQT), optional period, actor, action, dataPeriod, data, securityLabel, and optional nested provision.provision exceptions. | . No draft purpose vocabularies: W3C DPV is a Community Group report and is refused (dpv:* or /dpv returns false in isKnownHl7PurposeOfUse). Always use HL7 v3 ActReason PurposeOfUse codes.

4cd2780e038b.title: 2. Translate — consentToOdrl() and the Four Implicit Policies
4cd2780e038b.content: consentToOdrl(consent, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts translates a FHIR R4 Consent into a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policy (PcfOdrlSet). 2.1 Field-by-field mapping (Consent → ODRL Set) . | FHIR R4 Consent element | ODRL 2.2 Set element | Translation rule | . | id + meta.versionId | uid | consentPolicyUid(consent) → urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId> (or urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id> when unversioned). | . | performer[0] (fallback patient) | assigner | The party granting or withholding consent. | . | status !== "active" | permission: [], prohibition: [] | Non-active consents emit an empty Set, which evaluates to "unknown" (or defers to implicitPolicy). | . | provision.type ("permit" / "deny") | permission / prohibition | Root provision defaults to "permit" when provision.type is omitted, per FHIR R4 Consent.provision.type. | . | provision.purpose[] (v3-ActReason) | constraint (odrl:purpose) | Each HL7 PurposeOfUse code becomes { leftOperand: "odrl:purpose", operator: "odrl:isA", rightOperand: code }, so ontological parent codes (TREAT, HRESCH, ETREAT, …) permit their sub-concepts (CLINTRL, BTG, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, …) via broaderOrSelf over HL7_PURPOSE_OF_USE (IHE PCF Vol 3 §3:5.8.2). Non-HL7 local project codes become odrl:eq. Multiple purpose codings expand into one rule per purpose (logical OR). | . | provision.period (start, end) | constraint (odrl:dateTime) | period.start → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:gteq", rightOperand: start }; period.end → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:lteq", rightOperand: end }. Date-only bounds (YYYY-MM-DD) expand to 00:00:00.000Z (start) and 23:59:59.999Z (end). | . | provision.actor[].reference | assignee | One rule per actor reference; defaults to ANYONE ("*") when actor is omitted. | . | provision.action[] | action | "read" → "odrl:display", "correct" → "odrl:modify", "access" / "collect" / "use" / "disclose" (and default) → "odrl:use". | . | provision.data[] (meaning: "instance") | target | Direct resource references (DocumentReference/ex-doc, Observation/ex-obs) become rule targets. | . | provision.data[] ("authoredby" / "related") | constraint (pcf:author / pcf:encounter) | meaning: "authoredby" → leftOperand: "pcf:author"; meaning: "related" → leftOperand: "pcf:encounter". | . | provision.dataPeriod | constraint (pcf:dataPeriod) | Clinical data creation/effective period (odrl:gteq / odrl:lteq on pcf:dataPeriod). | . | provision.securityLabel[] | constraint (pcf:securityLabel) | Confidentiality / sensitivity tags (R, V, ETH, PSY, SDV, HIV, …) become odrl:eq or odrl:isAnyOf on pcf:securityLabel. | . | Nested provision.provision[] | permission / prohibition + conflict | Child provisions inherit parent period (intersected via mergePeriods). A root permit with nested deny exceptions sets conflict: "odrl:prohibit". A root deny with nested permit exceptions (e.g. dissent except for Break-Glass BTG) sets conflict: "odrl:perm". | . 2.2 The four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets . When a patient has no explicit active Consent on file (or when their explicit Consent has expired), IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 and §1:53.4.2.4 define four overarching jurisdictional baseline policies, exported in PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS and resolved by getImplicitPolicySet(uriOrAlias): . | Canonical URI (PCF_POLICY_*_URI) | Alias(es) | Constant | Semantics | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-basic-normal | "basic-normal" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BASIC_NORMAL_SET | Permit Clinical Treatment: permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA TREAT (including ETREAT, BTG, CLINTRL, POPHLTH); non-treatment purposes return deny. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-all-normal | "all-normal", "opt-out" | PCF_IMPLICIT_ALL_NORMAL_SET | Permit All Authorized (opt-out baseline): permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA PurposeOfUse. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-break-glass-only | "break-glass-only" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BREAK_GLASS_ONLY_SET | Break-Glass Only: prohibits all uses except when odrl:purpose isA BTG (medical patient-safety override). | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-deny | "deny", "opt-in" | PCF_IMPLICIT_DENY_SET | Deny All (opt-in baseline): prohibits all odrl:use until an explicit active Consent permits access. | .

e01b7619f535.title: 3. Decide — Three-Valued Evaluation, ITI-108 Reads, obtainConsent, and PROV Citations
e01b7619f535.content: 3.1 decide() and evaluatePcfPolicy() (permit | deny | unknown) . decide(consentOrPolicy, req, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts evaluates a PcfDecisionRequest (actor, actorRoles, actorGroups, action, and scope / top-level purpose, dateTime, target, securityLabel, dataPeriod, author, encounter): . | Active explicit Consent governs: if one or more active, non-expired Consent resources (or translated PcfOdrlSets) are supplied, any deny across them returns "deny" (odrl:prohibit), any "permit" (with no "deny") returns "permit", and unresolved scope operands return "unknown". | Missing Scope Operand is "unknown", never "permit": if a rule constrains odrl:purpose, odrl:dateTime, pcf:securityLabel, target, or assignee and the request omits that dimension, evaluation yields "unknown". Under conflict: "odrl:perm" (such as a root deny with a Break-Glass permit exception), if the exception’s constraint is unresolved, evaluatePcfPolicy() returns "unknown" rather than prematurely denying before purpose is supplied. | Expired or absent Consent: . | If options.implicitPolicy is provided, decide() falls back to the configured implicit-policy Set (IHE PCF Vol 1 §1:53.2.2 & §1:53.4.2.5). | If no implicitPolicy is configured: an expired active Consent returns "deny", and an absent or non-active Consent returns "unknown" — never a silent "permit". | . | . 3.2 Reading consents via IHE ITI-108 (findAccessConsents) . findAccessConsents(query) and Iti108ConsentClient in fhir-harness/schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts implement the IHE ITI-108 (Find Access Consent, [ITI-108]) RESTful search transaction (GET <baseUrl>/Consent) as a Consent Consumer: . | Search parameters (buildIti108SearchUrl): patient / patient.identifier, status (defaults to "active"), actor, purpose, security-label, period, date, data, _profile, and _count. | Client-side validity filtering (evaluateConsentValidity / filterIti108Bundle): every Bundle.entry.resource of type Consent is verified against FhirConsentSchema. Entries whose status !== "active", whose patient does not match the queried patient, or whose provision.period is expired (end < now) or future-dated (start > now) are excluded from consents and recorded in ignored[] with a structured Iti108IgnoredReason ("not-active", "expired", "not-yet-valid", "patient-mismatch", "invalid-period", "invalid-consent"). | Third-state failure handling (status: "unknown"): network failures, DNS errors, request timeouts, non-2xx HTTP responses, malformed JSON, non-searchset payloads, or OperationOutcome errors return { status: "unknown", reason, detail } — never an empty consents: [] that a caller could mistake for “no consent on file”. When passing an ITI-108 result into decide(), check result.status === "unknown" first and propagate "unknown". | . 3.3 Fulfilling odrl:obtainConsent duties on DSAs via injected createPcfConsentEvaluator . cat-harness/schemas/content/odrl.ts holds no FHIR resource types or pcf:* keys. A Data Sharing Agreement (@type: "Agreement") carrying an { action: "odrl:obtainConsent" } duty evaluates consent through an injected consentEvaluator: createPcfConsentEvaluator(consents, options) callback from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts, which returns { verdict, consent: { id, versionId, uid } } to permits() / permitsWithConsent() / decideWithConsent(): . | DSA + no Consent (or unreachable ITI-108 registry) → "unknown": when odrl:obtainConsent is due and no active matching PCF Consent (or consent-verification record) is provided, permits() returns "unknown". | DSA + matching deny Consent (or expired Consent) → "deny": when the patient’s PCF Consent denies the requested actor, action, purpose, or target, the decision is "deny". | DSA + matching active permit Consent → "permit": when an active, in-period PCF Consent permits the request’s actor, action, purpose, and target (and any other DSA constraints and duties hold), permits() returns "permit". | . 3.3a Consent rules for agreements . Four rules govern consent-based agreements. Rules 2 and 4 are enforced here; rules 1 and 3 are authored in the agreement itself (the dsa document kind and its lifecycle process in folio-assistant-core). | Legal basis. An agreement carries odrl:obtainConsent only when consent is its legal basis. Agreements resting on treatment, public-health law or a research waiver carry no such duty, and this evaluator is never asked. | Version pinning. A Consent names the agreement’s fixed-version URL in R4 Consent.policy.uri. createPcfConsentEvaluator counts a Consent only when that URI equals the agreement’s version (the agreement policy’s uid, or agreementPolicyUri); consentsCitingAgreement() is the filter. An amendment that widens use is a new version URL, so the old Consent no longer counts. An amendment that narrows use needs no new consent: pass the agreement’s DCAT 3 version chain as agreementVersions (each version’s ODRL policy and its dcat:previousVersion), and an older Consent still counts while every step back to its version is a narrowing amendment. isNarrowingAmendment() decides that from the ODRL rules alone: every newer permission sits inside an older one (same or narrower action, same target and assignee, each older constraint matched by one at least as tight, each older duty kept), and every older prohibition and obligation remains. A widening step, a missing version or anything it cannot compare (such as inheritFrom) stops the walk, and new consent is needed. | Plain language. Every agreement that needs consent publishes a plain-language summary, hashed with the agreement. That summary is what the person consents to. | Scale. The jurisdiction picks one of PCF’s implicit default policies (opt-in or opt-out) and passes it as implicitPolicy. Registry reads may be cached: new Iti108ConsentClient(base, defaults, { ttlMs }). An entry ends at its TTL, at the earliest provision.period.end of its Consents, or when consentWithdrawn(id) is called for one of its Consents. | . 3.4 Citing Consent.id + Consent.meta.versionId in PROV-O decision records . Every consent-based access decision recorded in the hash-chained W3C PROV-O decision log (cat-harness/schemas/content/prov.ts, cat-harness-tools/src/workflow/prov-record.ts) must cite the exact Consent resource version used: . | Use extractConsentCitation(consent) / consentPolicyUid(consent) from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts to obtain { id, versionId, uid, status, patient, performer, policyUris }. | Include the translated consent policy uid (urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId>) in "cat-harness:underPolicy" on the prov:Activity decision record alongside the governing DSA Agreement uid, and record the Consent’s id and meta.versionId citation so any auditor can verify which version of the patient’s consent directive was in force when the decision hash (cat-harness:recordHash chained via cat-harness:previousHash) was computed. | . 3.5 One-way renderer: ODRL 2.2 Agreement to FHIR R5 Permission (output only) . HL7 FHIR R5 Permission (Trial Use) is output only: W3C ODRL 2.2 is the source of truth and nothing reads Permission back. schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts provides odrlAgreementToFhirR5Permission(agreement, options) and fhirR5PermissionToFsh(permission, options): . | FhirR5PermissionSchema and its required value-set code lists are built from hl7.fhir.r5.core#5.0.0’s StructureDefinition-Permission.json and CodeSystem-*.json (permission-status, permission-rule-combining, consent-provision-type, consent-data-meaning), so no field outside FHIR R5 Permission is ever invented. | Maps conflict (prohibit / perm) to combining (deny-overrides / permit-overrides); assigner to asserter; shared dateTime constraints to validity; the agreement’s fixed-version uid and dcterms:source to justification.evidence / justification.basis; permission / prohibition to rule.type (permit / deny); target to rule.data.resource; assignee, action (consentaction), and purpose (HL7 v3-ActReason PurposeOfUse) to rule.activity; and delete duty roughly to rule.limit (v3-ActCode#DELAU). | Every ODRL 2.2, DCAT 3, or SPDX term with no exact home in FHIR R5 Permission (including @type, profile, inheritFrom, spdx:checksum, isA, exclusive lt/gt bounds, elapsedTime, refinement, and duties or duty constraints) is returned explicitly in dropped: DroppedOdrlTerm[] rather than dropped silently. | .

11d8928ec59e.title: pcf-consent (skill)
11d8928ec59e.content: The skill pcf-consent as its source file fhir-harness/skills/content/fhir-ig-authoring/pcf-consent.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

f1da3ff3e3ce.title: Placement — decide where it goes before you write it
f1da3ff3e3ce.content: Skill placement: Establish where a new node belongs BEFORE you create it — which layer, which declared graph, which kind of node, and which of the two “stub” conventions applies. Read before adding a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision table, schema, tool or content object, and before writing any literal that names one folio. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Code node review, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, SMART Guideline end to end, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review . One question, answered before the first file exists: . Which layer owns this, which of its declared graphs does it go in, and what kind of node is it? . An agent that starts writing and works the answer out afterwards produces a node in the wrong repository, under a hardcoded path, named by a composed string. All three are silent: the tests pass, and the damage lands on the next consumer. This is a decision procedure. Four steps and a stop. Run it in order; the later steps are meaningless if an earlier one is a guess.

74189d37d40f.title: Step 1 — which layer?
74189d37d40f.content: folio-assistant is the platform, not the content. It holds skills, schemas, the pipeline and the MCP server an agent uses to author a folio — a paper, a WHO SMART Guideline, an IG — and the folio lives in a separate repository. Ask of the thing you are about to write: . Does this name, assume, or default to one folio? . A paper directory, a document title, a badge URL, an owner/repo, a Lake library prefix, a workflow filename, a simulator path, a licence block, a vocabulary, a constant with a subject-matter value. If the answer is yes, it does not belong in platform code. There are three destinations, not two, and collapsing the third is the common mistake: . | destination | what goes there | test | . | the platform | the mechanism, parameterised | the same code is correct for every folio | . | the folio’s tree | the subject matter itself | a reader of that folio would look for it | . | the folio’s config | the value the mechanism reads | it varies per folio but platform code needs it | . A value that varies per folio and is consumed by platform code is a config field — <name>.config.json, <name>.json, lakefile.toml — never a literal in a script and never a file the platform has to go and find. A Lake prefix, for example, is read from lakefile.toml, and left unprefixed when no lakefile names one, because a wrong namespace is worse than none. Do not infer the layer from the directory you are standing in. Read the declaration at the repository root, carrying name, stub and directories. basename($PWD) is not an identity — a repo cloned into a differently-named directory resolves to nothing, and reports no config rather than an error.

a31811337bf0.title: Step 2 — which declared graph, and where does that layer put it?
a31811337bf0.content: A node’s location is not a path you memorise. Every layer declares the directories it scans in <name>.json, and each entry names the kind of graph it holds — cat-harness (skills, roles, workflows, decisions, requirements, permissions), schemas, tools, qa, beans, folio and the rest. The vocabulary is open. | Ask for a skill, do not open a file. skill_list for what exists here, skill_fetch to load one, work_plan_prime for the work plan. With no MCP, resolve the graph from the declaration (readDeclaration in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) and read the directory it names. | In this repository the skills graph’s path is skills/. That is a fact about this layer, not a convention you may carry to another one. Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. | Overrides match on the entry’s id, never on its path. A layer that sites its knowledge graph elsewhere redeclares the same id with a different path. Matching on path makes two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | Declare only what exists. A declared-but-absent directory is worse than an undeclared one: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. | . Full rules, inheritance order and the three read states: directory-conventions.md. The docs graph, and the filing question it answers . docs is an authorable destination like the others, and the one an agent most often forgets to consider when it derives a destination list: deriving the list is not enough if the derivation drops a declared graph. What goes there: a design-memory asset — something produced while BUILDING, rather than the thing built. kg-contribution-offer carries the one question that identifies the class and why fsh-guts is the tempting wrong answer (its content may be thrown away; a design record’s value is that it survives). WHOSE docs/ comes first, and it is Step 1’s question again. Detailed information, design and planning for a harness, feature or tool go into that harness’s docs/: docs is a declared graph, and the layer that owns the feature owns the record of why it is shaped that way. A feature’s reasoning filed in the wrong layer’s docs/ reads fine and is unreachable from the place that needs it. Then where inside it, which is this skill’s question and not kg-contribution-offer’s: . | the asset is | it files under | . | why a subsystem is shaped as it is — requirements, options, rulings | <instance>/docs/architecture/, with parent: Architecture in the front matter | . | options for a decision not yet taken, with what each costs | <instance>/docs/proposals/, kind: proposal, and a row in its index.md | . | what was FOUND — prior art, a survey, a measurement, a comparison — that informs a decision without proposing one | <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/, kind: research, and a row in its index.md | . | how a person does a task with it | <instance>/docs/guides/ | . | how to REACH a data source the content describes — endpoints, shapes, quirks | <instance>/docs/, beside the subject it serves | . | what a declared thing IS, generated from source | <instance>/docs/reference/ — never hand-edited | . Three rules that catch the usual mistakes: . | A design record is dated and says what it was true OF. It is history, so it carries the commit, PR or issue it describes. A record written in the present tense becomes a claim about today, and goes stale invisibly. | It states what it could NOT establish. A requirement referenced but never defined, a measurement not taken: named as such. A design record that reads complete when it is not is worse than a short one. | It is prose for a person, not instructions for an agent. If you find yourself writing “the agent SHALL”, it is a skill and it is in the wrong graph. | . The line between the two, stated as a test: . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls: real, worth keeping, and none of it needed to act. Both directions fail silently — a skill that swallows them makes every agent read a chapter to find a rule, and a rule filed in docs/ because it arrived with context is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Inheritance . A layer inherits its dependencies’ directories and skills, deepest dependency first and root last so the root wins: declarationChain + resolveDirectories for directories, and resolveSkillDirs in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts for the cross-layer skill overlay. So a skill placed in the platform reaches a downstream folio through its declaration; never copy a skill into the folio, which mints a second copy free to drift.

95c4d8b6f215.title: Step 3 — which KIND of node?
95c4d8b6f215.content: The axes below are distinct. Ask the separating question; do not pattern-match on what the thing resembles. | you are about to write | ask | the two answers | . | a new content type | does it need different code, or only different rules? | different code → an adapter; only rules → a profile plus a subclass | . | something a participant is or does | must the performer know it, or may the participant do it? | know → a skill, on the lane’s role; do → a permission, on the actor | . | a participant | does it persist across processes, or is it a position inside one? | persists → an actor; a position → a role, which is the BPMN swimlane | . | a sequence of steps | does it have actors, activities and a control flow? | yes → BPMN under the workflows directory, not a Mermaid fence and not prose | . | a branch at a gateway | is the answer computed from facts, or chosen by a person? | computed → a DMN table plus a <cat-harness.processes:decision/> ref; chosen → an ordinary gateway | . | a durable fact for one agent | does it govern, or summarise what governs? | governs → a skill; summarises → a memory entry under the memory nodes | . | subject matter | would a reader of one folio look for it? | yes → the folio, as data — never the platform | . Adapter vs profile is the expensive one. Adapters (paper, dak) partition block kinds into disjoint namespaces, and adapterForKind — what QA-criterion scoping reads — must stay total and unambiguous. Profiles (document, paper) nest: every document kind is also a paper kind. Making document a third adapter would make adapterForKind ambiguous on every shared kind. Actor / role / skill / permission. One sentence carries the model — an actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Permissions stay on the actor: moving them onto Role, which looks right, conflicts wherever a permission is held by some but not all actors sharing a role. Resolution rules, how to bind a lane, and how to add a role: role-model.md. Do not re-derive them here. A .md under the cat-harness path that declares its own $schema is not a skill. The audit walks that directory recursively; declaration beats location, the same contract part-of: carries. Adding a graph typology is a registry change, not a new top-level directory. If nothing in the open vocabulary fits, that is a decision to hand over (Step 5), not one to settle by creating a folder.

f97888d9243c.title: Step 4 — which stub? There are two, and they are unrelated
f97888d9243c.content: This is the step most often skipped, because “stub” reads as one word. The agent-file stub — a pointer, never a home . AGENTS.md is the agent-generic source of truth. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are thin stubs whose entire content is a pointer to it; scripts/init-folio.ts writes all three for a new folio. | Never put guidance in a stub. It reaches one tool’s agents and nobody else, and the other two stubs are then quietly wrong. | And prefer not to put it in AGENTS.md either. That file’s own banner says it: it is a bootstrap pointer, and the discipline lives in the skills graph. A rule that exists only in AGENTS.md is not in the generated reference, not in the published skill docs, and not found by an agent that went looking for the skill first. | . So: new guidance is a skill. Add a pointer from AGENTS.md if it needs one, and register the skill in its package manifest. The artefact stub — resolve it, never compose it . The declaration carries stub, the filename stem of every artefact this layer publishes. artefactStub() is the one function that answers it (stub when declared, otherwise name), and renderingPath() / siteDir() derive the published paths from it: . <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld <base>/<name>/<stub>.json <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json <base>/<stub>/ docs/<stub>/ . The graph document is under the layer’s own directory, the host’s included: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document (instance-publication §”Which base an @id is minted against”). Compose nothing; resolve everything. A hand-written path such as /kg/ 404s, because the real path comes out of renderingPath. A naive guess is not merely fragile, it is wrong on real layers. WHO’s SMART Base IG publishes under a stub shorter than its repository name, so “the stub is the repo name” fails on the reference implementation the convention was modelled on. The declaration file itself is NOT stub-named: it is <name>.json, found by findDeclarationFile() matching a file’s stem to its own name. Everything it describes is named after the stub, because by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration that names them.

9d2e35120c92.title: Step 5 — when you cannot tell, stop and ask
9d2e35120c92.content: Placement has three states, like everything else here: determined, determined-empty (this layer genuinely has no such directory — a real answer), and could-not-determine. The third is never to be rendered as the first. Do not guess and do not pick the repository you happen to be standing in. A misplaced node is not a typo: it is a second copy of something, free to drift, that a later agent will find and believe. Hand the decision over the way interaction-modality.md §4.1 requires — context → options with what each costs → your recommendation, marked → what happens if they say nothing → the question. The test is one pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . Every identifier expanded on first use. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. I need to place <thing>, which <one sentence on what it does>. Two candidates: A. <instance/graph> — costs <what this makes harder, concretely> B. <instance/graph> — costs <…> Recommend B, because <the property that decides it>. If you say nothing I will do B and note it in the PR body. A or B? .

a62e7134ee75.title: The worked failure this skill exists to prevent
a62e7134ee75.content: A platform script that writes a whole README holding one folio’s title, badges and licence destroys the README of every other folio it runs in, because prose about a folio belongs to that folio. Every step above catches it: Step 1, the content names one folio; Step 2, a helper path is composed rather than resolved; Step 4, published paths are built by convention and checked against nothing. The pattern that replaces it: the folio owns the file; the platform owns the markers, and writes a section only where the README carries its marker pair (readme-sections).

a1e100d747fe.title: Checklist
a1e100d747fe.content: Before you create a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision, schema, tool or content object: . | Layer — platform, folio, or the folio’s config? Does anything in it name one folio? | Graph — which declared entry, resolved from <name>.json by id? Not a path you remember. | Kind — which side of the separating question in Step 3, and can you say why in one sentence? | Stub — if it is guidance, is it a skill rather than a stub or AGENTS.md? If it publishes, does every path come from artefactStub() / renderingPath()? | Registered — bun run cat skill:register (skill-registration), and bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts run, so the published mirror is not stale. | Could not determine? Stop. Ask in the Step 5 frame. Do not default to the repo you are in. | .

93159176e000.content: The skill placement as its source file cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/placement.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

86f83755d7e5.title: The platform’s own gates — run what CI will run
86f83755d7e5.content: Skill platform-gates: bun test passing is not the gates passing. What to run before you push, why the list is derived from the CI workflow rather than written down, and what a *:check failure is actually telling you to do. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Wireframe design review, An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes, Questionnaire wireframe review, Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch, SMART Guideline end to end, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . One command: . bun run cat gates # the fast set bun run cat gates --all # plus the jobs that need a browser bun run cat gates:list # see them without running them . Run it before you push, not after CI tells you. The push itself runs the precheck (owner, card 2026-11-18): git’s pre-push hook, which the session-start primer installs, runs bun run cat precheck — only the fast checks whose inputs the push changed, 15–60 s, and nothing when it changed none of them: . | the push changes | the precheck runs | . | index.lock.json / index.config.json | lock:coherence:check (agreement and freshness), mount:remote:check | . | .github/workflows/ | check:workflow-pins | . | a .ts file | the typecheck | . A red one refuses the push; fix it, since CI would fail on it and every red run emails the owner. It never runs the full tier, never installs anything, and lets the push through with one line when bun, the cat runner or node_modules is missing or a check could not determine. --dry-run prints the plan; git push --no-verify skips it. It is a floor, not this skill: bun run cat gates is still the sweep.

25ec434e070d.title: The CI workflow is the list
25ec434e070d.content: This skill does not list the gates, because a written list drifts from CI and a stale list reads as authoritative, so nobody checks it. bun run cat gates derives the set from .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml at the moment you run it, so a gate added to CI is in your next local sweep. package.json is not the authority: many of its check: scripts appear in no workflow, and running all of them would fail you on things CI does not gate. The workflow’s own comments name the scripts it deliberately excludes, with a reason beside each (for example check:ci-health is a report about main, not a gate on your diff). Read the reasons there.

3834eab11c99.title: bun test green is not the gates green
3834eab11c99.content: The test suite, tsc --noEmit and the *:check gates fail independently. One cause can also fail two gates at once. Run the gate set, not just the tests.

7a514df02afd.title: …and the gates green is not the PUBLISHED PAGE green
7a514df02afd.content: Gates read sources. A defect that exists only in a renderer’s output — for example markup that Kramdown escapes because a Liquid whitespace-strip joined two attributes — passes every gate. | Gate coverage is bounded by what a gate can look at. Ask what the gates read, not how many there are. | When your change alters a rendered page, build the page. The site build is not in the fast loop. check:escaped-markup asks one narrow version of “the output is well-formed”, and only in docs-site.yml, where _site/ exists. If the real build will not run locally (the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway; never substitute the thing under test. continual-progress §”A template is not a page” carries the discipline. | .

4796cb7fbcd7.title: …and a green gate is not a VERIFIED FACT
4796cb7fbcd7.content: A gate can see the artefact and still answer a different question from yours. A rule that lives only in prose has a compliance ceiling nobody measures. When you write a rule into prose, ask what would fail if somebody ignored it; if the answer is nothing, you have written a wish. The measurable form is a check, a schema field, or a test. A gate’s silence is bounded by its stated scope. check:stale-paths, for example, judges two shapes — an id adjacent to an arrow, and a numbered step under a path heading — and declines everything else. Prose that merely mentions a closed work item passes it while carrying the same defect. Likewise check:ci-health labels workflow files that produced no run unjudged, not green. Green over a narrow rule is worse than red, because red is examined; a gate that does not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed. Before quoting a tick as evidence: . What does this gate say it judges, and is my claim inside it? . Read the check’s own header — every one here states its scope and its declined cases — rather than inferring the scope from the fact that it ran.

e898ed290578.title: Fast versus full is job membership
e898ed290578.content: The split is read from the workflow at run time. | fast — the typescript job. No browser. This is the inner loop. | --all — adds the jobs that install Chromium. render:bpmn:check is there because bpmn-js renders through a browser, so it can pass locally only because a browser happened to be installed. | . render:bpmn:check and node-views:report are QA reports, not merge gates: their results go to the qa-reports branch and show on each layer’s QA page, and neither is in index-gates.json or always-green. The node-view report needs a built site or a live base, so it is not in the fast set either; its author’s check is node-views:judge --against main, which fails only on a finding new against the baseline.

1209bcaeba9c.title: Running “the gates that relate to my change” is not running the gates
1209bcaeba9c.content: Pick the gate set by JOB MEMBERSHIP, never by which gates you judge relevant. bun run cat gates --all is the whole point of there being a command. A subset chosen by an author tests the author’s model of the change, and CI tests the change; they differ precisely where the bug is. gates --all takes minutes; a red CI run costs a push cycle. A verification names a tree . A verification names a TREE, not a branch. Anything edited after the run started is unverified, however green the run was. bun run cat gates reads the WORKING TREE, not the commit. An edit made while it runs leaves the change unverified, and can make the run report failures that were never in any commit. Nothing looks wrong when this happens: the run really passed, about a different tree from the one pushed. Run the gates after the last edit, not alongside it — if you edit while they run, the run is spent and needs doing again. A skill edit is the case most likely to produce this, because a skill body has two committed artefacts generated from it. A skill edit is three files: . | file | regenerate with | . | the body, skills/<pkg>/<name>.md | — you edit it | . | test/results/kg-qa/.../<name>.kg-qa.json | bun run cat kg:audit | . | docs/reference/skill-instructions/<name>.md | bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts | . The kg-qa row is a derived QA result whose record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch. While a committed copy exists, kg:audit:check compares against it, so regenerate it. bun run cat skill:register does all of it in one command. A minted term needs a gloss . termIri("X") MINTS a term, and a minted term needs a gloss. Adding a new @type or a new property in kg-export.ts is therefore a TWO-file change: the emitter, and schemas/content/vocabulary.ts (CLASS_GLOSSES for a type, PROPERTY_GLOSSES for a property). ns:check refuses the half done alone. This is a different gate from the export’s own undeclared-term report: one checks that the JSON-LD @context binds the term, the other checks that the namespace DEFINES it. Both must pass, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

6d0d00330093.title: What a *:check failure is telling you
6d0d00330093.content: Most of these gates compare a committed artefact against what its generator would produce now. A red one almost never means “the artefact is wrong”. It means you changed an input and did not regenerate. So the fix is to run the generator and commit its output — never to hand-edit the artefact into agreement, which makes the next regeneration noisy and detaches the artefact from its source. QA gates have a different shape. A gate over the qa graph computes and judges: --check writes nothing, and fails only on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — the committed working copy, or --against <ref> on the qa-reports branch. A missing baseline is UNKNOWN, printed and never a pass, never a fail. The four judge states are ok (0), finding (1), unknown and error (2) — JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. A red one of THOSE is a real finding your change introduced; regenerating does not clear it, fixing the subject does. Which gates have this shape is in each script’s own docblock. Each *:check script has a generator beside it under the same stem; bun run cat gates:list shows the check, and the script it checks is named in the check’s own output when it fails.

0a2ac7d569df.title: …and a green gate set is not a CLEAN RUN
0a2ac7d569df.content: bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) carries the two causes, the one command that tells them apart, and the question that settles the second: does the churning field describe the subject the artefact is about, or the run that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write.

15cc610a92aa.title: Three things this skill will not do for you
15cc610a92aa.content: It does not replace reading the failure. The runner names the failing command and the CI step it belongs to, so a local failure and a red PR are findable by the same string. Read what the gate printed. It does not tell you a gate is wrong. A gate whose purpose you cannot state gets “fixed” by being made to pass, which turns the check into decoration. Every gate in that workflow carries a comment saying what it catches; if you think one is wrong, that comment is what you are arguing with. It does not make --all optional before a push that touches a diagram. Anything under processes/ changes a rendered SVG, and the check for that is in the browser job.

fef38e5137b3.title: If bun run cat gates reports no gates
fef38e5137b3.content: It fails rather than exiting clean: an empty sweep that exits 0 is indistinguishable from a passing one. If you see that refusal, the workflow was renamed or restructured and the reader needs fixing — not the gate list.

bb27a0bf3e0e.title: Related
bb27a0bf3e0e.content: |   |   | . | .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml | the authority, with a comment per gate saying what it catches | . | scripts/gates.ts | the reader, and the vacuity guard | . | continual-progress | commit early, open the PR at the first commit — this is the step before the push | . | prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | the pre-merge recipe, which runs these plus content-type gates | . | ci-health | whether the workflows themselves are working — a different question | . | gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | reading NOT clean — a green gate set over a tree a gate repaired | .
