074a0d314d54.title: symbiotic-interaction — the three registers of author input
074a0d314d54.content: Skill symbiotic-interaction: Recognize and respond to the three epistemic registers of author input — Socratic steer (known-answer correction), honest gap (flagged unknown), and intuition seed (tenuous cross-domain identification) — with the coactive-learning measurement spec (per-arc correction quality and turns-to-convergence) and the prompt-lexicon convention. Carries the STRICT rule that a steer correcting a RULE is written into the skill that governs it, in the same turn, quoted and dated — use whenever the author corrects, settles or overrules anything. Generic platform skill. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, SMART Guideline end to end, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review .

a4dc44f5dbf7.title: 0. Why this skill exists
a4dc44f5dbf7.content: Session transcripts show the author’s inputs arriving in three distinct epistemic registers, and mis-classifying them wastes passes in three distinct ways: treating a flagged-gap question as a steer produces sycophantic confirmation; over-verifying a steer wastes the author’s good correction; demanding rigor before cheaply testing an intuition seed kills the division of labor the methodology depends on. The formal backbone is coactive learning (Shivaswamy–Joachims): the author’s feedback is α-informative — an improvement toward the target, not the gold standard — and convergence speed is governed by correction quality.

9e91d7f9c87d.title: 1. The three registers
9e91d7f9c87d.content: | register | seed lexicon (v0 — expanded by transcript mining) | agent protocol | . | steer (author knows or nearly knows) | “isn’t X essentially Y?”, “shouldn’t this be …”, “what about Z here?”, “I think the other point is …” | Treat as a correction near the truth: update the working proposal toward it, verify cheaply rather than relitigate, and do not require the author to repeat the correction. | . | gap (author doesn’t know, and says so) | “I don’t recall …”, “I wish I remembered …”, “is it true that …?”, “not sure”, typed uncertainty markers | The marker REMOVES the presumption of author knowledge: raise the evidence threshold, verify from primary sources or the corpus before adopting, never confirm sycophantically. | . | seed (author suspects a novel link) | “tenuous”, “hunch”, “could A be linked to B?”, “feels like”, any cross-domain identification offered without a citation | Corpus-grep first (is it already known here?); then the cheapest decisive (in)validation — a structural argument or a small probe per the formalize-first discipline — reported fast; survivors get rigorized. Record novelty attribution: author-origin, with a literature-absence check. | . The division of labor the third row encodes: the human is the generator of low-probability / high-value cross-domain hypotheses that exist in neither the literature nor the model’s usable priors; the machine is the fast validator and rigorizer. Once a tenuous identification is made, (in)validation is cheap — so the protocol optimizes for never letting a seed die unexamined and never letting an unvalidated seed masquerade as a result.

fd8cb3c9f3f3.title: 2. A steer that corrects a RULE lands in the SKILL — same turn (STRICT)
fd8cb3c9f3f3.content: §1’s steer row ends “do not require the author to repeat the correction.” Applied to the artefact alone, that clause is broken — just not within the session where it looks kept. The proposal is fixed, the rule that produced the proposal is not, and the next session is a fresh context that never saw the chat. It produces the same proposal, and the author corrects it again. Requiring the correction twice is requiring it repeatedly, and for an author with limited hand function that cost is keystrokes (interaction-modality §0). A steer that corrects a rule is not applied — it is WRITTEN DOWN: in the skill that governs the thing corrected, in the same turn. The rule and its reason go in the narrative; the author’s words, quoted and dated, go in that document’s provenance log. Is this steer rule-level? Three questions . A steer about the artefact in front of you is an edit. A steer about how that kind of artefact is decided is a rule, and the difference is not tone — the author says both in the same register, often in the same sentence. Ask: . | Would an agent with no memory of this chat make the same mistake again? If the correction lives only in a file that agent will not read as a rule, yes. | Does it generalise past this artefact? “Call it voices/ here” is an edit. “Voices belong to the instance that owns them semantically” decides every future placement. | Is there already a rule that this CONTRADICTS? Then the edit is not optional and not additive: the old rule is wrong and stays wrong until it is replaced; a correction filed beside it leaves the next agent two answers. | . Any yes makes it rule-level. A gap or a seed (§1) never is — a flagged unknown is not a ruling, and treating one as a rule is §3’s first anti-pattern with a durable artefact attached. Same turn, quoted, dated — in the provenance log . | Same turn. Not “noted for later” and not a work item saying the skill should be updated. A work item that records a rule is a rule in the wrong graph: beans/ is state, the skills are context, and a reader looking up how something is decided reads the skill. | Quoted. The author’s own words, verbatim, typos included — they are the primary source, and a paraphrase is the agent’s reading of them standing in for the ruling itself. | Dated. A rule with no date cannot be told from a rule that was superseded. | In the log, not the narrative. The quote and its date go in the document’s provenance log, <document>.prov.jsonld beside it (PROV-O), which the renderer shows in the page footer. The narrative states the rule and the reason the author gave, in the present tense, so a reader learns what holds without reading who said it when. | A log may name any layer. It quotes verbatim, so it carries the issue and repository names the original text did, including layers above this one. A log is a record of where a rule came from, not a reference the document depends on, so check:reference-direction exempts *.prov.jsonld. | . You do NOT ask permission to fix a rule the author just corrected . kg-contribution-offer says the agent never picks a destination silently, and that is about manufacturing a node from agreed requirements — work whose shape nobody has ruled on. This is the opposite case: the node exists, it is wrong, and the author has just said so. Asking “shall I write that into the skill?” asks them to repeat the correction, which is the failure at the top of this section. The two do not overlap, and the line is: does the rule already have a home? If yes, the correction goes there now. If the correction implies a skill that does not exist, that is a new node and kg-contribution-offer governs it — except where the author said outright it should be one. Worked examples . | the steer | where it lands | why there | . | “that should be a skill: a collision means coordinate” | the named skill (coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)), as new triggers | rule-level on all three questions, and the author named the destination | . | “voices belong to the instance that owns them semantically” | the schema module that states voice ownership, replacing the old rule | question 3: it contradicts a standing rule, so filing it beside that rule would leave two answers | . | “the harness handler wins” (a collision between two path rules) | schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes — TWO rules, not three”, beside the two rules | question 2: it settles every such collision, not one generator’s | . A refusal is a ruling. An answer that declines your recommendation carries at least as much rule as one that accepts it — the reason it gives is a durable claim about the domain, and it goes into the governing skill or schema gloss in that turn, with the quote and date in its provenance log.

ff2f32d94574.title: 3. Measurement spec (new sessions and retroactive)
ff2f32d94574.content: An arc is (initial agent proposal y₀; author inputs u₁…u_T with register labels; terminal state ŷ). Metrics, computed offline by a discussion-corpus miner — agents do not annotate live chat: . | T — author turns to acceptance. | α̂ — mean fractional gap closed per steer (successive-proposal distance toward ŷ; the miner’s distance proxy is recorded with the estimate). This is the empirical constant of the coactive bound. | outcome ∈ {converged, abandoned, diverged}. | gap-honored? — after a gap marker, did the agent verify independently before adopting? | seed metrics — validation latency (turns to verdict), verdict ∈ {validated→rigorized, refuted, undecidable-cheaply}, and the literature-absence check for novelty attribution. | . Linkage to artifacts is via the existing commit-trailer ↔ session mapping; no extra ceremony in-session.

fca148e0c02e.title: 4. Anti-patterns
fca148e0c02e.content: . | Treating a gap-marked question as a steer (sycophantic capture). | Relitigating a steer the author has already given (wasted α). | Requiring a derivation before running the cheap probe on a seed — or the inverse, promoting an unvalidated seed into prose. | Flattening the registers: answering every input at the same evidence threshold. | Applying a rule-level steer to the artefact and not to the rule (§2) — the cross-session form of anti-pattern 2. | Filing a rule-level steer as a work item instead of editing the skill. A work item says work is outstanding; the work here is the edit. | .

2ec63dbe5745.title: 5. Lexicon maintenance
2ec63dbe5745.content: Register lexicons above are seeds: a corpus miner’s prompt-lexicon records expand them with observed phrasings, usage counts, and outcomes; updates land as mining PRs citing source sessions. This skill is adapter-generic.

7af937714005.title: Task authorization — four questions before every task
7af937714005.content: Skill task-authorization: The check every BPMN task execution runs before anything is recorded: is the actor authenticated, assigned to the role the lane binds, authorized by an ODRL policy to perform the task, and allowed access to the content it acts on? One generic check in the engine rather than a step drawn in some diagrams; strict, with GitHub as the authenticator. Also how the HTTP routes ask the same policies. Triggers on: may this actor, who may perform, authorization, authentication, access rights, permission check, RBAC, rbac.ts, workflow_complete refused, not eligible for role. Named by: A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Hand back to the discussion . Before an actor performs a task or answers a decision, the BPMN executor asks: who is this, may they act in this lane, does a policy let them do it, and may they touch this content? .

d8b1f49db68b.title: The four checks, in order
d8b1f49db68b.content: | # | question | answered from | a “no” | . | 1 | Authenticated — who is the actor, and how do we know? | the executor’s Principal (src/core/access.ts) | recorded as a finding | . | 2 | Assigned — may this actor take the role the lane binds? | ActorDef.roles in cat-harness/scenarios/actors/; the lane’s roleRef | refuses | . | 3 | Authorized — may they perform-task in this process, for this task, as this role? | ODRL policies in policies/*.jsonld | deny refuses; unknown is a finding | . | 4 | Access — the same, on the content (target) the task acts on | the same policies, rule target | deny refuses; unknown is a finding | . It is one function, authorizeTask in src/workflow/authorize.ts, run by the interpreter’s complete() and by workflow_gate. It is not drawn as a task in any diagram. A check drawn into some processes is a check missing from the others. The verdict is written into the instance history (HistoryEntry.authz) and the task-end log line, so the record of a step says who did it and on what authority, not only that it happened. Why checks 2 and 3 stay separate . A role is what the actor is acting as; a permission is what the actor may do (role-model §”Three questions about an actor”). An actor permitted to perform-task everywhere still cannot sit in a lane its roles do not include. So the role check does not wait on the policy and cannot be overridden by it.

35524e47fa0e.title: One action for every task
35524e47fa0e.content: A task always asks for perform-task, scoped by cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task and cat-harness:role constraints and by target. A step needing a narrower right gets it as a constrained rule in a policy, never as a new attribute on the diagram: . { "assignee": "content-reviewer", "action": "perform-task", "constraint": [{ "leftOperand": "cat-harness:role", "operator": "odrl:eq", "rightOperand": "reviewer" }] } . Remember the direction of includedIn: a grant of a broader action covers a narrower one. perform-task sits under odrl:execute, so granting adjudication (which is included in perform-task) does not grant perform-task. It is the other way round.

a0951127e281.title: Authentication is the executor’s job, and GitHub is today’s authenticator
a0951127e281.content: Whoever executes a process (the MCP workflow tools, a script, a swarm orchestrator) must say how it knows who the actor is. A Principal carries authenticatedBy: . | value | meaning | today | . | github | GitHub authenticated the caller | a GitHub Actions run (GITHUB_ACTOR, set by the runner) | . | http-gateway | the auth-gateway’s OAuth session, as headers | the HTTP routes, once deployed (deployment-auth) | . | asserted | an actor id the caller typed | every local agent session | . | none | nobody named | a step recorded with no actor | . The second half of GitHub as access control needs no code: the KG data store is a git repository on GitHub. An instance file, a work item or a content change becomes durable only through a push GitHub has authorised. The in-process check decides whether the step may be recorded; branch protection and push rights decide whether the record lands. Do not treat asserted as authenticated. Report it as asserted. policies/ never holds identity.

a458309c9254.title: Asking who you are: the auth_whoami Tool
a458309c9254.content: The user-auth Tool node (MCP auth_whoami, src/tools/auth.ts) answers three questions in one call: . | Who am I? It asks GitHub (src/core/github-auth.ts). With a person’s own token, GET /user gives the login and the permissions block of GET /repos/{o}/{r} gives their role. In an Actions job the token is the workflow’s, not the person’s, so it asks GET …/collaborators/{GITHUB_ACTOR}/permission instead. | What does GitHub let me do? That role, mapped onto the gateway actors policies/http-gateway.jsonld already grants: admin → owner; maintain and write → collaborator; triage and read → viewer; none → nobody. A GitHub caller and an HTTP-gateway caller therefore get the same answer from the same policy, and no login is written into the repository. | What does policy let me do here? The ODRL answer for an action, or the full four-check verdict for a BPMN step when process and task are given. | . It answers in three states: authenticated, unauthenticated, and unknown (GitHub could not be asked). unknown is never shown as a pass. A role that cannot be read stays unknown and maps to nobody; it is never guessed. An actor you name is reported as claimed, because GitHub vouched for the login, not for the BPMN actor. One resolver for preferences and permissions, two thresholds. The same identities feed both, through resolveIdentities (cat-harness-tools/src/core/identity.ts): GitHub’s answer is the one auth_whoami gives, and the other providers — GitLab CI, the agent host’s account, the user-level store, the git author — are listed beside it, each marked vouched or self-asserted. A preference may follow a self-asserted identity (interaction-modality §3.1). A permission never does: only an identity GitHub vouched for maps to an actor, and a self-asserted one maps to nobody. There is no login-to-actor table. A personal-account repository has exactly three GitHub permission levels, and they are the whole mapping (PERSONAL_ACCOUNT_LEVELS in src/core/github-auth.ts): . | GitHub level | GitHub role | actor | . | owner | admin | owner | . | collaborator | write | collaborator | . | anyone else, public repository | read | viewer | . | anyone else, private repository | none | nobody | . The consequence is stated in every auth_whoami answer: there is no read-only or triage collaborator on a personal-account repository, so every collaborator can write the whole graph. Telling an author from a reviewer is left to the per-lane ODRL rules. The actors are owner, collaborator and viewer, and nothing finer is mapped from a login. At the GitHub level author, reviewer, adjudicator and release manager are all collaborator; sign-off stays with owner by the merge, as the CRDM process has it. Access granularity is a property of the tool that holds the data, not of the actor: a GitHub-backed write is all or nothing for the whole repository, and a different tool, such as a future data store in front of the graph, may give the same actor finer grain.

80b14da89547.title: GitHub as the auth layer: what it is good at, and where it stops
80b14da89547.content: The knowledge graph’s data store is a git repository on GitHub, so GitHub is the authenticator and the outermost access control. That choice has real strengths and one structural weakness, and every answer auth_whoami gives ends by restating the weakness. Strengths . | Real identity at no extra cost. Accounts with two-factor authentication, organisation SSO where it is configured, per-repository fine-grained tokens, and a runner-set GITHUB_ACTOR in Actions. There is no second identity system to run. | Access to the graph is access to the repository. One place to grant, and revoking a collaborator takes effect on the next request. | Every write is attributable. A change lands as a commit with an author, and PR reviews and merges are recorded. That is the durable half of the audit trail that the PROV-O report (below) reads. | Write governance exists. Branch protection and rulesets can require reviews and passing checks before a merge, and CODEOWNERS makes review requirements path-scoped. | . The weakness: all of the knowledge graph, or none of it . | Read is whole-repository. Anyone with read sees every sub-graph, every node and every file. GitHub cannot say “the glossary, but not the unpublished chapters”. | Write is whole-repository too. write lets a person push to any path on any unprotected branch. Path scoping exists only for reviews (via CODEOWNERS), and it binds merges into protected branches, not pushes. | No query-path control. GitHub serves files, not queries. It cannot authorize a traversal that starts in a sub-graph you may read and reaches a node you may not, because it does not know the edge exists. | Five roles, no actions. admin, maintain, write, triage and read are its whole vocabulary. Authoring, adjudicating and releasing are all just write. The ODRL profile’s actions cannot be expressed in it. | Once read, it is copied. A clone or a fork keeps the data after access is revoked. Revocation stops the next read, not the last one. | A login is not an actor. GitHub says who pushed, not which lane or role they were acting in. | . What follows from that . | Where a boundary must hold against a reader, it is a repository boundary. Sub-graphs with different read audiences belong in different repositories. | Everything finer is ODRL, enforced in process. The engine’s four-check verdict and the HTTP routes govern callers that go through them. They are not a security boundary against someone who can clone the repository. Do not describe a scoped ODRL rule as protecting data from a GitHub reader. | Real per-node or per-query enforcement needs a data store in front of the graph (the auth-gateway, and later a relationship engine such as OpenFGA). The policies do not change when it arrives. Only the place that evaluates them does. | .

1309592068fd.title: The engine is strict
1309592068fd.content: policies/http-gateway.jsonld grants perform-task to owner and collaborator in every lane; viewer gets nothing beyond the anyone floor. The principal is the one GitHub vouches for (githubPrincipalFor), not an actor name the caller types. Together these are what make strict mode workable: without a permit in every lane and an authenticated principal, strict would stop every process. workflow_gate and workflow_complete run in strict mode (ENGINE_MODE in src/tools/workflow.ts). Strict refuses deny, a role mismatch, unknown, an asserted identity, nobody, and an undeclared actor. The actor a caller passes is still written to the history, as what it said it was acting as; it does not decide anything. With a GitHub-authenticated principal, every task and gateway in processes/ is allowed for owner and collaborator and refused for viewer (unknown) and for nobody. scripts/tests/task-authorization-strict.test.ts pins this. What strict costs: if GitHub cannot be asked (no token, no network, rate limit), no step can be recorded; that is the price of authentication being real rather than typed. authorizeTask itself still defaults to advisory, so a reader that re-checks history (the PROV-O report below) is not strict by accident.

324c26b4882e.title: The HTTP routes ask the same policies
324c26b4882e.content: src/core/rbac.ts asks the ODRL policies: . | a route names the action it performs: allows(req, "content-authoring"); | the gateway’s three sessions are three declared actors (viewer, collaborator, owner), and what each may do is policies/http-gateway.jsonld; | at the HTTP boundary unknown refuses. A route is a door, and a door nobody has decided about stays shut. That is the one place the two callers differ. | . | route | action | . | edit content, revert content, upload documents, save glossary curation | content-authoring | . | delete feedback | review-comments | . | adjudicate a relevance verdict | adjudication | . Every gated route allows collaborator or owner, and task-authorization.test.ts pins that.

0300505ef577.title: When a step is refused
0300505ef577.content: . | Read the verdict line: it names which of the four checks said no. | Role mismatch: you are acting as the wrong actor, or the lane binds a role you do not hold. Hand the step to an actor who may take the role (process-state). Do not edit your actor’s roles to get past it; that is actor-role-administration.bpmn, and it belongs to the administrator lane. | deny: a prohibition was written on purpose. Ask the user; never remove it yourself (deletion-requires-confirmation). | .

85d8e70b701d.title: The engine writes its own PROV-O record
85d8e70b701d.content: complete() attaches a prov:Activity to each history entry it records under an authorization context (src/workflow/prov-record.ts, HistoryEntry.prov): . | prov:agent is the actor GitHub vouched for, not a typed name; | prov:hadRole is the lane’s role, and prov:hadPlan is <process file stem>#<node id>; | cat-harness:underPolicy is every policy in force, because decide evaluated every one; | prov:used is the target, when the step names one. | . It is written at the moment it is true, which the after-check below cannot do from a name alone. The same no-invention rule applies: a refused step, a step with no actor, or a step in a lane that binds no role gets no activity.

ef2cc9f0b3ad.title: The after-check: the PROV-O QA/QC report
ef2cc9f0b3ad.content: The engine checks before a step. An agent swarm acts first, so the same policy is checked after, from the record (docs/source/concepts-agentic-harness/bpmn-execution.md). scripts/prov-qaqc.ts reads every instance in beans/workflows/, including its subprocesses, and for each history entry on an activity or decision: . | writes one prov:Activity (schemas/content/prov.ts): prov:agent is the entry’s actor, prov:hadRole is the role the lane binds (laneBinding), prov:hadPlan is <process file stem>#<node id>, and cat-harness:underPolicy is every policy evaluated. One log per instance goes to docs/assets/prov/<instance>.prov.jsonld; | re-runs authorizeTask itself. For an entry recorded under a verdict it re-checks the principal that verdict recorded (the actor GitHub vouched for); for an entry that records just a name, it uses that name, asserted; | emits the engine’s own prov:Activity when the entry carries one, and derives one only for an entry without one. | . Findings: unknown, deny, not-eligible, undeclared-actor, a recorded authz that disagrees with the recomputed one (authz-disagrees), and gaps in the record itself: no-actor, no-role, node-not-in-model, source-moved and source-missing. An entry with no actor, or in a lane that binds no role, gets no prov:Activity, because the schema requires both and a guessed value is fabrication. It gets a finding instead. bun run cat prov:qaqc # write docs/prov-qaqc/index.md and the logs bun run cat check:prov-qaqc # CI: fail when they are stale . It is advisory, unlike the engine: findings are listed on the /prov-qaqc/ page and never fail the build. check:prov-qaqc fails only on stale outputs, a prov:Activity that does not validate, or an internal error. Quote the counts from a run, not from the page you remember.

710461dff88d.title: Code
710461dff88d.content: . | src/workflow/authorize.ts: authorizeTask, describeVerdict | src/core/access.ts: loadAccessContext, principalFromEnv | src/core/rbac.ts: principalOf, authorize, allows, forbidden | src/core/github-auth.ts: githubIdentity, principalFromGithub, GITHUB_ROLE_ACTOR | src/tools/auth.ts: auth_whoami (Tool node user-auth), whoami, grainNote | schemas/content/odrl.ts: decide (every policy; any deny wins), PERFORM_TASK | src/workflow/prov-record.ts: provActivityFor (the engine’s record) | scripts/prov-qaqc.ts: buildReport, reportInstance (the after-check) | tests: scripts/tests/task-authorization.test.ts, scripts/tests/task-authorization-strict.test.ts, scripts/tests/user-auth.test.ts, scripts/tests/prov-qaqc.test.ts, scripts/tests/prov-record.test.ts | .

edc46e050d9d.title: terminology-management
edc46e050d9d.content: Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . Skill id: terminology-management · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Named by the calling layer’s authoring process, in its Terminologist lane. Bind a DAK’s data elements to standard terminologies, and manage the value sets and concept maps that result. Sourcing. ICD-11, SNOMED CT and LOINC are external code systems with their own licences, release cycles and editorial rules; FHIR’s terminology layer is HL7’s. This skill states how binding is worked in this harness and defers to those authorities for the semantics. Which code to choose for a given concept is the terminologist’s judgement, not this skill’s.

a2db825100a8.title: Inputs and outputs
a2db825100a8.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/terminology-management/: . | in — operation (required), targetStandard, inputFile | out — resources (required), unmappedConcepts | . unmappedConcepts is the important output. A binding pass that maps everything is either a small dictionary or a pass that guessed. Concepts with no defensible code are a normal result, and reporting them is what lets the clinical SME see where the DAK is asserting a local meaning.

9fa816c2ca16.title: Why this has its own lane
9fa816c2ca16.content: The authoring process gives the terminologist a lane of their own because a wrong binding is invisible downstream: a data element bound to a plausible-but-wrong code compiles, validates, publishes, and is wrong in every derived artefact. The person who chooses codes is not the person under pressure to finish the dictionary. The terminologist role carries this skill and clinical-sme does not: they are different judgements. A clinician rules on whether the concept is right; the terminologist rules on whether the code denotes it.

e24337dbec62.title: Do not invent a code
e24337dbec62.content: If no code in the target standard denotes the concept, the answer is unmappedConcepts, not the nearest neighbour. A “close enough” binding changes what the data element means, and cannot be recovered once downstream systems have consumed it.

0aa6b713098f.title: Tooling
0aa6b713098f.content: The extractors and generators that read a source dictionary and write vocabularies and schemas belong to the layer whose model they read; its own tooling skill says how to load them. An absent toolchain degrades this skill to skip, never to a clean run. Validation of the resulting artefacts is fhir-validation, not this skill.

b43c61e8563f.title: Input and output contracts
b43c61e8563f.content: What this skill takes and gives, as a class diagram drawn from its JSON Schema contracts by the schemas viewer’s own renderer. 7197fa6eb870.title: Theme art intake
7197fa6eb870.content: Skill theme-art-intake: Accept or refuse a set of three theme/avatar layouts arriving through document ingestion, with a named reason for every refusal. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . Art arrives — three crops for a theme or an avatar — and the answer is either accepted, with the declaration written, or refused, with what to fix.

e55dc630ec79.title: This is a step in document ingestion, not a process beside it
e55dc630ec79.content: Document ingestion already answers the question art arrival poses — something unstructured has arrived; is it acceptable, and if not, why not — with a pipeline and a completeness gate. Theme art is the same event with a different payload, so what exists is a check keyed on the payload, not a second pipeline: a parallel “avatar ingestion” would be a second answer to one question, free to disagree with the first. |   | where | . | the check | schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts — pure, no I/O, no clock | . | the CLI face | scripts/check-theme-art.ts, bun run cat check:theme-art | . | the arrival | uploads/, per content-acquisition and document-intake | .

6a340a51a36a.title: The constraints
6a340a51a36a.content: Each constraint answers a failure that has happened. Do not add one that has not: a rule with no failure behind it is one whose next maintainer cannot tell whether it still matters. | constraint | verdict | why | . | all three layouts | refuse | resolveThemeBackdrop refuses an incomplete backdrop wholesale, so a theme missing one crop renders with no art — not two thirds of it. | . | distinct content | refuse | two byte-identical files for two named layouts or avatars means one is missing. | . | orientation per layout | refuse | a portrait crop is not a landscape crop scaled down. The quiet area the sticky’s text sits in moves. | . | a declared destination | refuse | art outside a declared directory (at the repository root, say) is seen by no gate: check-declared-assets walks declared→disk. | . | dimensions measured | structural | intake takes bytes and emits the declaration, so there is nowhere for a retyped (or copied) number to enter. | . | weight and format | report | heavy PNGs still render, so refusing them would block work over a bandwidth judgement. | .

d9f4e0385932.title: Refuse, report, or neither
d9f4e0385932.content: . | Refuse when the art cannot do its job, or when intake cannot tell which of two readings is intended. A missing crop and two identical files are both “somebody has to decide something”. | Report when the art works but costs. Weight and format are the cases: a 1.6 MB PNG renders correctly. | Neither — say nothing — for anything intake did not actually measure. | . remedy is a required field on every failure: a refusal that says invalid teaches nobody what to fix. All failures are collected rather than thrown one at a time, because art arrives as a batch, and reporting the first problem of three means three round trips to learn three things.

6e0382c37a40.title: Do not repair somebody’s art
6e0382c37a40.content: deletion-requires-confirmation applies, and so does its spirit. When intake refuses, the outputs are the report and a work-plan item — not a re-crop, not a converted file, and not a quietly removed declaration. What looks like a missing crop may be a duplicate that was uploaded by mistake, and that is a question for the person who has the original. check:theme-art:check runs in CI, so a refusal of declared art is a regression.

15d54ef4246b.title: Reading the report
15d54ef4246b.content: ✓ landing-engineer: 3 layouts accepted · laptop 1672×941 docs/assets/img/harness/landing-engineer-laptop.png ! [heavy] laptop: … is 1560 KB, over the 391 KB budget → convert to webp — the measured gap on this art was about 16× ✗ landing-architecture: refused, 1 problem(s) · [missing-layout] mobile: no file offered for the mobile layout → supply all three layouts … . Three rules for reading it, the same three ci-health states: . | declared-but-absent is not a refusal and not a pass. The declaration names a file that is not on disk. It is reported on its own line because “the file is not there” and “the file is the wrong shape” are different facts, and a reader who cannot tell them apart fixes the wrong one. | A check that fires on every subject is wrong. docs/ is not a declared directory, and should not be — a declared entry names a graph, and the site is the render target — so art under it is not undeclared-destination. When a new check’s first run lights up broadly, ask which of these are correct? before how do I fix the repository?, and test any exclusion in both directions: a test of the excluded case alone passes equally for a check that never fires. A check that fires on legitimate subjects gets switched off, and a switched-off check still reads as coverage. | Warnings do not accumulate into a refusal. Twelve heavy files are twelve reports, not a failure. | .

33daad5fc3f1.title: Adding a constraint
33daad5fc3f1.content: . | Name the failure it answers. No failure, no constraint. | Decide refuse vs report by the line above — can the art do its job? | Write the remedy before the detection. If you cannot say what to do about it, the check is not ready. | Prove it fires, with a test that fails when the check is removed. | Check it against art already shipped. The aspect bands are deliberately wide because the shipped laptop crops run 1.50–1.78; a tighter band would refuse work that is fine. | . The stages of theming, and which owns which question, are in theming.

5dded5d91849.title: What is NOT here
5dded5d91849.content: The theming code — schemas/ui/themes.ts, schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts, scripts/check-theme-art.ts, scripts/gen-themes-css.ts, scripts/gen-avatars-css.ts — stays where it is. This is the kg graph: the instructions an agent follows, not the implementation. A skill and the code it describes are different node kinds, and moving code beside its documentation would make the partition meaningless.

2d3ee627352e.title: At ingestion, and only at ingestion
2d3ee627352e.content: Skill theme-ui-review: Review graphical assets AS THEY ARE INGESTED, in the context of the website or app design they are for — accessibility, branding, languages — to determine what the assets and the UI will be. At ingestion only; called from ingest-theme. Measures rather than asserts, and raises findings rather than fixing them. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . This skill runs in exactly one place: theme-ui-review.bpmn, called from ingest-theme.bpmn Task_Review, whose agent lane is ingestion-agent. It is not part of a post-MVP SDLC step and is not called from crdm-deliver.bpmn.

ef109d31de01.title: What it reviews
ef109d31de01.content: It looks at the arriving graphical assets laid out in the design they are for, so a finding is a decision about what the assets will be, taken while it is still cheap. The questions: accessibility measured rather than asserted, branding against the layer’s own declaration, and every declared locale. Theme choice is an authoring judgement. There is no role-to-theme mapping (theme.ts records why), so nothing here checks a binding. What gets reviewed is the ingested art in its design context.

da62f59ada70.title: What this gives up — accepted
da62f59ada70.content: An ingestion review answers “what will this turn into?” only as far as the assets can be laid out in their design before the site exists — not how a crop reads in the finished page. That gap is accepted; do not add a post-MVP review call on your own initiative.

5b04cf9b5c3e.title: A person is in the loop, inside ingestion
5b04cf9b5c3e.content: R_Judge is a human step: a person looks at the assets laid out at a web and a mobile width, so ingesting a theme source is attended at that step. Ingesting anything else stays unattended — Gateway_ThemeSource in document-ingestion.bpmn routes non-theme documents past ingest-theme.bpmn entirely.

c65b131bced9.title: Measure; do not assert
c65b131bced9.content: Contrast is computed, against the real ground. A theme with a backdrop has no single ratio — ink over a photograph varies pixel to pixel — so the number that matters is the worst case the art can present. Every shipped scrim in this repository is measured over pure black for that reason, and the check is written so it can fail: without a case that fails at a thin scrim, passing assertions prove nothing about the value. Colour is never the sole carrier (SC 1.4.1). Where it carries meaning, look for the second channel — the priority stripe is a width as well as a hue precisely so a monochrome reader still sees it. An automated pass is necessary and not sufficient: . | axe accepts a non-empty placeholder as an accessible name, so a label removed from the accessibility tree can pass the automated check. | A CSS selector that matches nothing raises no error in any tool, and can leave a backdrop at its intrinsic size across the viewport with every gate green. | . So a person looks at the assets laid out in their design (R_Judge). That is a step in the diagram, not an optional extra, because no automated check catches either case above.

f7cac9b3e977.title: Branding is a question about the LAYER, not about taste
f7cac9b3e977.content: Marks, palettes and art are checked against the layer’s own declaration rather than a remembered style. The sharpest form of the question comes from downstream: would a folio depending on this platform inherit something it did not choose? landing.html states it as a rule — “a downstream folio should not inherit a grumpy cat it did not choose” — and it is why a theme names an image role rather than a path.

b38c6fce72d6.title: Languages: new UI is where untranslated strings enter
b38c6fce72d6.content: Check that every user-facing string reaches the .pot, that each declared locale renders without clipping, and that right-to-left is laid out rather than mirrored by accident. The distinction worth keeping: a name is translatable and a value is not. A theme’s display name goes through the pipeline; its palette does not, because a colour is not language-dependent and translating one invites a locale to diverge on a value the CSS must agree on.

ae282d23c1a4.title: Raise findings; do not fix them
ae282d23c1a4.content: A finding goes back to whoever authored the choice, because the choice was theirs. There is no mapping to correct instead, and a reviewer who quietly re-themes a note has substituted their judgement for the author’s without saying so — which is the same objection decision-audit makes to editing a finding rather than overruling it with a note. The one exception is the one this repository already allows everywhere: a defect that is not a judgement call at all — a selector matching nothing, a string missing from the .pot, a contrast ratio below the floor — is a bug, and bugs get fixed.

771754291102.title: What this does NOT cover
771754291102.content: Not the choice itself. Whether a sticky should be engineer or library is an authoring decision, and this review does not second-guess it; it asks whether what was ingested will render legibly, consistently and in every declared language in the design it is for.

0da9802dc071.title: Both viewports, always
0da9802dc071.content: . | Every surface is inventoried and judged at a web width and at a mobile width. | A review done at one width is incomplete, not passed. | The surface’s wireframe, in wireframe-design-review, states what each layout was meant to be, so the review compares the build against an intent rather than against memory. | .

dfcb65165dcb.title: Todo Review Skill
dfcb65165dcb.content: Skill todo-review: Monitor and triage open feedback across all content blocks. At session start, ask the author if they’d like to work on feedback. Provide overview, let them pick a chapter/section, then review and iterate until done. Named by: Adjudication, Wireframe design review, DTH authoring . Disambiguation: . | todo-review (this file) = triage of content feedback stored under feedback/<paper>/ (paper-scope; persistent across sessions; surfaced via /todos dashboard). | todo-manager = the agent’s session work-plan via work items (durable, committed under beans/). | . Both can be active in one session: the agent’s work-plan (todo-manager) may include “process N feedback items via todo-review” as a single task.

e18600cbdda4.title: Where the feedback came FROM — this skill starts mid-air without it
e18600cbdda4.content: Materialized content (held by reference or materialized from elsewhere) is read-only; a reviewer cannot annotate it in place. The first step of review is copy-out-materialized (diagram: library/processes/copy-out-materialized.bpmn): the reviewer copies the materialized sub-graph into their own folio/, carrying provenance.local back to the original, annotates the copy, and those annotations arrive here. While triaging: . | Feedback is on the COPY, not on the original. Resolving an item edits the copy. The original still hashes to its recorded digest, and check:materialized-fixity fails if somebody annotated held content in place. | provenance.local makes a resolved item traceable to the thing it was about; without it the copy is indistinguishable from original work one rename later. | .

3cd5e7b6d631.title: Role
3cd5e7b6d631.content: Monitor open feedback across the manuscript. At session start, offer a structured todo workflow. Provide triage, context-aware selection, and a feedback cycle until the author is satisfied.

d474979a1461.title: When to Use This Skill
d474979a1461.content: . | Session start (automatic): ask if author wants to work on feedback | User asks: “show todos”, “what feedback is pending”, “review todos” | User asks: “what needs attention”, “any open items”, “work on todos” | After completing a block of work, to check if related items can be closed | .

a31c127fe29f.title: Feedback Storage
a31c127fe29f.content: Feedback lives in feedback/<paper-dir>/ (tracked in git, committed to main via worktree). Each content block with feedback has a TypeScript file: . feedback/ <paper-dir>/ <block-a>.ts <block-b>.ts ... Each file exports an array of FeedbackItem (extends TodoItem with author/authorEmail): . import type { FeedbackItem } from "../../schemas/types"; export default [ { "id": "todo-mn159z53", "summary": "short description of the issue", "comment": "longer description of the issue", "status": "open", "priority": "medium", "origin": "human", "assignee": "editor-agent", "createdAt": "2026-03-22T02:35:33.543Z" } ] satisfies FeedbackItem[]; .

98fbee480575.title: Session Start: Todo Workflow
98fbee480575.content: When the editor skill enters the session start protocol and open feedback exists, follow this flow: . Step 0 — Offer the todo workflow . Present a brief overview and ask: . You have N open feedback items (X critical, Y high, Z medium). Would you like to work on feedback today? . Options: . | Yes, let’s review feedback → proceed to Step 1 | No, I have something else in mind → exit to normal triage | . Step 1 — Overview and scope selection . Show a quick summary grouped by chapter: . ## Feedback Overview | Chapter | Open | Critical/High | Sample |---------|------|---------------|--------| Ch 1: Introduction | 12 | 3 | "this does not need to hold in general" | Ch 4: Methods | 4 | 1 | "missing cross-ref to prior section" | Ch 11: Results | 6 | 0 | "clarify the derivation" | . Then ask: . Where would you like to start? . Options (dynamically generated): . | High priority first — all critical + high items across paper | **Ch N: ** — one option per chapter that has feedback | Show all — flat list sorted by priority | . Step 2 — Present the selected feedback . Show the filtered items as a table: . ## Open Feedback — Ch 1 (12 items) | # | Priority | Block | Summary |---|----------|-------|---------| 1 | high | initial-conditions | this does not need to hold in general | 2 | high | main-point | need a supporting statement for the claim | 3 | medium | core-definition | clarify notation convention | ... | . Ask: Which item(s) would you like to address? (pick by number or “all”) . Step 3 — Review and address each item . For each selected feedback item: . | Show the feedback — full comment, author, date, priority | Read the block — load content/<paper>/<chapter>/<rootName>.md and .ts manifest for context | Propose a fix — suggest specific edits to the .md content | Ask for approval — show the proposed changes and ask: Does this address the feedback? (yes / revise / skip) . | Apply if approved — edit the file, mark todo as in_progress | Iterate if “revise” — ask what to change, re-propose | . Step 4 — After each item, offer next steps . After completing (or skipping) an item: . Done with “this does not need to hold in general”. What next? . Options (context-aware): . | Next item on this block (if more exist) | Next item in this section/chapter | Back to overview — re-show the chapter summary | Done for now — exit todo workflow | . Step 5 — Wrap up . When the author says “done” or all items in scope are addressed: . Session feedback summary: . | Reviewed: 5 items | Addressed: 3 (edits applied) | Skipped: 2 | Remaining open: 9 | . The addressed items are marked in_progress. You can resolve them from the viewer feedback panel when you’re satisfied with the changes.

858142afbee3.title: Resolving Feedback
858142afbee3.content: Only the human author may resolve or remove a FeedbackItem. Agents must never set status to resolved or wontfix, and must never delete items. Agents may set status to in_progress after making edits. Resolution happens in the viewer’s feedback panel (click the status badge on any feedback item).

871fb9f96387.title: Translation adjudication — the review loop
871fb9f96387.content: Skill translation-adjudication: A person’s word on a translation, carried from the translation review page or a block’s 🌐 pane to the record: anyone proposes text, which joins the ranked candidates; an owner, member or collaborator adjudicates, by accepting a catalogue or choosing one string’s translation with a reason; it is filed as a translation-adjudication/v1 issue; a workflow checks the author and the catalogue’s hash, writes the records, re-runs the auto-pick and opens a PR; a maintainer merges it. Use for “review the translations”, “this string is mistranslated”, “why was my review not recorded”, and when wiring a layer for review. Locale sign-off is a separate act, not this one. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Review task, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes, Questionnaire wireframe review, Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, DTH authoring, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Skill id: translation-adjudication · Package: library-core . The process is translation-review-adjudication.bpmn; this page is what each lane of it needs to know. translation-manager is the reference for every term used here (catalogue, msgstr, fuzzy, translation node, official).

0cf0a7b35e75.title: What it records, and what it never does
0cf0a7b35e75.content: What one person said about one catalogue, against the exact bytes they saw. Who they are decides what it counts as: anyone proposes; only an owner, member or collaborator adjudicates, and that is read from the issue event’s author_association, never from the body. | what was filed | by | what is written | . | a suggestion | anyone | appended to the catalogue’s candidates sidecar as a human candidate (id: github:<login>, by, issue, its msgidHash and placeholder QA), beside every other candidate; never refused for a changed catalogue | . | a suggestion with Choose as the translation (choose: true, reason) | a collaborator | the suggestion is also the string’s msgstr, not fuzzy, and the sidecar entry’s chosen records how: adjudicated, by, at, issue, reason and which candidate | . | the same | anyone else | refused as a choice, with a comment; kept as their proposal | . | acceptable | a collaborator | the catalogue’s translation node gets signedOffBy / signedOffAt, and each fuzzy string in it is adjudicated as it stands; the review page shows it reviewed, and stale once its bytes change | . | acceptable | anyone else | refused, with a comment | . | any of the above | — | an entry appended to the catalogue’s translation-qa attestation, criterion human-adjudication (or human-proposal), naming the issue and the hash the person saw | . After the writes, every string nobody has adjudicated is auto-picked by rank (below). It never makes a translation official. The PO header X-Folio-Official and the locale’s status.json are left alone: locale sign-off is the translation coordinator’s act in human-translation-workflow (Task_Signoff), checked by check-translation-officiality. A reviewed catalogue is evidence for that sign-off, not a substitute for it.

05a6ff4fe9e0.title: Candidates are never a barrier to having a translation
05a6ff4fe9e0.content: A string may have several candidate translations, from several sources; they live beside the catalogue in <locale>/<catalogue>.candidates.json (translation-candidates/v1), and translation-candidate-source is how they are produced. The rule that binds every writer: . | the .po keeps one msgstr; the sidecar keeps the rest; | when a string’s msgstr is empty, the writer also puts the first candidate there, marked #, fuzzy — the page always has something to show, the status page counts it as needing review, and it stays the default until a person adjudicates; | an existing msgstr is never replaced by a candidate, only offered beside it; | a candidate is never a verdict, whoever produced it. | .

847e4aded32d.title: The rank, and the default pick
847e4aded32d.content: When no collaborator has chosen, a string shows its best-ranked candidate. The rank is one function, rankCandidates: the tool that writes the strings projection ranks with it, the 🌐 pane restates it for a bare candidates sidecar, and a test holds the two equal, fixture for fixture. | tier | score | . | official — an official publication’s text | 0 | . | human-adjudicated — the text a collaborator chose | 1 | . | human-proposed — a person’s proposal | 2 | . | platform — a translation platform (Weblate, Crowdin, Transifex) | 3 | . | agent — an agent model | 4 | . | mt — open machine translation, or a machine-translation web service | 5 | . A QA failure (glossary, placeholders, round trip) adds 10. A check not run is not a failure. Ties go to the newest source.at, then the order recorded. A stale candidate — its msgidHash is not the string’s now, because the source text changed — is listed after every other and is never auto-picked. The auto-pick fills an empty msgstr, or replaces one that is itself an earlier auto-pick; it never overwrites a collaborator’s choice, or text whose provenance is not an auto-pick. It is written fuzzy and unofficial (chosen.how: auto), except an official candidate whose sourceText is the msgid exactly: whitespace, case and punctuation included. That one is written without fuzzy, as auto-official.

9c816d0a4f75.title: The reviewer’s lane
9c816d0a4f75.content: There are two ways in, and both file the same issue. | The review page (review.html, beside the translation status page): a layer’s catalogues × locales. A cell is machine, flagged, stale or reviewed when it can be adjudicated; none, empty and official cannot. | A block’s 🌐 pane, in the block’s 📣 panel, on every page — source-language pages included. It lists every locale’s current translation of the block: its status (official, adjudicated, proposed, agent, mt, missing, stale, unattributed) and how it came to be (chosen.how, chosen.by). On a translated page that page’s locale comes first and the others are collapsed. It reads assets/translation-status/review.json and each catalogue’s strings projection (folio-translation-strings/v1), which every site build publishes wherever the checkout has translations. | . Then: . | Read the strings against their source. ✎ Fix translation shows, per locale, each string’s candidates as a ranked table: the text; the source’s kind, id and version; who, linked to the issue it came from; the date; the QA results; a stale mark; whether an official source’s English matched exactly; and which one is the default. | Either mark the catalogue acceptable, or, for each wrong string, pick a row (its text fills an editable box, and its source is recorded while the text is unedited) or write your own text. | If you are an owner, member or collaborator and mean it as the translation, tick Choose as the translation and say why. Anyone else may tick it too, but only a collaborator’s choice is recorded; anyone else’s becomes a proposal. The help text says so. | Submit. The page opens GitHub’s new-issue form prefilled with a readable summary — per string, whether you propose or choose — and the translation-adjudication/v1 JSON block, labelled translation-adjudication and titled [translation review] …; when the record is too long for a URL, it copies the body for you to paste. Filing the issue is the act of proposing or, for a collaborator who chose, of adjudicating, under your own login. | . Do not edit the JSON block by hand. It carries the hash of each catalogue you saw, and a hand edit that changes what you reviewed is a record of something you did not read.

a67077c60941.title: The workflow’s lane — and every refusal
a67077c60941.content: layer-translation-adjudication.yml (a reusable workflow; a layer’s caller is a few lines) runs translation:adjudicate on the issues event. It reads the event file and parses the body only as JSON. It refuses rather than guesses, and says why on the issue: . | refusal | why | what to do | . | already recorded | the issue’s branch exists | nothing: one issue, one record | . | could not determine (exit 2) | no event, no issue author, or no declaration | the run FAILS; it is never read as “nothing to record” | . | an acceptable or a choice from an author who is not an owner, member or collaborator | identity comes from author_association, never the body | nothing: their suggestions are recorded as proposals; a collaborator can choose among them | . | invalid record, wrong repository, wrong translations directory | the record is not for this layer | file it from this layer’s page | . | a choice or acceptance against a catalogue that changed since the page showed it | the poHash no longer matches | reload the page and choose again; the proposal is kept | . | a choice whose current text is no longer the catalogue’s | the string moved under you | reload and choose again; the proposal is kept | . | node or attestation will not parse | the attestation is append-only and never overwritten | fix the file; nothing is recorded for that catalogue | . Proposals are never refused for a moved catalogue: the pins bind adjudication only. When every item is refused, nothing is written and no PR is opened (exit 3). When some survive, those are recorded and the refusals are listed beside them in the PR body and the issue comment — never a partial record dressed as a whole one.

9fa200e57cdd.title: The maintainer’s lane
9fa200e57cdd.content: The workflow commits on translation-adjudication/issue-<n>, authored by the issue’s author, and opens a ready PR. A PR opened with the workflow’s token starts no other workflows, so the layer’s checks run once a maintainer pushes to it or re-opens it. The maintainer judges whether the PR writes down what the issue decided and nothing else — not the translation, which was the reviewer’s verdict. Closing it records nothing.

9b02524ac6b5.title: Tools
9b02524ac6b5.content: Every Tool here is one concrete way of doing a step; another forge or another engine is another Tool satisfying the same skill. | step | Tool | . | produce candidates | any translation-candidate-source Tool: translation-candidates-agent, or the open machine-translation engines through translation:candidates | . | build the review page | translation-status-viewer (translation:status writes review.html) | . | read and submit a verdict | translation-review-page, or a block’s 🌐 pane (cat-harness site-chrome/assets/js/translation-review.js) | . | publish what the pane reads | publish-translation-review.ts, run by every site build | . | carry the issue, run the workflow, hold the PR | github | . | the workflow itself | translation-adjudication-workflow | . | plan and write the records | translation-adjudicate | .

215eb28a34aa.title: Do not
215eb28a34aa.content: . | Do not treat reviewed as official, or sign a locale off from this loop. | Do not accept a catalogue whose suggestions you just wrote: they are fuzzy until somebody else reads them. | Do not paste an issue body into a shell or an expression: it is untrusted text, read only as JSON from the event file. | Do not let a candidate’s source stand in for a verdict: an agent model’s candidate is as unreviewed as an open model’s. | Do not treat a high rank as a review. The auto-pick is a default to show, fuzzy and unofficial, not a choice anyone made. | Do not let a source change block a pull request on its translations: the strings go stale and re-enter this process. | .

290792548f64.title: Translation candidate source — one interface, many engines
290792548f64.content: Skill translation-candidate-source: The one interface every candidate-translation engine meets: for a layer’s catalogues, append candidate translations per string to the translation-candidates/v1 sidecar, each carrying its source, and seed an empty msgstr with the first candidate marked fuzzy. An agent model and the open machine-translation engines (OPUS-MT, LibreTranslate / Argos) are interchangeable behind it. Use when adding an engine, choosing one, or producing candidates for review. Skill id: translation-candidate-source · Package: library-core . A candidate is a translation somebody or something proposes for one string. This skill states what producing candidates means, independent of the engine. A Tool that satisfies it runs one engine or several — the open machine-translation Tool picks its engine by flag — and which engine produced a candidate is recorded on the candidate. The reviewer’s choice among candidates is a step of translation-adjudication.

acb201b82984.title: The contract
acb201b82984.content: What makes engines interchangeable is what they WRITE, not how they are called: every Tool of this skill walks a layer’s catalogues for the locales asked and leaves the same two things behind. |   |   | . | input instance | the layer root whose catalogues to propose for | . | input locales | the target locales; absent means every locale the layer declares | . | output candidates | translations/<locale>/<catalogue>.candidates.json, translation-candidates/v1, appended to | . | output catalogues | the .po catalogues whose empty msgstr got the first candidate, #, fuzzy | . Engine-specific inputs (which engine, a server’s URL, a model) belong to the Tool that runs that engine. Each Tool states its selection — when to reach for it, where it stops, what it costs — so an agent can choose among them. The sidecar holds, per string (msgid, with msgctxt when there is one), a list of candidates and, once there is one, the chosen translation. | field | what it says | . | text (forms for a plural) | the translation | . | source.kind | official, agent, open-mt, web-service or human | . | source.id | the model, service or publication (opus-mt-en-fr, a model id, weblate); a person as github:<login> | . | source.version, source.at | when known; at breaks ties in the rank, newest first | . | source.by, source.issue | who proposed it, and the issue it came from: every proposal filed from the review page or a block’s 🌐 pane, by any GitHub author, is appended as a human candidate | . | msgidHash | sha16 of msgctxt U+0004 msgid U+0000 msgid_plural when the candidate was made; when it no longer matches, the candidate is stale and never auto-picked | . | sourceText | for an official candidate: the English as the publication prints it. Only an exact match with the msgid makes its auto-pick official | . | qa | glossary, placeholder and round-trip results; a failure costs it 10 in the rank | . | basedOn | a person’s proposal that repeats another source’s candidate names it | . chosen is { text, how, by, at, issue, reason, candidate }: how is adjudicated (a collaborator chose it), auto-official (an exact-match official candidate) or auto (the best-ranked candidate, fuzzy). How they are ranked is translation-adjudication.

a80e45e88adf.title: The rules every engine keeps
a80e45e88adf.content: . | Append, never overwrite. Another engine’s candidates stay. | Seed an empty msgstr, marked fuzzy. Candidates are never a barrier to having a translation: when a string has no translation, the first candidate also goes into the .po as its msgstr with #, fuzzy. An existing msgstr is never replaced. | Keep what must not be translated. Placeholders, code, math, URLs and tags shielded by extraction must survive; the deterministic gates of translation-manager judge the .po after any engine has written to it. | Say what you are. A candidate without a source is refused by the sidecar’s schema; an engine that cannot name its model and version names what it can. Record the msgidHash of the string you translated, so a later change to the source text shows your candidate stale. | A candidate is never a verdict. Nothing an engine writes makes a catalogue reviewed or official, and no engine writes chosen with how: adjudicated: only the adjudication workflow does, for an owner, member or collaborator. | .

6309debbd48a.title: Adding an engine
6309debbd48a.content: A new engine is either a new value of an existing Tool’s engine flag — the open machine-translation engines are one Tool, translation:candidates --engine opus-mt,libretranslate — or, when it is a different mechanism (a person, an agent, a paid service), a new Tool node under tools/<id>/<id>.json that satisfies this skill, writes the outputs above, states a selection, and — when it reaches a host — requires.network: true with a remedies entry naming what to do when that host is refused. Nothing in the process changes: the process names this skill, never an engine.
